### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@1OF1Research

## Applicant & Organization

### Organization or Individual Name

Agent Embassy

### Additional Team Members

None

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

The official call for proposals on the Zcash Community Forum.

## Project Overview

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

50000

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

zpop issues signed, hash-chained Proof-of-Production receipts for Zcash mining fleets — blocks found, coinbase rewards, production share over a window, and shielded treasury inflows — that any stranger can re-verify from public chain data without the operator exposing wallet internals. The completed tool, a worked example over a full day of real mainnet production, and a two-mode verifier are public and runnable today.

### Project Description

Zcash mining has industrialized faster than its public accountability. In August 2026, Cypherpunk Technologies (Nasdaq: CYPH) launched the world's largest Zcash mining fleet — 4,902 Antminer Z15 Pros acquired with their hosting agreements in a $33.33M equity transaction with Winklevoss Capital, roughly 4.2 GSol/s, about 18% of network hashrate at launch (Bloomberg reported roughly 20% by late October 2026) — alongside the largest corporate ZEC treasury (about 323,394 ZEC at launch; the company's September 22, 2026 release disclosed its first production: 3,023.13 ZEC mined August 18–31, added to treasury). Its chief investment officer has said the company plans to add its own data center and power assets over time. A second fleet is scaling toward a similar share.

Yet none of this production can be bound to its operator from public data. Explorers show coinbase outputs to addresses and label miner attribution as a guess; no explorer binds an operator's identity to its payout addresses with a signature. Shareholders, hosts, power providers, and partners all take production numbers on trust — and the fleet's own filings list dependence on third-party hosting as a risk factor precisely because counterparties cannot independently verify what they are hosting, financing, or powering.

zpop closes that gap. A Proof-of-Production receipt joins the two halves that are each insufficient alone: public chain facts, and a signed operator claim with cryptographic proof of control over the claimed payout addresses (a Zcash message signature per address, verified by secp256k1 key recovery). Receipts are canonical JSON, Ed25519-signed by the issuer, and hash-chained. Three kinds:

1. **Network window receipts** rebuild a closed production window from two independent public sources (lightwalletd compact blocks and Blockchair) that must agree field by field: per-block subsidy asserted against the consensus schedule, the ZIP-1016 funding split (miners 80% / ZCG 8% / coinholder lockbox 12% — the ZCG stream address is derived from the data, never hardcoded; the deferred lockbox accrual is cross-checked against Blockchair's pool delta and agrees), total fees, average hashrate by the node method (Δchainwork/Δtime), and production concentration by payout address.
2. **Shielded payment receipts** (the engine's core) bind any transaction — e.g. a shielded treasury inflow an operator chooses to disclose — by fetching and parsing the raw transaction (v4 Sapling, v5 Orchard, v6 Ironwood): pool value balances, component counts, expiry, anchoring block. Verification re-fetches and re-parses independently.
3. **Operator production receipts** verify a claim's control proofs, then measure the claimed addresses' coinbase receipts in the window. The tool proves negatives as rigorously as positives: a claim over addresses the operator does not control fails, and a claim over idle addresses verifies as a proven zero. That is what makes its positives mean something. Shielded coinbase value is never attributed to anyone — public data cannot attribute it, and the receipts say so.

The worked example is entirely real mainnet data: the full UTC day 2026-11-02 (1,149 blocks; 179,531,250,000 zats of subsidy; 17 distinct miner payout addresses; top address 23.131% of subsidy), one real shielded (Orchard, version 6) transaction as a payment receipt, and a demonstration operator claim by a clearly labelled lab identity whose address honestly measures zero production in the window. Anyone can re-verify the example offline against the bundled hash-pinned dataset, or online, re-deriving every fact from the live public sources. During final verification we found and fixed a real defect — an early cross-check sampled an indexer's pages relative to its current tip, which is not reproducible; the shipped check is pinned to the window's own heights, and the fix is documented in the code and README. We would rather ship a verifier that caught its own author than one that was never re-run.

Cypherpunk Technologies is named as the motivation and the class of user this serves. It is not a user or customer of this tool, and no company data appears in it. The class is what matters: any fleet, host, or data-center operator that must prove production to counterparties — and an ecosystem that gains independent, re-runnable production and supply verification at the moment a fifth of its hashrate sits inside public companies.

**The road this grant funds.** zpop's receipt core — anchor, claim, evidence, signature, hash chain — is vertical-neutral by design; Zcash mining production is its first claim family, chosen because the public chain gives free, incorruptible ground truth. The same core is shaped for the proof every data center owes the people who do not trust it: AI compute delivery against signed job manifests, energy draw and source mix against grid settlement data and granular certificates, uptime against independent probe networks — each family is named in the README with the public anchor it would stand on, and each receipt is labelled with the strength of its own anchor, so a weaker anchor never borrows a stronger one's name. This grant funds the completed first vertical and the open core it proves out. The class of user widens from mining fleets to any operator whose counterparties — shareholders, hosts, lenders, tenants, insurers — must be shown, not told.

Build note: zpop was designed, built, and completed on November 3, 2026, on an encrypted laptop in our lab (full-disk LUKS encryption), entirely against live mainnet data. It is open source under the MIT license.

Repository and worked example: https://github.com/1OF1Research/zpop

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Pure Python 3.12; all cryptography implemented in-tree on the standard library (Ed25519, secp256k1 with Zcash message signing and key recovery, base58check, RIPEMD-160) and tested against published vectors — the only third-party dependencies are grpcio/protobuf for the lightwalletd protocol. One computation path is shared by the receipt builder and the verifier, so a receipt cannot drift from the method that checks it. Dual-source by design: lightwalletd (zec.rocks) for structure and coinbase outputs; Blockchair as the independent cross-check for chainwork, difficulty, timestamps, coinbase totals, and value-pool deltas — used only where it is exact, with its known inexactness (its reward field counts transparent coinbase outputs only; its fee totals do not reconcile on shielded blocks) documented in the code, and fees derived from the consensus identity instead. Cross-checks are reproducible by construction: closed-window data and height-pinned queries only. 31 automated checks: 22 unit (crypto vectors, subsidy/halving boundaries, the 80/8/12 streams) and 9 negative-path receipt/claim tests, each naming the tampering it must catch (edited fact, edited value balance, spliced chain link, forged control proof, a stranger's producing address claimed with and without a well-formed wrong-key proof, edited claim window).

### Time Period of Work Completion

Designed and completed on November 3, 2026. The worked example covers the 2026-11-02 UTC production day (mainnet heights 3538694–3539842). The artifact was complete and publicly verifiable before this submission, as the program requires.

## Budget

### Total Budget (USD)

50000

### Budget Breakdown

- Window production engine with dual-source cross-verification — $14,000
- Operator claims and proof-of-control cryptography — $10,000
- Shielded payment receipt engine (v4/v5/v6 transaction parser, incl. Ironwood) — $9,000
- Receipt format: canonical signing, hash chain, two-mode (offline/online) verifier — $7,000
- Worked example on real mainnet data with bundled public dataset — $5,000
- Test suites (31 checks incl. tamper/forgery negatives), documentation, open-source release (incl. CONTRIBUTING.md) — $5,000
Total: $50,000

### Previous Funding

No

### Other Funding Sources

No

## Impact & Evidence

### Success Metrics

Already true at submission: the artifact is public under MIT; a stranger can run the full verification (offline and online) from the README alone; the reference window re-verifies deterministically. After the award: (1) first production claim by a real fleet operator verified by an independent third party using only the public tool; (2) verifier runs and issues from outside our lab (repository clones, issue reports, reproduced receipts); (3) additional production windows receipted beyond the reference day; (4) at least one host, auditor, or data-center counterparty workflow documented using a receipt as its evidence.

### Proof of completion

https://github.com/1OF1Research/zpop — worked example at examples/ (window dataset + three chained receipts + demonstration claim); verification commands in README ("Verify it yourself"); test suites in tests/.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

None. Agent Embassy is the developer of zpop. We have no relationship with Cypherpunk Technologies or any mining operator; the company is named in the proposal text as motivation and class of user only.

## Zcash Community Forums Post Requirement

issues.body:
### Terms and Conditions

- [x] I agree to the [Grant Agreement](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_6ff6db4095fd4c4ba21babec361e927e.pdf) terms if funded

- [x] I agree to disclose conflicts of interest
- [x] I understand that this grant program is only eligible for completed work, as it is a retroactive grant program. Applications for planned or partially completed work will not be considered. All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.
- [x] I agree that for any new open-source software, I will create a CONTRIBUTING.md file that reflects the high standards of Zcash development, using the [`librustzcash` style guides](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#styleguides) as a primary reference.
- [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (`@octocat`, `@octocat1`)

@Anirudh-712

### Organization or Individual Name

Cryppit (Anirudh Tumuluru, solo)

### Additional Team Members

None.

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

The FPF "Plan Ahead" post with the 2026 dates and the Q3 call on the forum.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$16,000

### Category

Integration

### Project Summary

Finished, public work from October 2026 that helps Zcash addresses and payments behave correctly across wallets and
tools: six merged fixes in Zebra, Zingo and ZecHub; address bug reports that Unstoppable fixed, Keystone scheduled and
a Zebra engineer confirmed; a test-vector set for ZIP 320 TEX addresses; a public NU7 readiness board covering 33
projects; a read-only helper that tracks ZEC and BTC deposits stuck in the Omni bridge and checks Zcash addresses
before anyone sends; and Shield Receipt, which shows whether a ZEC withdrawal landed shielded.

### Project Description

All of it is open source (MIT) or merged upstream, and all of it can be checked today.

1. **Upstream fixes, merged.**
   - Zebra #11880 (merged 23 Oct): TEX addresses print as Bech32m per ZIP 320 instead of as the `t1` address of the
     same key hash. I reported the bug in #11826 and wrote the fix.
   - Zebra #12150 (written 31 Oct, merged 4 Nov): a Testnet or Regtest config that gives an activation height to an
     upgrade with no consensus branch ID now stops at config load with an error naming the upgrade, instead of
     panicking at that upgrade's activation block. Fixes #11482.
   - Zingo mobile #1663 and #1665 (merged 19 Oct): the swap address check accepted only some valid recipient formats;
     it now accepts every valid NEAR account ID and stores uppercase Bech32 and CashAddr addresses in lowercase.
   - Zingo mobile #1754 (merged 26 Oct): in privacy mode the Insight screen hid amounts but still showed each row's
     address. It now shows the mask, and a tap shows the address for a short time. Closes #1542.
   - ZecHub #2444 (merged 21 Oct): the Ironwood and turnstile pages show the amount of a transfer between pools.
2. **Address bug reports and spec input that other teams acted on.**
   - Unstoppable iOS: I traced the TEX memo bug (#7295) to `ZcashAdapter.validate(address:)` returning `.shielded` for
     TEX. Unstoppable shipped the fix in #7300 the next day.
   - Keystone firmware #2313: a TEX output fails the transparent output check. Keystone replied that TEX support comes
     in its next feature release.
   - Zebra #11803: `z_validateaddress` rejects unified addresses that carry an item with an unknown typecode, which
     ZIP 316 says a consumer must ignore. A Zebra engineer confirmed it on 20 Oct; the team is deciding whether the fix
     belongs in Zebra or in `zcash_address`.
   - librustzcash #468: a ready-made test address for the change (mainnet Revision 0, one P2PKH receiver plus one item
     of experimental typecode 0xFFFC).
   - zips #936: ZIP 320 is now Active but still has no Deployment section, and its Rationale points to ZIP 316
     Revision 1, which is withdrawn (the elements it names are in Revision 2).
   - zecblock: the explorer reports TEX addresses as invalid (#136); PR #137 looks them up by the P2PKH address they
     encode. Both open.
3. **ZIP 320 TEX test vectors** (github.com/cryppit/zcash-tex-vectors). ZIP 320 publishes one example pair. This adds
   21 cases: Mainnet, Testnet and Regtest forms, edge values, and 13 invalid inputs that implementations get wrong
   (a Bech32 checksum where Bech32m is required, 19-, 21- and 22-byte payloads, mixed case, a P2SH address). Each case
   has the expected result or error category. A six-point integrator checklist lists the bugs above that the cases
   would have caught. The Testnet and Regtest strings match Zebra's tests.
4. **NU7 readiness board** (cryppit.github.io/nu7-readiness). 33 wallets, hardware wallets, libraries, bridges and
   swaps, each checked against public GitHub state and source code for NU7 support (v5-only transactions, the branch
   ID 0x77190AD9, the Mainnet activation height). Every row links its evidence. The check on 5 Nov (06:48 UTC) showed
   12 fixed, 1 in review, 9 broken and 10 to watch, plus 1 it could not read. Problems it found by reading source code:
   KeepKey firmware signs Ironwood spends only under the NU6.3 branch ID; Unstoppable Wallet pinned pre-NU7 SDKs on both
   apps (both have since moved: iOS on 29 Oct, Android on 2 Nov); the original MIT Android and Swift SDKs end at 4.0.0 with no NU7;
   ShapeShift fixes the branch ID to NU6.3 (reported in shapeshift/web #12794). KeepKey and Unstoppable had no public
   NU7 issue when I found these. I also got two rows wrong: Keystone firmware and the Zodl Swift SDK. str4d corrected
   both on the forum on 29 Oct, I fixed them the same day, and I re-checked every row.
5. **Zcash Refund Helper** (github.com/cryppit/zec-refund-helper, live at cryppit.github.io/zec-refund-helper). Three
   read-only pages, no keys of any kind, nothing signed:
   - Deposit check: paste a transaction hash; it shows where a ZEC or BTC deposit to the Omni bridge is, whether it was
     credited, the exact refund steps and their cost, and the only address the coin can go back to. It parses ZIP 316
     unified addresses (Bech32m, F4Jumble, BLAKE2b) to check a refund address before anyone uses it. Its steps were
     used for one refund (0.1 BTC, 15 Oct).
   - Address check (27 Oct, a Zcash-only port of the Where's My Swap address check): says offline whether a transparent-only or a shielded wallet can pay a Zcash address
     (t1, t3, TEX, Sapling, unified), and which refund the bridge could make to it.
   - Watch page (28 Oct): up to 25 deposit hashes re-checked every 10 minutes while the page is open, with what
     changed and a summary to paste into a support ticket. The list stays in the browser.
   - Scan of the Omni indexer on 26 Oct (665 candidates): no ZEC deposit stuck uncredited; 54 ZEC deposits absorbed
     below the connector's 0.001 ZEC minimum with no refund path, 33 of them funded from a shielded pool. On the Bitcoin
     side, 36 deposits (7.61 BTC) were never credited, and 15 of them (5.56 BTC) can still go back to their senders'
     refund addresses.
6. **Shield Receipt** (github.com/cryppit/shield-receipt, live at cryppit.github.io/shield-receipt, 31 Oct). Paste a
   transaction ID and the address you gave; it shows whether a ZEC withdrawal landed transparent or shielded, and in
   which pool. No keys of any kind, and only the transaction ID leaves the page. 113 offline tests.
7. **Forum help.** Answers in stuck-funds and tooling threads (Zodl swap refund, the ztrash trace write-up, Sapling's
   one-month report) and an Address Checker topic. After my reply, Sapling's founder said its withdraw screen will
   label the address type in plain words.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

- Upstream fixes followed each project's contribution rules: an issue first where the project asks for one, a test
  for every fix, review changes made in the same PR.
- Address work started from ZIP 316 and ZIP 320 and the `zcash_address` behaviour, then read each wallet's and node's
  address code to find where TEX or unknown items fall through to the wrong branch.
- The test vectors come from a small Python reference codec (Bech32/Bech32m, Base58Check, TEX to P2PKH). A test fails
  if `vectors.json` differs from what the codec generates, or if any case disagrees with it. CI runs on every push.
- The NU7 board is one stdlib Python script (`check.py`, 22 tests) run by GitHub Actions on every change and on a
  schedule, several times a day. Each row's signals (open blockers, fix PRs, releases, patterns in source files)
  resolve to fixed, in review, broken or watch, and a failed lookup never counts either way. New rows were found by
  searching GitHub for NU7 issues and for source files that still carry the NU6.3 branch ID, then reading each one. The
  page marks itself stale if the last check is more than 8 hours old.
- The refund helper is TypeScript, read-only: public explorer GETs and NEAR view calls. 55 commits and 240 offline
  tests, with tests and a typecheck in CI before each Pages deploy.

### Time Period of Work Completion

13 October 2026 to 31 October 2026. Zebra #12150, written on 31 October, merged on 4 November.

### Total Budget (USD)

$16,000

### Budget Breakdown

A fixed price for each finished item. No infrastructure costs (GitHub Pages and Actions, free tier).

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| Zcash Refund Helper (deposit check, address check, watch page, scans) | $6,800 |
| Upstream fixes (Zebra #11880 and #12150, Zingo #1663, #1665 and #1754, ZecHub #2444) | $2,800 |
| Address bug reports, spec input and ZIP 320 test vectors | $2,400 |
| NU7 readiness board | $2,400 |
| Shield Receipt | $1,200 |
| Forum help | $400 |
| **Total** | **$16,000** |

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

None.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

- **ZCG #513** (Zcash Community Grants, pending, not awarded): future milestone work to make transparent ZEC swaps in
  Vultisig/SwapKit produce v5 transactions. Nothing in this application is in #513's scope; the Vultisig probe behind
  #513 (vultisig-android #6115) and the board rows about Vultisig are not claimed here.
- **ZECATHON 2026**: the refund helper was entered in the Cross-Chain track. Winners are announced after this window
  closes. If it wins a prize, I will say so in the forum thread and take the prize off this ask, up to the $6,800
  refund helper line.
- **Free Society Hack (4 Nov 2026)**: my entry there, zshagun, is a separate project built that day. Nothing in this
  application claims it, and any prize it wins is unrelated to this work.

### Success Metrics

- 6 merged PRs in 3 Zcash projects (Zebra, Zingo mobile, ZecHub); 2 more teams fixed or scheduled a fix from my
  diagnosis (Unstoppable #7300, Keystone #2313); 1 more bug confirmed by the Zebra team (#11803).

- 33 projects tracked for NU7 with linked evidence; 4 problems found by reading source code, 2 of them (KeepKey,
  Unstoppable) with no public NU7 issue when found; 2 wrong rows corrected in public the same day.
- The refund helper checks any Omni ZEC or BTC deposit from its hash, and its scans put numbers on the ZEC absorbed
  below the connector minimum (54 deposits, 33 from shielded pools) and the BTC never credited (36 deposits, 7.61 BTC).
- A request delivered: on 26 Oct a member of Gem Wallet's support team asked on this forum for a plain answer to "can
  my wallet send to this?", for example that a TEX address needs a transparent balance. I built that on the Where's My
  Swap address page, and they replied that the two answers were easier to understand and that they'd share it with their
  team. The Refund Helper page is a port of that check, and I never sent it to Gem. This is one support person's reply
  about a different page, not a test or acceptance by Gem (corrected 5 Nov, after a reviewer's question).

Zcash Community Forum — Q4 2026 CDRGP call for proposals thread ### Requested Grant Amount (USD) $9,100 ### Category Media ### Project Summary The Zcash Daily is a sourced, opinionated editorial digest covering what happened in the Zcash ecosystem each day and why it matters. 50+ editions published to the Zcash forum between August 27 and November 3, 2026, with 417 inline source links, a structured log.json, and an automated publishing pipeline. Every edition is publicly verifiable. This is a retroactive request for work already completed. ### Project Description The Zcash Daily is a sourced, opinionated editorial digest covering what happened in the Zcash ecosystem each day and why it matters. Every edition draws from 8+ source channels — price action, governance debates, GitHub commits, on-chain metrics, external press — and publishes to the Zcash forum, Notion, and X. Across 10 weeks, mostly weekdays, it has built a daily public record with rotating thematic focus: community pulse early in the week, builder spotlights midweek, broader ZK ecosystem context to close it out. This is information infrastructure. The community has funded this kind of work before — the Arborist Call note-taker role exists because someone recognized that protocol-level conversations needed a reliable, consistent communication layer between developers and coinholders. The Zcash Daily extends that logic to the full ecosystem — governance, community sentiment, builder activity, external coverage — on a daily cycle. Same category, broader scope. ZecHub already does valuable work as a weekly education hub with its DAO model. The Zcash Daily isn't a replacement — it's a different instrument. Daily vs. weekly. Editorial voice vs. encyclopedic reference. Real-time tracking vs. macro explainers. Major events covered during the period: - NU7 activation countdown and Zondax/Ledger migration warnings - ZCG governance crisis — all four competing proposals, the $455K ZSA grant controversy, ZCG taper withdrawal - Grayscale ZCSH ETF inflow tracking (eight consecutive inflow sessions tracked in the digest) - Zcon7 Cancun event spotlighted - Zcash 10th birthday (October 28) - CoinShares/Euronext ETP suspension on debut day - Shielded pool usage tracking across the period (supply in shielded pools, transaction share trends) - HashSmash launch, ROZO shielded payments, Kestrel WalletConnect, 10-second block spacing ZIP ### Technical Approach (how you did it) I designed the editorial system: the voice, format rules, source methodology and themed calendar. Claude drafts from that system. I review, correct, decide what publishes, and write it myself when the draft doesn't meet the bar. A typical day is 45 minutes to an hour of editorial work. Early sessions ran longer while I built the framework, and heavy news days took more. Across the full run, that averages about 1.5 hours per digest. Automation handles the publishing mechanics, so my time goes to editorial decisions. The publishing pipeline is at github.com/oolu4236/zcash-digest: - GitHub Actions automated workflow (daily + manual dispatch) - Claude API integration for generation assistance and fact-checking - Automated link verification (HEAD requests to all inline URLs) - Notion API integration (child pages with rich text and hyperlinks) - Twitter/X OAuth 1.0a integration (automated tweet condensing and posting) - Structured log.json tracking every published digest - Batch tweet backfill system for missed posts - Format validation (char counts, link counts, paragraph structure) ### Time Period of Work Completion August 27, 2026 – November 3, 2026 ### Total Budget (USD) $9,100 ### Budget Breakdown - Compensation: - $(USD): 5,625 - Justification: Editorial work: 50 digests x 1.5 hrs avg x $75/hr ($112.50/digest). Designing the voice and format system, scanning 8+ source channels, verifying facts against primary sources, reviewing and correcting Claude's drafts, deciding what publishes. Early sessions were longer (building the editorial framework); later ones shorter (45 min – 1 hr). Average across the full run: 1.5 hours per digest including building the editorial framework. The automation handles publishing mechanics — the paid hours go to editorial judgment. - Technology/Software: - $(USD): 475 - Justification: API costs (Anthropic, X/Twitter) - Infrastructure/Hosting: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: GitHub Pages hosting (free) - Services/Contractors: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: N/A, sole operator - Other: - $(USD): 3,000 - Justification: Publishing pipeline development (~40 hrs x $75/hr) - Total $(USD): 9,100 ### Previous Funding No ### Previous Funding Details _No response_ ### Other Funding Sources Yes ### Other Funding Sources Details I moderated engineering meetings for ZingoLabs' Zaino team, which receives ZCG funding. - [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners

@AArnott

### Organization or Individual Name

Andrew Arnott (nerdcash)

### Additional Team Members

None

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Zcash Community Forum

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$16,000

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

Kept Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies, the ZF-funded .NET Zcash light wallet library, working through NU6, Ironwood and NU7. Built faster sync and view-only wallet support in the nerdcash/librustzcash fork that powers it.

### Project Description

Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies, originally funded by two Zcash Foundation Minor Grants, is the only known way for .NET apps to embed a Zcash light wallet. Since the grants ended I have kept it current with each network upgrade, unpaid: adapting to new zcash_client_sqlite releases, preloading Ironwood subtree roots, adding full Ironwood pool support ([#713](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/713), released in [v0.5.53](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/releases/tag/v0.5.53)), mempool reporting, NativeAOT builds and signed releases.

To make it fast and useful for watch-only and merchant scenarios, I extended librustzcash in the [nerdcash fork](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/tree/nerdbank) with UIVK import and IVK-only scanning (proposed upstream as [zcash/librustzcash#3206](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/3206)), a view-only scan mode that skips note commitment trees, an opt-in sandblast spam filter, multicore trial decryption, and faster commitment-tree and nullifier writes. They ship today in the library, which eZcash builds on, and in MoneyStream, which uses the fork directly. NU7 support (zcash_protocol 0.11, branch ID 0x77190AD9) came through upstream merges into the fork.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

C# library over a Rust FFI layer that builds on the nerdcash/librustzcash `nerdbank` branch, a submodule that merges upstream regularly and is never rebased. Changes ship through reviewed PRs with CI and mainnet benchmarks.

Selected library work (nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies, all merged after Feb 19, 2024):
- [#713](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/713) Add missing support for the Ironwood pool (Nov 1, 2026; released in v0.5.53)
- [#709](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/709) Send a block range end on open GetTaddressTxids requests (Oct 30, 2026)
- [#699](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/699) Opt-in sandblast trial-decryption filter on sync (Oct 29, 2026)
- [#693](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/693) Update the librustzcash submodule to the nerdbank tip (Oct 29, 2026)
- [#669](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/669) Scan view-only wallets without note commitment trees (Oct 28, 2026)
- [#646](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/646), [#647](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/647), [#650](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/650), [#658](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/658) Sync profiling, faster lightwalletd reads, larger subtree chunks, faster note-commitment tree updates (Oct 27, 2026)
- [#649](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/649) Preload Ironwood subtree roots so older birthdays finish syncing (Oct 27, 2026)
- [#648](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/648), [#620](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/620) Adapt to zcash_client_sqlite 0.23.0 and 0.22.0 (Oct and Sep 2026)
- [#632](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/632) Authenticode signing (Sep 7, 2026)
- [#591](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/591) Import UIVK accounts into the light wallet (Jul 31, 2026)
- [#575](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/575), [#506](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/506) librustzcash updates, including a fix for [zcash/librustzcash#2096](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2096) (Jan 2026)
- [#568](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/568) Incoming payments to a particular address (Jan 24, 2026)
- [#561](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/561) Report mempool transactions (Jan 12, 2026)
- [#541](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/541) NativeAOT libraries and tool (Jan 5, 2026)
- [#479](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/479) Move CI from Azure Pipelines to GitHub Actions (Jan 8, 2025)

Fork-only improvements (nerdcash/librustzcash, merged Oct 27–29, 2026):
- UIVK import and IVK-only account scanning (upstream PR [zcash/librustzcash#3206](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/3206))
- View-only scan mode with no note commitment trees, its own scan queue and optional anchor retention ([#8](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/8), [#9](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/9), [#14](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/14))
- View-only rewind by height and block hash; balances without witnesses ([#10](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/10), [#11](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/11))
- Opt-in sandblast spam filter in the scan API ([#20](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/20))
- Trial decryption across every core, plus a mainnet benchmark ([#16](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/16), [#17](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/17))
- Faster commitment-tree writes: cached updates, larger subtree chunks, folded checkpoints ([#4](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/4), [#15](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/15))
- Bounded nullifier-map growth; staged nullifier writes off the SQLite writer ([#22](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/22))
- Idempotent subtree-root appends past a stored prefix, so Ironwood roots can be preloaded ([#12](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/12))
- pasta_curves 0.6.1 assembly field arithmetic on aarch64 ([#23](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/23))

Not claimed here: fork commits from Dec 29, 2023 to Feb 17, 2024, which fall under the prior grant, and the separate zcash-payment-service scanner work, which is its own proposal.

### Time Period of Work Completion

February 19, 2024 (where the prior grant's work ended) to November 2, 2026 (v0.5.53 release)

### Total Budget (USD)

$16,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 16,000
  - Justification: 40 hours of Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies upkeep ($8,000) and 40 hours of librustzcash fork improvements ($8,000), including the UIVK import proposed upstream as [zcash/librustzcash#3206](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/3206), at $200/hour.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: None claimed.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: None claimed.
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: None claimed.
- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: None claimed.
- Total $(USD): 16,000

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

No previous funding from the Coinholder program. For transparency: two Zcash Foundation Minor Grants for this library: $750 (April 2023, Unified Address library) and $18,000 (October 2023 to February 19, 2024, full lightwallet for .NET). This proposal covers only work after those grants were completed.

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

None

### Success Metrics

- Releases v0.4.1, v0.4.9, v0.4.79, v0.5.29 and v0.5.53 (Ironwood support).
- Upstream PR [zcash/librustzcash#3206](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/3206) proposes the UIVK import work.
- Fork PRs [#4](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/4) to [#23](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/pull/23) merged.
- In use by MoneyStream (through the fork) and eZcash (through the library).

### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies) - the .NET library
  - [Ironwood support PR #713](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/pull/713) - full Ironwood pool support
  - [nerdcash/librustzcash nerdbank branch](https://github.com/nerdcash/librustzcash/tree/nerdbank) - the fork

  - [All releases](https://github.com/nerdcash/Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies/releases) - v0.4.1 through v0.5.53
- Other Evidence:
  - [NU7 in zcash_protocol 0.11.0](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/commit/92859218) - arrived in the fork through upstream merges

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

I own MoneyStream, a paid app that depends on the nerdcash/librustzcash fork, so the fork improvements also benefit that commercial app. MoneyStream does not use Nerdbank.Cryptocurrencies. The improvements are public and open source, and MoneyStream is not a funded deliverable.

The Q4 2026 call for proposals on the Zcash Community Forum, and seeing other Zebra security researchers file their applications this round.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

25000

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am the original reporter of GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v, a High-severity (CVSS 3.1 7.5) Zebra vulnerability fixed in Zebra 7.0.0: one permissionless 2 MB transaction could stall block verification for minutes, because the transparent signature-hash cost of a transaction grows with the square of its input count. I reported it privately to the Zcash Foundation on 17 September 2026 with a working, reproducible proof of concept, and I am asking for $25,000 — my equal share of ZCG's published High-severity base payout, split among the three researchers ZF credits on the advisory.


### Project Description

### How this claim is scoped

- **One advisory, one share.** I'm claiming my reporter share of GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v only — the advisory ZF credits me as reporter on. Nothing else.
- **Three credited researchers, one base payout.** ZF credits me, @x15-eth and @janneh2000 on this advisory. I'm asking for one third of ZCG's published High base rate: $75,000 ÷ 3 = **$25,000**. If the other two claimed identically, all three shares together would sum to exactly one payout — no more.
- **Coordinate with, not competing against, the other claims.** @x15-eth has filed his own application this round for his share of this same advisory (issue #79). Both claims use the same split; together they total half the advisory's base payout, leaving the third researcher's share unclaimed.
- **Unpaid to date, no bonus.** I've received nothing from any source for this advisory, and I'm not requesting anything above the base rate.

| Advisory | Severity | Researchers ZF credits | My role | My share |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v: quadratic signature-hash cost, so one transaction stalls block verification for minutes | High, CVSS 3.1 7.5 | **asafmod (reporter)**, @x15-eth and @janneh2000 (independent rediscoveries) | Original reporter, first private disclosure, with proof of concept | $75,000 ÷ 3 = **$25,000** |


| Advisory | Severity | Researchers ZF credits | My role | My share |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v: quadratic signature-hash cost, so one transaction stalls block verification for minutes | High, CVSS 3.1 7.5 | **asafmod (reporter)**, @x15-eth and @janneh2000 (independent rediscoveries) | Original reporter, first private disclosure, with proof of concept | $75,000 ÷ 3 = **$25,000** |

### The completed work

**The bug.** Zebra's ZIP-244 (v5 transaction) signature hasher cached only the `txid_parts` digest, not the per-transaction `hash_amounts` and `hash_scriptpubkeys` digests. Every input's signature hash therefore re-hashed data covering all of the transaction's inputs. The per-input cost grows with the input count, so the per-transaction cost grows with its square. One permissionless, at-most-2 MB transaction could make Zebra perform minutes of hashing work on the same thread pool that verifies blocks — and the work kept running after the transaction was rejected, with no misbehavior score attached.

**My report.** I found the issue by reading `zcash_primitives`' ZIP-244 implementation and confirming that the transparent sighash digests were recomputed per input rather than computed once per transaction. I reported it privately through ZF's GitHub security advisory process on 17 September 2026, and included a working, reproducible proof of concept: a transaction densely packed with signature-checking (stub-P2PK) inputs that, submitted to a live Zebra node, pinned the node's CPU for the duration of the quadratic hash work. ZF acknowledged on 19 September, reproduced the finding, and built the fix on top of it.

**The fix.** `zcash_primitives` 0.31.0 adds `PrecomputedSighashData`, which computes the ZIP-244 amounts and scripts digests once per transaction and reuses them for every input — reducing the cost from quadratic to linear. It also precomputes the ZIP-243 (v4 path) prevouts, sequence and outputs digests once per transaction. The fix shipped in **Zebra v7.0.0** (released 22 October 2026), the release every node needs for NU7. The advisory was published the same day.

**ZF's published description of the effect** (from the advisory, verified verbatim): "The reporter measured roughly 1,700 CPU-seconds for one such transaction, which is about 7 minutes of stalled verification on a 4-core node and 14 minutes on a 2-core node," and "A mining node cannot verify new blocks during that time and its templates go stale." The advisory's credit line reads: "Reporter @asafmod; @x15-eth and @janneh2000 (independent rediscoveries)." The "reporter measured" figure in ZF's advisory is my measurement, from my proof of concept.

**What this bug is not.** It is an availability bug. As ZF's advisory says, it does not crash a node, corrupt state, split consensus or touch funds, and the effect stops when the attack stops. The case for paying it rests on reach and persistence: any peer, or any caller of `sendrawtransaction`, on every default node, for as long as the attacker likes — and a 2 MB transaction is cheap and reusable.

### Why I'm bringing this here

- **The work is finished, public, and checkable.** ZF published the advisory on 22 October 2026, crediting me as reporter and quoting my measurement ("roughly 1,700 CPU-seconds… about 7 minutes of stalled verification on a 4-core node"). The fix shipped in Zebra v7.0.0 the same day.
- **There's no other route to be paid for it.** Zebra's `SECURITY.md` states ZF does "not currently operate a bug bounty program and do not pay for reports," and ZCG's disclosure program closed in May 2026.
- **I did the patient version of disclosure.** I reported privately on 17 September and kept the details confidential for five weeks until the fix shipped and operators had been told to upgrade. Retroactive recognition is what makes that patience a rational choice over publishing immediately or after an embargo period.


### Basis for the $25,000 request

| ZCG Core Node tier | Base payout | Discretionary bonus (not claimed) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Critical | $150,000 | $75,000 |
| **High** | **$75,000** | $37,500 |
| Medium | $37,500 | $18,750 |
| Low | $18,750 | $9,375 |

- One High advisory, three credited researchers: $75,000 ÷ 3 = **$25,000**.
- I'm not asking coinholders to set a price — ZCG's closed program already priced this class ("Non-distributed denial of service against an individual node or wallet") at $75,000 per Core Node High; I'm asking for my third of it.
- Splitting a payout across credited researchers has precedent: in Q3, coinholders funded a researcher's share of GHSA-8m29 alongside the original reporter's own claim ("Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities", 96% approval).


### Technical Approach (how you did it)

I ran this review with Kimi 3 (Moonshot AI's model) as the research engine, and directed it.
Rather than relying on unverified model output, I used it to trace the real code paths, to search for the strongest possible amplifiers of the cost, to build and run the demonstrations that confirmed or killed each lead, and to draft the report for the finding that survived.

My part:

1. **I chose the target and the threat model** — post-zcashd-EOL, Zebra is the main full node the Zcash network runs on, so unauthenticated per-peer cost amplification is the highest-value class of bug to hunt.
2. **I traced the actual signing path** through `zcash_primitives`' ZIP-244 implementation and identified that the transparent `amounts_digest` (BLAKE2b, personal `ZTxTrAmountsHash`) and `scripts_digest` (`ZTxTrScriptsHash`) were recomputed on every per-input `sighash()` call instead of once per transaction.
3. **I searched for amplifiers that make the stall as long as possible.** The cost per transaction grows with the square of the input count, so the attack hinges on maximizing inputs within the 2 MB transaction-size limit — i.e. minimizing bytes per input. I evaluated input constructions for the best cost-per-byte ratio: the winner was small stub-P2PK inputs (compact signatures spending short P2PK-style outputs), which pack roughly 39,000 inputs into a single at-most-2 MB transaction. That amplifier choice is what took the quadratic from a theoretical scaling flaw to a measurable, minutes-long stall — and ZF's advisory quotes the resulting measurement.
4. **I confirmed it with a live demonstration, not a model's word.** I built that 2 MB, ~39,000-input transaction and submitted it to a real Zebra node pinned to one core: the node's CPU stayed pinned for the length of the quadratic work. The demonstration was reproducible and used Zebra's real code paths, with honest transactions as the negative control (no cost amplification).
5. **I reported privately and reproducibly** through Zebra's private advisory process on 17 September 2026, with the full transaction construction so ZF could reproduce it — and kept the details private until the fix shipped on 22 October.
6. **I verified the fix** in `zcash_primitives` 0.31.0: `PrecomputedSighashData` computes the digests once per transaction and reuses them per input, restoring linear cost — on both the ZIP-244 (v5) and ZIP-243 (v4) paths.


### Time Period of Work Completion

September–October 2026: reported privately 17 September 2026 (first private disclosure; acknowledged by ZF 19 September), independently rediscovered by two other researchers in early October, fixed in Zebra v7.0.0 and published as GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v on 22 October 2026.

No

I have not received funding from the Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program.

### Other Funding Sources

No

I have not received any payment, from any source, for GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v. ZF does not operate a bug bounty program and did not pay for this report.
If any payment for this advisory ever arises from another source, it will be disclosed and deducted dollar-for-dollar before disbursement.


### Success Metrics

- **Severity assigned by the remediation team:** High, CVSS 3.1 7.5 (GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v).
- **Exposure:** every zebrad release before 7.0.0, every default configuration; reachable by any connected peer or any caller of `sendrawtransaction`.
- **Measured effect:** a single at-most-2 MB transaction stalled block verification for about 7 minutes on a 4-core node (ZF's published figure); the work continued after rejection and no misbehavior score was assigned to the sender.
- **Fix:** O(N²) → O(N) per transaction via `PrecomputedSighashData` in `zcash_primitives` 0.31.0; shipped in Zebra v7.0.0, the NU7 release.
- The report was the first private disclosure of the issue, with a reproducible proof of concept ZF could run, five weeks before coordinated publication.
- The fix protects every Zebra operator on the network, and restores linear signing cost for both ZIP-244 (v5) and ZIP-243 (v4) transactions.

Severity High, CVSS 3.1 7.5, CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption). Affected: all zebrad < 7.0.0.
- **Release/Deployment (the fix, shipped):** [Zebra v7.0.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v7.0.0) — released 22 October 2026, the NU7 release; fixes the vulnerability via [zcash_primitives 0.31.0](https://crates.io/crates/zcash_primitives/0.31.0) (`PrecomputedSighashData`: digest computation O(N²) → O(N) per transaction).
- **Other Evidence (timeline, all dates in ZF's advisory and private triage):** reported privately 17 September 2026 via ZF's private security-advisary channel; acknowledged 19 September; independently rediscovered by two other researchers in early October; coordinated publication 22 October 2026.

The analysis identified a version and consensus-branch combination accepted by the parser but rejected by the writer, turning an assumed-infallible operation into a process abort in Zebra 6.4.0 and 6.4.1. The [published advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h5rr-8pqv-grp9) documents the vulnerability analysis, reproduction conditions, and reporter credit.

### Project Description

#### At a glance

| Finding | ZF severity | My contribution and other credited finders | Fix | Requested share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| [GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8): checkpoint verifier left ahead of state | High | Reported by @SphereDonout with an end-to-end P2P proof of concept; independently reported by @x15-eth | Zebra 7.0.0 | $37,500 |

| **Total** | | | | **$75,000** |

#### The completed findings

**GHSA-2w9f: checkpoint sync stalls until restart.** A peer could serve a forged checkpoint block body and a second invalid block so that a sync restart cancelled the verifier's rewind to the state tip. Zebra then treated honest missing blocks as already verified and stopped making checkpoint sync progress until an operator restarted it. The [advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8) credits my end-to-end P2P proof of concept and negative control, and credits @x15-eth's independent analysis. Zebra 7.0.0 moved recovery into the commit task. My $37,500 request is the other half of the High reference amount; [@x15-eth separately requests $37,500](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/79).

**GHSA-6v36: process abort on peer disconnection.** If Zebra disconnected a peer while an outbound socket send was blocked, an unresolved response handle could trigger an assertion. Under release settings, the panic terminated zebrad. The confirmed trigger required a timing overlap while the node was syncing; the [advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-6v36-c42v-v98p) reports no consensus, funds, privacy, or persistent-state impact. It credits my report and @professorsolderin's independent report. Zebra 7.0.0 fixed the response-handle lifecycle. I request half of the Medium reference amount.

**GHSA-5h3r: honest peers banned over lock time.** A Zebra node one block behind a peer could treat that peer's valid, newly relayed transaction as a ban-worthy lock-time violation. On 6.4.x the resulting peer-group ban lasted 24 hours; on earlier affected releases it lasted until restart. The node itself kept running. The [advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w) credits my private two-node reproduction and @sangsoo-osec's independent public report. Zebra 7.0.0 stopped assigning peer misbehavior scores to mempool lock-time rejections. I request half of the Medium reference amount.

#### Basis for the amount

The former [ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545) classified Zebra as a Core Node and published reference amounts of $75,000 for High and $37,500 for Medium findings. I use those historical amounts to propose shares for this separate coinholder-directed retroactive grant application; they do not guarantee an award. Each finding has an independent public record, a named credit, and a released fix. I request no bonus and make no claim on behalf of the other credited reporters.


### Technical Approach (how you did it)

I used LLM-based vulnerability discovery tool to scan the core logic components to find these issues, followed by carefully manual review to triage these findings.

My manual review followed each candidate from an untrusted network input or peer interaction through the relevant parsing, verification, synchronization, or error-handling code to its observable effect. I checked the conditions needed to trigger each issue and distinguished the affected releases from versions where the path was already blocked or fixed:

- **GHSA-2w9f:** I traced checkpoint-verifier progress, state commits, sync-round cancellation, and the rewind after a failed commit. I submitted an end-to-end P2P proof of concept with a negative control showing how a forged checkpoint block body and a second invalid block could leave the verifier ahead of the state and stop checkpoint sync until restart.
- **GHSA-6v36:** I examined the lifetime of an outbound request's response handle while a socket send was blocked and a peer connection was removed. The analysis identified the cancellation window in which the handle was dropped unresolved, causing an assertion and a process abort in release builds.
- **GHSA-5h3r:** I compared mempool lock-time validation and peer scoring at two nodes whose chain tips differed by one block. A two-node reproduction showed that a transaction valid for the ahead peer could cause the lagging node to ban that honest peer at the lock-time boundary.

The published advisories for [GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8), [GHSA-6v36-c42v-v98p](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-6v36-c42v-v98p), and [GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w) document the vulnerability analyses, reproduction conditions, and reporter credit for these findings.



### Time Period of Work Completion

September–October 2026. These three advisories and their Zebra 7.0.0 fixes were published on October 22.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This is an outcome-based retroactive award request. No salary, software, hosting, contractor, or other expenses are submitted for reimbursement, so the total expense budget is $0.


### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

None. I have not received funding from the Coinholder Grants Program.

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

None. I have not received funding from other sources for these three findings.

### Success Metrics

- Three published Zcash Foundation advisories credit @SphereDonout: [GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8) is rated High; [GHSA-6v36-c42v-v98p](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-6v36-c42v-v98p) and [GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w) are rated Medium.
- Three fixes shipped in [Zebra 7.0.0](https://zfnd.org/zebra-7-0-0-release/): the checkpoint-sync stall, the peer-disconnection abort, and the incorrect bans of honest peers. The Zcash Foundation announcement acknowledges my reports by name.
- The [checkpoint-sync advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8) acknowledges my end-to-end P2P proof of concept and negative control. The [lock-time advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-5h3r-fpmj-483w) acknowledges my two-node reproduction.
- The fixes address distinct availability and peer-connectivity harms: initial sync halted until restart, a timing-dependent process abort, and bans of honest peers. The advisories describe the impact and limits of each finding; none of these three is claimed as a consensus or funds vulnerability.
- The $75,000 request covers only my proposed shares. Other credited finders are named above, and [@x15-eth's separate application](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/79) requests the other share of GHSA-2w9f.

issues.body:

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@metaforismo

### Organization or Individual Name

Individual — Independent security researcher

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
Francesco Giannicola (@metaforismo) — principal investigator (elliptic-curve cryptography researcher, co-author of ECDSA.Fail, secp256k1 research). AI-assisted audit methodology disclosed below; all findings human-verified with executed proofs-of-concept.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through the Zcash ecosystem: following the Q3 2026 round (including the Orchard incident response and the $1.5M Hornby award), the ZIP-1016 ratification discussions, and the FROST/ZIP-312 standardization work. The retroactive model — paying for completed, verifiable security work rather than promises — is the natural vehicle for independent audit work of this kind.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$40,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

Independent, in-depth security audit of FROST v3 (Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures) as specified for Zcash shielded multisig in ZIP-312 — covering frost-core v3.0.0, the RedPallas/RedJubjub ciphersuites, the DKG implementation, and the frost-tools application layer. Headline result, stated honestly: no critical vulnerability was found; the codebase is in excellent shape — this audit independently confirms it across 21+ investigated leads, each chased to a documented kill reason.

### Project Description

## Why FROST, why now

FROST is the threshold Schnorr signature scheme selected for Zcash shielded multisig (ZIP-312, IETF standardization track). Threshold signatures are a historically subtle class — nonce handling, DKG robustness, and cheater detection are where the real bugs live. The v3 codebase (2026) is new: it has not been through the "AI bug crisis" re-auditing wave that covered Orchard and Zebra. An independent audit *before* wallets ship FROST signing to users is precisely the kind of preventive security work the retroactive model exists to reward.

## What was audited (real code, not specs)

- ZcashFoundation/frost, frost-core v3.0.0 (0966bd1): round1 (nonces), round2 (signing), aggregate, cheater detection, DKG, refresh, identifiers
- frost-rerandomized v3.0.0: ZIP-312 re-randomization mechanism
- RedPallas/RedJubjub FROST ciphersuites (reddsa pre-removal commit 3a1533b): custom ciphersuite overrides (highest-risk zone per the Mina audit lesson)
- frost-secp256k1-tr (workspace): cross-check of sign/verify symmetry
- frost-tools (frostd, coordinator, participant, zcash-sign) main @ 2026-10-14: application layer — session management, relay, signing UX
- ywallet / Zallet / FROST Book flow HEAD Oct 2026: production wallet integration check

## Methodology (AI-assisted, human-verified)

AI-assisted analysis with a strict protocol: no lead is closed without a proof-of-concept or a formal kill reason. Two Round-1 candidates were later debunked by the same methodology (documented below); this is presented as evidence of rigor, not hidden. This follows the demonstrated precedent in the ecosystem: the $1.5M Orchard finding (Q3) was produced with AI assistance. AI is the instrument; the judgment and verification are human.

## Round 1 — Library audit (frost-core v3.0.0): 14 leads, all killed, code excellent

- Nonce management: hedged generation per RFC 9591 (H3(random || secret)); binding factor correctly covers (group VK || H4(msg) || H5(commitments) || id); IncorrectCommitment check in sign() blocks in-session commitment substitution by a malicious coordinator. Correction (post-publication): this check does NOT prevent cross-session reuse of the same nonce/commitment pair — the library holds no cross-session state, and fresh nonces per session remain the application's documented responsibility (RFC 9591). The original report's reasoning overstated the check's scope; the library is sound per its threat model.
- DKG robustness: Schnorr PoK with verified domain separation (FROST_RedPallasD); rogue-key defense per FROST paper; VSS share verification with culprit identification (cheater detection default-on in v3).
- Binding & context: challenge H2 verified against Zcash spec (Zcash_RedPallasH); complete domain separation across all hash contexts; serialization headers prevent cross-ciphersuite confusion; re-randomization sound. Correction (post-publication): in frost-rerandomized, the randomizer is derived from both the seed AND the signing commitments (regenerate_from_seed_and_commitments) — repeating a seed alone does not reproduce the same randomized key. The original report's reasoning on coordinator seed-reuse was imprecise; the no-forgery conclusion stands.
- Rogue-key attacks: defenses complete for DKG, trusted dealer, and Taproot (BIP-341 unspendable tweak).
- RedPallas custom ciphersuite (577 lines, recovered from pre-removal commit — the highest-risk zone): EvenY algebraic consistency verified; DKG participant coherence verified. Two robustness nits noted (an .expect() on derivable data; an undocumented-but-sound PoK skip).

Full report: https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review/blob/main/reports/frost-library/AUDIT-REPORT-2026-10-17.md

## Round 2 — Application layer: 1 confirmed, 2 debunked, rest negative

- frostd memory exhaustion — CONFIRMED (mechanism). Unbounded recipient buffering in send confirmed by source-code review and local fan-out test; filed as ZcashFoundation/frost-tools#611. The original report's specific RSS measurements and 29,000-recipient SIGABRT kill test are as-reported without published execution logs — the mechanism, not the exact numbers, is the verified claim. Honest caveat: frostd is explicitly demo/reference code; requires self-registered login.
- Noise_K peer impersonation — DEBUNKED (two independent verifications). Round 1 applied Noise X-pattern logic to the K pattern; in K the initiator transmits no static key and Dh(Ss) requires the victim's private key — impersonation is cryptographically impossible. The proposed fix was retracted as tautological. Residual: K-handshake replay -> slot-squat DoS (low, known).
- Missing cheater detection — DEBUNKED (Round 1 was factually wrong). cheater-detection is in frost-core 2.2.0's default features; the culprit IS identified (InvalidSignatureShare { culprit: ... }). Lesson documented: always verify default features before claiming their absence.
- Fuzzing — honest negative. ~1,270 requests against frostd (malformed inputs, state-machine sequences, races, boundaries) on release AND debug builds (overflow checks active): 0 crashes, 0 panics, 0 bypasses. Notable: the fuzzer had to construct a valid XEdDSA signer to test the real login path.
- Chaining — honest negative. Systematic composition matrix of all candidates: no chain escalates from DoS/design-gap to funds or keys. The #2 debunking kills the chains built on it.
- ywallet/Zallet integration check: neither contains FROST signing code (exhaustively verified; Zallet has it only as a transitive dependency). The FROST Book demo flow is broken in HEAD. Blind-signing gap documented: traced the sighash end-to-end — every human checkpoint (zcash-sign, coordinator, participant) displays only opaque hex. A malicious coordinator could get honest co-signers to sign an attacker-crafted PCZT. No production wallet consumes this flow today -> documented as a design gap for future integrators, not filed as a vulnerability.

Full reports: https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review/tree/main/reports/frost-application-layer

## What this work gives the ecosystem

1. Assurance: independent confirmation that FROST v3 — the foundation of shielded multisig — is sound. This is not the team auditing itself.
2. One real bug (frostd DoS) with a reproducible PoC the maintainers can fix.
3. A documented design gap (blind signing) that every future FROST wallet integrator should address before shipping.
4. Methodology transparency: including the debunked false positives, so the community can trust what is claimed.

## What this work is NOT

- Not a critical vulnerability. Stated plainly: the $150k+ Q3 security grants were for actual vulnerabilities. This application does not claim that tier of impact.
- Not production-code findings: the confirmed DoS is in demo/reference code; no production wallet was affected.
- The amount requested ($40,000) reflects this honestly.

All reports, PoC code, and fuzzing harnesses: https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Audit di sicurezza indipendente con metodologia AI-assisted ma human-verified: nessun lead chiuso senza proof-of-concept eseguito o kill reason formale. Round 1: revisione manuale del codice frost-core v3.0.0 (round1/round2, aggregate, cheater detection, DKG, refresh, identifiers), frost-rerandomized, ciphersuite RedPallas/RedJubjub e application layer frost-tools. Round 2: fuzzing (~1.270 richieste contro frostd, build release e debug), test di fan-out locale, verifica end-to-end del flusso sighash/PCZT, controllo integrazione ywallet/Zallet.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Q4 2026 (October 2026)

### Total Budget (USD)

$40,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 40000
  - Justification: Independent security audit of FROST v3 (library + application layer), October 2026
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Total $(USD): 40000

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

N/A

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

N/A

### Success Metrics

21+ lead investigati con kill reason documentate; conferma indipendente che FROST v3 è solido; 1 bug reale (frostd DoS) segnalato come ZcashFoundation/frost-tools#611 con PoC riproducibile; gap di progettazione (blind signing) documentato per i futuri integratori; tutti i report, PoC e harness di fuzzing pubblicati e verificabili.

### Proof of completion

- Repository:
  - https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review
- Library audit report:
  - https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review/blob/main/reports/frost-library/AUDIT-REPORT-2026-10-17.md
- Application-layer reports:
  - https://github.com/metaforismo/frost-security-review/tree/main/reports/frost-application-layer

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@binqbit

### Organization or Individual Name

Dmytro Sysoliatin

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
N/A
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through AI-assisted research and the official announcement on the Zcash Community Forum.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

15000

### Category

Non-Wallet Applications

### Project Summary

Void Market is an open-source sealed-bid auction application that combines confidential bid comparison with Zcash shielded payments. It demonstrates a workflow for selecting an eligible winning bid and settling the resulting transaction without publicly exposing bid amounts or the seller’s reserve price.

### Project Description

Void Market is an open-source sealed-bid auction application combining confidential bid comparison with Zcash shielded payments. Buyers submit confidential bids, while sellers keep their reserve prices private. The application determines the eligible winning offer without publicly disclosing these amounts and uses shielded Zcash payments to settle the resulting transaction.

The current version implements this workflow through an automated arbiter operated by the project. Under honest execution, the arbiter processes the auction without learning individual bid amounts. This version retains a trust assumption: the operator must not collude with a participating bidder to disclose unauthorized competitive information.

The project’s goal is to make confidential auctions and shielded settlement usable as a practical, integrated workflow, demonstrating how Zcash can support private commerce beyond standalone payments.

The planned version 2 aims to enable independently operated arbiters. We intend to develop additional cryptographic proofs that make specified deviations from the agreed auction rules verifiably attributable to the arbiter, including misconduct that could expose confidential information. Combined with an enforceable collateral and compensation mechanism, this would make proven abuse financially punishable and give independent operators an incentive to follow the agreed rules. The objective is to reduce reliance on a trusted operator through verifiable accountability.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Void Market v1 separates confidential auction evaluation from payment settlement. The application coordinates buyer bids, the seller’s private reserve price, an automated arbiter, and Zcash shielded payment verification.

Auction evaluation uses homomorphic computations and comparisons, together with one-time masks for intermediate values exchanged during the protocol. Homomorphic operations support computation over protected inputs, while masking limits disclosure during intermediate verification steps. Participant responses are checked for consistency with the protocol. The intended output identifies the winning eligible offer and whether it satisfies the seller’s reserve, rather than publishing the underlying bid amounts or reserve price.

Version 1 uses an automated arbiter operated by our platform. During normal protocol execution, the arbiter does not learn individual bid amounts. The identified confidentiality risk involves collusion between the platform operator and a participating bidder, which could expose confidential competitive information. The current threat model therefore requires trust that the platform will not engage in such collusion.

The settlement workflow uses Zcash shielded payments. After auction selection, the winning buyer receives a payment request. Payment is verified against the agreed auction outcome, and the seller confirms the transaction. Relevant payment information can be selectively disclosed for dispute resolution without publishing the entire payment history.

The application also coordinates an Ethereum-side asset-release workflow. The asset remains under arbiter control until the required payment conditions are met, after which it can be released to the buyer or returned on cancellation. This is coordinated cross-chain execution, not an atomic swap.

The work followed a research-first process over approximately one month. Several weeks were devoted to developing the core protocol: brainstorming the mechanism, working through its mathematical and cryptographic reasoning, analyzing its guarantees and threat model, comparing alternative designs, and checking its behavior through exploratory prototypes and test examples. The protocol’s guarantees were considered together with their trust assumptions, including the collusion-related limitation of version 1.

During the final week, the protocol rules and conditions were consolidated into documentation and technical specifications, followed by implementation of the integrated application workflow. This brought together confidential auction evaluation, automated arbiter coordination, shielded payment verification, and coordinated asset release in version 1. The source code was published for review and reuse.

Version 2 is planned to support independently operated arbiters through additional cryptographic evidence of specified misconduct and a collateral-backed compensation mechanism. These mechanisms are future development goals and are not claimed as implemented version 1 capabilities.

### Time Period of Work Completion

October 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

6525

### Budget Breakdown

  - $(USD): 6,000
  - Justification: Compensation for my own development work on the completed Void Market v1, including protocol implementation, application integration, and testing.

- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 500
  - Justification: $300 in additional Codex credits purchased specifically for this project, plus an estimated $200 allocation of my ChatGPT/Codex subscription cost based on the project's share of my development usage. The subscription allocation is an estimate, not an exact metered project charge.

- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 25
  - Justification: Estimated combined allocation for server hosting and domain registration associated with the project.

- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: No external contractor costs included in this budget.

- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: No other costs included in this budget.

- Total $(USD): 6,525

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

_No response_

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

Void Market has been submitted to ZECATHON, a Zcash hackathon. The results are pending, and no prize funding has been received to date. If awarded, I intend to use the prize to support further development of the project. This is a potential funding source, not a confirmed award.

### Success Metrics

### Completed contribution

Void Market v1 is an open-source application combining confidential auction evaluation with Zcash shielded payments, payment verification, and selective disclosure for disputes. Its source code is publicly available for inspection and reuse.

We do not yet report verified external adoption or transaction-volume metrics. The evidence below supports the relevance of the problem; it is not a claim of measured product adoption.

### Evidence of community need

- **Commerce privacy beyond payments — December 1, 2025.** In [Shielding the Context of Commerce: Closing the Metadata Gap](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/shielding-the-context-of-commerce-closing-the-metadata-gap/53596), GGuy discusses how private payments can still leave purchase context, identity, and receipts exposed.

- **Marketplace privacy — August 26, 2026.** The [ZEC Market team](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zec-market-a-private-non-custodial-marketplace-built-on-zcash/57200) describes a goal of enabling commerce without a middleman holding funds or seeing what users buy. Its description also includes public listings and prices. This is a developer-stated objective, not an independent customer testimonial.

- **Operator visibility into auction bids — October 2026.** [ShadowBid was described on the Zcash forum](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/we-need-support-with-a-testnet-zec-faucet/57087/19). Its [documented privacy model](https://github.com/sopskistar/shadowbid#privacy-and-trust-model) states that the server receives bid amounts and secrets during reveal, and that the operator can access valid revealed bids. This illustrates the distinction between hiding bids from the public and hiding them from the auction operator.

### Void Market’s approach and current trust boundary

During normal execution, Void Market v1 does not reveal individual bid amounts to its automated arbiter. It retains a trust assumption: collusion between the platform operator and a participating bidder could expose some confidential information.

The planned version 2 aims to support independent arbiter operators through cryptographic evidence of specified misconduct and collateral-backed compensation. These are future development goals, not completed outcomes.

### Evaluation outlook

The sources above establish relevant community discussion and documented implementation trade-offs. They do not establish adoption or independent validation of Void Market.

Future evaluation should measure independent reproduction of the complete workflow, real auction usage, and the reliability of settlement and dispute handling.
