### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@octocat, @octocat1

### Organization or Individual Name

@x15-eth

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual, for my own share of each advisory.

Each advisory's other credited researchers are named below. I claim only my equal share, and
nothing on their behalf. Remediation was done by the Zcash Foundation's Zebra team (structured
credits include @conradoplg, @upbqdn, @oxarbitrage and @mpguerra).
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Zcash Community Forum: the Q3 call for proposals and the Q3 results thread.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

100000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

**In plain terms:**
- Zebra 7.0.0, the release every node needs for NU7, fixed four High-severity bugs that credit me.
- Before the fixes, a single connected peer could make any Zebra node burn its CPU for as long as it kept sending, slow its block verification, or stop its initial sync, and was never banned.
- I am asking for $100,000: my equal share of ZCG's published High rate on the three of them where ZF names what my report contributed.
- I claim nothing for the fourth, GHSA-9hq5, where ZF names no contribution of mine.
- I also claim nothing for an earlier advisory I was already paid for, and no bonus.


### Project Description

### Claim policy

- **Only findings the Zcash Foundation has fixed and published,** where ZF credits me as a reporter, first or independent, and names what my report contributed.
- **I claim only my equal share of each advisory's ZCG base payout,** split among every researcher ZF credits on it. If every credited researcher claimed the same way, the total paid per advisory would never exceed one payout.
- **High-severity advisories only,** at ZF's published rating.
- **Anything already paid is deducted.** No bonus.
- **If ZCG reopens a bounty program,** I will use it before asking coinholders.

<!-- TODO(you): keep the "If ZCG reopens a bounty program" line only if you're happy to commit to it. If you delete it, delete it from the forum post too. -->

### The completed work

| Advisory (all High) | Researchers ZF credits | My named contribution (ZF's words) | My share |
|---|---|---|---:|
| [GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x): transparent script failures are never scored, on the mempool, block-sync and block-gossip paths | **me (reporter)**, @ouicate (independent rediscovery and further analysis: ZF says ouicate "showed the block-sync and block-gossip consequences") | "Reported by @x15-eth, who also measured the combined effect with GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v" | $37,500 |
| [GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2w9f-9wx8-f5c8): a sync restart during a failed checkpoint commit loses the verifier rewind, stalling checkpoint sync until restart | @SphereDonout (reporter), **me** (independent) | "showed that the issue affects every NU5 or later checkpoint range and identified the unscored `UnexpectedSideChain` trigger and the `AlreadyVerified` path, with crate-level tests" | $37,500 |
| [GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-j4cw-58mj-7w6v): quadratic signature-hash cost, so one transaction stalls block verification for minutes | @asafmod (reporter), **me** and @janneh2000 (independent rediscoveries) | "Independently reported by @x15-eth who also measured the v4 path and the effect on block verification and memory" | $25,000 |
| [GHSA-4m69-67m6-prqp](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-4m69-67m6-prqp) (CVE-2026-52736): block suppression via same-header body poisoning, fixed in 4.5.0 | @ipwning and **me** (co-reporters) | "first reporter, with E2E reproduction and control experiment" | $37,500 − $37,500 already paid = **$0** |
| **Total** | | | **$100,000** |

All three claimed advisories are rated CVSS 3.1 7.5, and were fixed in Zebra 7.0.0. GHSA-4m69 was fixed earlier, in 4.5.0.

**Not claimed:** GHSA-9hq5-pfgc-cx5h (High). ZF lists me as one of four independent re-discoverers, after the original reporter, with no contribution of mine named.

**What my independent work added,** where I wasn't the first reporter:
- **GHSA-2w9f:**
  - ZF's advisory lists the unscored `UnexpectedSideChain` trigger I found as one of its two confirmed triggers. It's the one that lets the attacker repeat the stall, because it carries a misbehavior score of 0.
  - ZF's fix also covers the `AlreadyVerified` path my report identified: the syncer now requests those honest blocks again.
- **GHSA-j4cw:**
  - ZF's credit names the v4 (ZIP-243) path, which I measured, and its effect on block verification and memory.
  - The fix covers that path too: it precomputes "the ZIP-243 prevouts, sequence and outputs digests for v4 transactions" once per transaction.
  - ZF's j4cw advisory also lists the GHSA-jq45 fix as part of the remedy, because it means "the sender of such a transaction is now banned".

### Why it mattered

**One connected peer could delay block verification on any synced Zebra node, or stop a new node's initial sync, and was never penalized.** With zcashd retired, Zebra is the main full node the network runs on.

- **CPU flood (GHSA-jq45).** This hit every synced node in its default configuration. In ZF's words, "any inbound or outbound peer can trigger it after the handshake", and "No configuration change exposes or protects you".
  - Zebra's 100-point ban score for invalid transparent scripts could never fire, because of a type-conversion gap. The node rejected every bad transaction but never banned the sender, like a smoke detector with its siren unplugged. That was true of every release from 2.3.0 (May 2025) to 7.0.0-rc.0.
  - So a peer could repeat the most expensive check in Zebra's transaction verifier without limit. In the 23,500-input transaction I measured, each attempt cost **about 85 CPU-seconds**, and a peer could keep five in flight per IP address. Most of that per-transaction cost came from GHSA-j4cw, below. The missing ban in jq45 is what let a peer keep repeating it.
  - ZF's GHSA-jq45 advisory gives the effect: "Block verification shares the same thread pool, so blocks were verified late while the attack lasted", and honest transactions waiting behind the same work "were dropped if they waited longer than the 73-second verification timeout."
  - Creating the 23,500 small outputs the transaction spends cost about 1.2 ZEC in fees, once. Because the transaction is always rejected, the outputs are never spent, and the sender is never banned. So the same outputs can fund the attack for as long as the attacker likes, against every node it can connect to.
- **Quadratic signature-hash cost (GHSA-j4cw).** This also hit every node, from any peer or any caller that can reach `sendrawtransaction`.
  - One transaction of at most 2 MB made Zebra do hashing work that grows with the square of its input count, on the same thread pool that block verification uses. The work kept running after the transaction was rejected.
  - For the original reporter's largest transaction, ZF's advisory puts the cost at "about 7 minutes of stalled verification on a 4-core node", adding: "A mining node cannot verify new blocks during that time and its templates go stale."
  - The rejection carried no misbehavior score, so the sender was not disconnected or banned.
- **Initial sync stall (GHSA-2w9f).** This one is narrower. It hits nodes doing checkpoint sync, which ZF lists as "a new node, a node re-syncing from scratch, or a node restarting from a cached state below the final checkpoint".
  - A single peer could stop such a node until restart, then do it again in the next range.
  - My report showed this covers every NU5-or-later checkpoint range, which is about 1.8 million blocks of Mainnet initial sync. It also found the unscored trigger that lets the attacker repeat it.

**What these bugs are not.** They are availability bugs. As ZF's advisories say, none of them crashes a node, corrupts state, splits consensus or touches funds, and the effects stop when the attack stops. The case for paying them rests on reach and persistence: any peer, any default node, never banned, for as long as the attacker likes.

**These are exactly what ZCG's own guide calls High.** ZCG's (now closed) disclosure program defined High with examples including "Non-distributed denial of service against an individual node or wallet", and priced a Core Node High at $75,000. The rate used here is ZCG's number for this class of bug, not mine.

### Why this is what the program is for

- **It is exactly the kind of work coinholders chose to fund.** In 2025, coinholders voted to run the Coinholder-Controlled Fund (ZIP 1016) as a *retroactive* program ([ratification poll](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/52013)): it pays only for finished, publicly verifiable work, so coinholders carry no execution risk. Every item here is already fixed, merged, released and published, and credited by name.
- **Anyone can check it.** ZIP 1016 aims for decentralized, accountable funding decisions. Each claim here is in ZF's public advisories, its changelog or the Zebra 7.0.0 release, so anyone can check it without taking my word for it.
- **There is no other paying route for security research.** ZF does not pay for reports (Zebra's `SECURITY.md`: ZF does "not currently operate a bug bounty program and do not pay for reports"). ZCG closed its program on 26 May 2026, after AI-generated, often unverified reports overwhelmed triage. I filed these reports on 6 and 7 October 2026.
- **It keeps responsible disclosure worthwhile.** Paying for fixed, verified disclosures keeps private reporting more attractive than exploiting a bug or disclosing it publicly. That is why Q3 coinholders funded the Orchard disclosure and several Zebra findings.
- **For scale:** in Q3, coinholders funded a single Critical Zebra DoS at $150,000. This request is $100,000 for my shares of three Highs.

### Basis for the $100,000 request

| ZCG Core Node tier | Base payout | Discretionary bonus (not claimed) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Critical | $150,000 | $75,000 |
| **High** | **$75,000** | $37,500 |
| Medium | $37,500 | $18,750 |
| Low | $18,750 | $9,375 |

Equal split per advisory, as funded in Q3:
- **GHSA-jq45:** $75,000 ÷ 2 = $37,500.
- **GHSA-2w9f:** $75,000 ÷ 2 = $37,500.
- **GHSA-j4cw:** $75,000 ÷ 3 = $25,000.
- **GHSA-4m69:** $75,000 ÷ 2 = $37,500, minus the $37,500 already received, which leaves $0.

This is the method sangsoo-osec used in Q3 ("Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities", funded with 96% approval, per the [published tally](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/57910/1)). He claimed half of GHSA-8m29, where ZF credits him as having "independently found the same issue" and shown an extra variant, alongside the original reporter's own claim.


### Technical Approach (how you did it)

I ran this review with Claude (Anthropic's AI model) as the research engine, and directed it. Rather than relying on unverified model output, I used it to generate focused hypotheses, to write and run the tests that confirmed or killed each one, and to draft the reports for the findings that survived. My part:
- I set the targets and the evidence bar;
- I chose which leads to pursue and which to drop;
- I decided what to report, and at what severity;
- I submitted each report, and saw it through ZF's triage.

1. **Learn from past advisories.** The review started from a model of what Zebra's published Critical and High advisories had in common: places where, by the time a failed check is acted on, the error no longer means what the code assumes.
2. **Generate focused hypotheses.** Each lead named one concrete place where that could happen, such as a ban score that can't fire, or a recovery step that can be cancelled.
3. **Confirm or kill with real code.** Every lead had to pass a test through Zebra's real code paths, such as the real transaction verifier, `CheckpointVerifier` and `StateService`, with a negative control. Leads that didn't survive were dropped, not reported.
4. **Measure the impact.** For jq45: CPU time per transaction, the queue against the 73-second timeout, and the attacker's setup cost. ZF's advisory uses those figures.
5. **Report privately and reproducibly.** Each report went through Zebra's private advisory process, with the full proof-of-concept diff and its control case. ZF reproduced, fixed and published each one.

**GHSA-jq45.**
- Every 100-point arm of the misbehavior table was traced back to the code that constructs its error. The `Script(_)` arm had no live constructor on the verification path, so script failures reached the table as `InternalDowncastError`, which scores 0.
- A proof-of-concept test against the real transaction verifier, with a negative control, confirmed it.
- The cost a peer could impose was then measured, including the v4 path: a 23,500-input transaction, its CPU time, and the queue behaviour against the 73-second timeout. ZF's advisories use those figures.

**GHSA-2w9f.**
- Following the checkpoint verifier's rewind path showed that the only step that rewinds it runs inside a future the syncer cancels on restart.
- The report then found an unscored way to force that restart (`UnexpectedSideChain`).
- Crate-level tests against the real `CheckpointVerifier` and `StateService`, using real NU5 Regtest blocks mined by `zebrad`, showed the stall in any NU5-or-later range, with honest re-deliveries dropped as `AlreadyVerified`.

**GHSA-j4cw.**
- Tests through Zebra's real signature hasher, with signatures that are well formed but never verify, showed that each input's signature hash re-hashes data covering every input. The cost per input grows with the input count, so the cost per transaction grows with its square.
- The tests covered both the v5 (ZIP-244) path and the v4 (ZIP-243) path, and then measured the effect on block verification and memory.

**Disclosure.** All reports went privately through Zebra's GitHub security advisory process. I worked with the team through triage, and kept details private until fixes shipped and operators had been told to upgrade.

## Time Period of Work Completion

October 2026: reports filed on 6 and 7 October 2026, fixed in Zebra 7.0.0, and published on 22 October 2026. GHSA-4m69 (listed, $0 claimed) dates from May 2026.

### Success Metrics

### Quantitative

- **Severity assigned by the remediation team:** High, CVSS 3.1 7.5, for each claimed advisory.

  - GHSA-2w9f: about 1.8 million blocks of Mainnet initial sync.
  - GHSA-j4cw: every zebrad release before 7.0.0.
- **Attacker cost:** ordinary peer connections, no proof of work, no keys. About 1.2 ZEC once for the CPU flood.
- **Measured harm:** about 85 CPU-seconds per 2 MB transaction in my measurement, five held in flight per IP, block verification delayed, honest transactions dropped, the attacker never banned. For j4cw, ZF's advisory gives about 7 minutes of stalled verification on a 4-core node for the original reporter's largest transaction.

### Advisories that credit me

### Qualitative

  - Script failures now get the sending peer banned.
  - The checkpoint verifier's rewind can no longer be cancelled.

- **Coordinated disclosure, done the way the ecosystem asks.** Private reports, test-backed evidence, help with triage, and no public details before the fixes shipped.

### On the arguments against this application

1. **"These are just DoS bugs, and High overstates them."**
   - They are DoS bugs, and I say so above. But GHSA-jq45 and GHSA-j4cw hit every node in its default configuration, from any peer. GHSA-2w9f hits syncing nodes, which includes every new node.
   - The severity isn't mine. ZF rated each advisory High (CVSS 7.5) after reproducing it, and ZCG's schedule defines single-node DoS as High.
   - The claim limits itself. I claim only my equal share, with no bonus and the earlier payment deducted. If each credited researcher claims an equal share, the total stays within the $225,000 that ZCG's schedule pays for these three advisories.
2. **"You're claiming bugs other people found, with AI help."**

All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@ouicate

### Organization or Individual Name

ouicate (Quorint)

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

The Zcash Community Forum: the Q4 2026 call for proposals, and the Q3 2026 retroactive grants for Zebra security findings.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$75,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I found and privately reported two Zebra vulnerabilities in how nodes handle forged block bodies served under genuine block hashes. GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x (High), which I reported independently of @x15-eth, let one connected peer hold a syncing node behind the chain tip without ever being banned. GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf (Medium, sole reporter) made nodes verify every proof in blocks that could never be committed. The Zcash Foundation fixed both in released Zebra (7.0.0 and 6.4.0). I am requesting $75,000: half of the $75,000 High base for GHSA-jq45, with x15-eth requesting the other half, plus the $37,500 Medium base for GHSA-3c94.

### Project Description

#### At a glance

- **GHSA-jq45 (High, CVSS 7.5):** one connected peer could hold a syncing Zebra node behind the chain tip, "never scored, never banned". It affected every Zebra release from 2.3.0 until 7.0.0, and no configuration removed it.
- **GHSA-3c94 (Medium, CVSS 5.3):** a peer could make a node verify every proof in a forged block body, including the Ironwood Halo2 batch, with no penalty. On the block-sync path, each forged body that won its download race also stalled sync for 67 seconds.
- **Credit and fixes:** independent reporter on GHSA-jq45, with @x15-eth, fixed in Zebra 7.0.0. Sole reporter on GHSA-3c94, fixed in Zebra 6.4.0.
- **Request:** $37,500 for GHSA-jq45, which is half of the $75,000 Core Node High base. x15-eth is requesting the other half, the same split coinholders approved for shared advisories in Q3 ([#58](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58)). Plus $37,500 for GHSA-3c94, the Core Node Medium base. The total is $75,000, at the severities ZF assigned. I am not requesting a bonus, and nothing has been paid for either finding.

#### The two findings

| Advisory | Severity | Affected | Fixed | My credit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x): Transparent script verification failures are never scored, on the mempool, block-sync and block-gossip paths | High (CVSS 7.5) | zebrad 2.3.0 up to 7.0.0 | Zebra 7.0.0 | Independent reporter, with @x15-eth |
| [GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf): Same-hash block body forces full proof verification with no peer penalty | Medium (CVSS 5.3) | zebrad 6.3.0 and earlier | Zebra 6.4.0 (the advisory lists 6.4.2) | Sole reporter |

#### How they connect

After NU5, a block's hash and Merkle root commit only to transaction IDs, and a v5 transaction's ID doesn't cover its authorizing data ([ZIP 244](https://zips.z.cash/zip-0244)). A peer can therefore take a real block, flip one authorizing byte, and serve a different body under the same hash. Zebra accepts that body as the answer to its own download request.

- **GHSA-3c94 (my report, 20 August).** Zebra ran every proof in the forged body, including the Ironwood Halo2 batch, before the state caught the mismatch. The serving peer was never scored. On the block-sync path, each forged body that won its download race also cancelled the sync round and idled the node for 67 seconds. The advisory calls a node catching up above the mandatory checkpoint "the most damaging scenario". Zebra 6.4.0 fixed it: the syncer now continues the round and re-requests the body from another peer.
- **GHSA-jq45 (x15-eth and me, independently).** Zebra scored transparent script failures at 0 on every path. x15-eth reported the issue, and I independently showed the block-sync and block-gossip consequences, and the same-hash construction that reaches them. If you flip a byte in a v5 transaction's `scriptSig`, script verification fails before the state's commitment check. As the advisory puts it, the GHSA-3c94 handling therefore "does not apply". The advisory describes the result: "A node syncing above the checkpoint range can be held back by one connected peer. [...] never scored, never banned. No funds, keys, proofs or mining are needed." Zebra 7.0.0 fixed it. Peers that send script-invalid transactions or blocks are now banned on all three paths, which limits the block-sync restart to once per banned address.

#### What the Zcash Foundation recorded

- GHSA-jq45, reporter field: "@x15-eth; @ouicate (independent rediscovery and further analysis)". Credit section: "Independently reported by @ouicate, who showed the block-sync and block-gossip consequences and the same-hash `scriptSig` construction."
- GHSA-jq45 lists GHSA-3c94 among its references as "the sync-round restart handling this fix must extend".
- GHSA-3c94, credit section: "ouicate, for the finding, the control-flow analysis, and the same-hash construction."
- [Zebra 6.4.0 release notes](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.0), on the GHSA-3c94 fix: "Thanks to @ouicate for reporting the issue."


### Technical Approach (how you did it)

**GHSA-3c94 (reported 20 August 2026).** I followed a downloaded block on v6.3.0 from the network layer to the state commit, checking four things in turn:

- What the download layer accepts a body by: the header hash only.
- What the semantic verifier binds: txids only.
- Where the authorizing-data commitment is checked: in the state, after every proof has run.
- How the resulting error is scored (0) and how the syncer handles it (a round restart and a 67-second idle).

I then built the same-hash body: an honest block with one authorizing-only byte flipped, which keeps both the header hash and the Merkle root. I reported it privately through a GitHub security advisory, with the code path traced line by line.

**GHSA-jq45 (reported 15 October 2026).** I checked how script-verification failures reach peer scoring. `impl From<BoxError> for TransactionError` downcast the shielded signature and proof errors but had no arm for `zebra_script::Error`, so every transparent script failure collapsed to `InternalDowncastError`, which scores 0. Zebra's own tests asserted that collapse. I then extended the same-hash construction to it. Flipping one byte of a v5 transaction's `scriptSig` keeps the block hash and the Merkle root, because ZIP 244 leaves `scriptSig` out of the txid, but script verification fails before the state's commitment check, so the GHSA-3c94 handling does not apply. On block sync the serving peer went unscored, the round restarted, the hash was dropped and the syncer idled for 67 seconds. On block gossip the peer also went unscored. I reported it privately with a runnable unit test for the root cause and network-level reproductions.

**Tools:** I used LLM-assisted code review to map the code paths and generate leads, and confirmed both findings by hand with tests before reporting.

### Time Period of Work Completion

August to October 2026. I reported GHSA-3c94 on 20 August; it was fixed in Zebra 6.4.0 (23 September) and published on 28 September. I reported GHSA-jq45 on 15 October; it was fixed in Zebra 7.0.0 and published on 22 October.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This is a retroactive request for completed work, not a reimbursement of costs. 

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

I have not received funding from the Coinholder Grants Program.

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

I have not received, and do not expect, payment from any other source for these two advisories. Both were reported after ZCG's bounty program closed on 26 May 2026. While that program was open, ZCG paid for two of my earlier Zebra reports ([public record](https://openzcash.org/zcg/recipient?r=ouicate)). Those are separate findings and are not part of this request.

### Success Metrics

**Quantitative**

- 2 published advisories crediting me: GHSA-jq45 (High 7.5, independent reporter) and GHSA-3c94 (Medium 5.3, sole reporter).
- 2 fixes shipped: Zebra 6.4.0 and Zebra 7.0.0.
- 3 paths (mempool, block sync and block gossip) that now ban peers sending script-invalid data. Before 7.0.0, none of them scored those peers.
- 67 seconds of forced sync idle per forged body that won its download race. 6.4.0 removed this for the commitment case. 7.0.0 limits it to once per banned address for the script case.
- Exposure closed for every zebrad release from 2.3.0 until 7.0.0 (GHSA-jq45), and for every release up to 6.3.0 (GHSA-3c94).

**Qualitative**

- Liveness for the nodes most exposed during an attack: nodes catching up above the checkpoint, such as new nodes, and exchanges and explorers coming back from downtime.
- A free, unauthenticated way to hold a node behind the tip is gone.
- The same-hash attack is now penalized on every path, not only in the commitment case that GHSA-3c94 fixed.

### Proof of completion

**Repository/Commit**

- GHSA-jq45 fix at 7.0.0: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/e8db87eb69254e0d4eedd058eadd48bdfa09065a/zebra-consensus/src/error.rs#L356-L370
- GHSA-3c94 fix, described in the Zebra 6.4.0 release notes: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.0

**Publication**

- GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x
- GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf

**Deployment/Release**

- Zebra 7.0.0: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v7.0.0
- Zebra 6.4.0 ("Thanks to @ouicate for reporting the issue"): https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.0

**Other Evidence**

- Q3 precedent for splitting a shared advisory: https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58
- ZCG's severity framework and payout schedule: https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545


### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

@x15-eth, the other reporter on GHSA-jq45, is requesting the other half of it in a separate application this round. We agreed to split it equally. I am also applying separately for two Critical Zebra consensus vulnerabilities, in [Two Critical Zebra Consensus Vulnerabilities (#77)](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/77). Apart from that, I have no employment, contracting or governance relationship with the Zcash Foundation, ZCG, FPF, or any keyholder organization.

### Community Forum Posting

- [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application. Note: If you are unable to post on the forum (for example, due to new user restrictions), please leave a comment below, and we will adjust your posting permissions.

### Terms and Conditions

- [x] I agree to the [Grant Agreement](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_6ff6db4095fd4c4ba21babec361e927e.pdf) terms if funded

All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.
- [x] I agree that for any new open-source software, I will create a CONTRIBUTING.md file that reflects the high standards of Zcash development, using the [`librustzcash` style guides](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#styleguides) as a primary reference.
- [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@ouicate

### Organization or Individual Name

ouicate (Quorint)

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual for my own security research contribution.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

The Zcash Community Forum: the Q4 2026 call for proposals, and the Q3 2026 retroactive grants for Zebra security findings.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$300,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I found and privately reported two Critical consensus vulnerabilities in the code headed for Zebra's next release: one would have let anyone split the Zcash network with a single transaction, and the other would have let any miner do it with a single block. The Zcash Foundation made them a release blocker, fixed both within six days (PR #11387), and shipped Zebra 6.4.0 without them, crediting me for "**identifying and mitigating what would have been a nasty consensus bug in Zebra before we shipped it.**"

### Project Description

#### At a glance

- **What:** two consensus vulnerabilities in the code headed for Zebra 6.4.0. In a release, either one would have split the Zcash network. C-01 would have needed only one transaction from anyone, and C-02 only one block from any miner.
- **Outcome:** I reported both privately on 2 September 2026. ZF made them a release blocker, merged the fix six days later, and shipped 6.4.0 on 23 September with both rules enforced. No node was ever exposed.
- **In ZF's words:** "Both findings identified and responsibly disclosed by @ouicate. We appreciate your contribution in identifying and mitigating what would have been a nasty consensus bug in Zebra before we shipped it." ([Issue #11383](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/issues/11383))
- **Request:** $150,000 per finding, which is the Core Node Critical base. That is the same per-finding amount coinholders approved for sole-reporter Zebra consensus findings in Q3, with 96.33% in favour. I am not requesting a bonus, and nothing has been paid for these findings.

#### What I found

[PR #10461](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10461) replaced Zebra's own transaction parser with the shared `zcash_primitives` library and was merged into `main` on 22 August 2026. Two rules that every Zcash node must enforce were lost in the move:

| | Rule | What Zebra's `main` branch did | Who could trigger it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C-01** | A non-coinbase transaction's `nExpiryHeight` must be at most 499,999,999 ([ZIP 203](https://zips.z.cash/zip-0203); protocol spec §7.1.2) | A new conversion turned every value from 2^31 to 2^32−1 into "no expiry", so about 2.1 billion invalid values were accepted | Anyone: one transaction, with no mining and no authentication |
| **C-02** | A coinbase `scriptSig` must be 2 to 100 bytes (protocol spec §7.1.2) | The check survived only in a function that production code no longer called. Its unit tests kept passing | Any miner: one block |

These are two separate findings. They break different rules, different people could trigger them, and each would have split the network on its own. PR #11387 fixes them in separate commits.

ZF's tracking issue, [#11383](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/issues/11383), says: "Both were reported by @ouicate." The fix, [PR #11387](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/11387), says: "Fixes #11383. Reported by @ouicate."

The full technical write-up, with code paths and deterministic tests, is on the Quorint research blog: [Two Critical Consensus-Divergence Vulnerabilities in Zcash's Zebra Node](https://quorint.xyz/research/zebra-pre-release-consensus-divergences/).

#### What would have happened

Since zcashd reached end-of-life in July 2026, Zcash has run on two full-node implementations: Zebra, and Zakura, an independent Zebra-derived node. Zakura v1.3.1 and Zebra 6.0.0 to 6.3.0 enforce both rules (#11383). Had Zebra 6.4.0 shipped with C-01, this is what would have happened:

1. Anyone broadcasts one transaction with an expiry height of 2^31 or more. Upgraded Zebra nodes accept it, relay it, and keep it as "never expires".
2. The next Zebra-based pool that calls `getblocktemplate` mines it.
3. Upgraded Zebra nodes accept that block and build on it. Zakura and older Zebra nodes reject it and follow the other branch.
4. Exchanges, pools, Zaino indexers and Zallet wallets now see two different chains. A deposit confirmed on one chain can be double-spent on the other.
5. Zebra does not roll back more than 1,000 blocks (`MAX_BLOCK_REORG_HEIGHT`, about 21 hours). After that, ending the split requires either resyncing every affected node or writing an exception for the bad block into the consensus rules.

C-02 leads to the same split. All it takes is a miner padding one coinbase `scriptSig` past 100 bytes.

#### Why these are Critical

ZF publishes severity ratings in its security advisories, and advisories are written for affected releases. No release was affected, so ZF tracked the fix in a public issue and published no rating. Three things show where these findings belong:

**1. ZCG's severity framework**, which this request uses as its reference. It defines Critical as a defect that, "at scale, directly causes" one of Zcash's core harms, and it lists "unintended chain splits" as one of them. Either finding would have split every upgraded Zebra node from the rest of the network at the same moment.

**2. ZF's own ratings for the same attack paths.** When bugs of these shapes shipped, ZF rated them Critical:

| My finding | Closest shipped Zebra advisory, in ZF's words | ZF's rating |
|---|---|---|
| C-01: anyone's transaction travels through Zebra's mempool and `getblocktemplate` into a block that the rest of the network rejects | [GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp): a transaction "accepted by `Zebra`, retained in `Zebra`'s mempool, selected into `Zebra` `getblocktemplate`, mined into a block, and then rejected by `zcashd`" | Critical |
| C-01: no mining needed | [GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443): "An attacker needs no mining capability." | Critical |
| C-02: a block that a miner builds and only Zebra accepts | [GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc): "A miner who produces such a block can split the network." | Critical |

**3. ZF's response.** ZF treated the findings as a release blocker and labelled the fix `consensus` and `security`. It described the outcome as preventing "a nasty consensus bug in Zebra before we shipped it."

These splits would not have healed on their own. C-01 could have been triggered by anyone, at any time after the release. Once a split passes Zebra's 1,000-block rollback window, ending it takes either a coordinated resync of every affected node or a hard fork. ZCG's framework lists an "unintended permanent chain split requiring a hard fork to resolve" as Critical.

#### What the Zcash Foundation did

- **2 September:** I reported both findings privately through Zebra's GitHub security advisory process. Each report included deterministic tests, the end-to-end split scenario and a suggested fix.
- **3 September:** ZF closed the private reports and opened #11383 the same day: "No released version is affected. [...] This is a release blocker for the next release cut from `main`."
- **3 to 8 September:** [PR #11387](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/11387) restored both rules, with tests through the production path that fail without the fix. It also merged Zebra's two deserialization paths into one checked path, and pinned tests for the rules the refactor had moved to the verifier. Finally, it added a permanent chapter to the Zebra Book, [Refactoring Consensus-Critical Code](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/main/book/src/dev/consensus-refactors.md), which the PR describes as "distilled from this incident". The chapter describes both bugs, and says its checklist "exists so the next refactor does not repeat that."
- **4 to 8 September:** ZF also restored a third check the refactor had changed, the null-prevout check ([PR #11400](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/11400)).
- **22 September:** ZF's [engineering update](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zf-engineering-update-7-20-september-2026/57756) reported "Security checks restored before release" and thanked "the Zakura security team and @ouicate for reporting these issues." My two findings are the checks it describes as covering "mining-reward inputs and transaction expiry".
- **23 September:** [Zebra 6.4.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.0), the first release after the refactor, shipped with both rules enforced.

#### Why I reported before release

I could have waited. I said so in [#11383](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/issues/11383#issuecomment-5527705406) on 3 September, before any grant was on the table:

> I could have waited for it to ship and then reported both as live, in-the-wild Criticals, with CVEs and published advisories — the same paper trail the earlier consensus-divergence findings carry. I chose the opposite: report them now and get two would-be Critical consensus splits eliminated before they touched a single production node. Catching a critical before it ships is a better outcome for the network than documenting one after it does — and that's the behavior I'd want the ecosystem to encourage.

On 22 September, in [ZF's update thread](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zf-engineering-update-7-20-september-2026/57756/2), I urged other researchers to do the same:

> To other researchers: report a consensus bug when you confirm it on the development branch. Waiting for a tagged release, a CVE, or a published advisory would have left these in the first release that carried them, and put Zcash at risk for no benefit. Finding them early is what kept them off the network. Credit in the issue and in this update is the right outcome.

That credit is the right public record for a bug that never shipped. Whether reporting early should also be paid like reporting late is the question this application puts to coinholders.

#### Why the full reference amount

Coinholders have already funded Critical security work at and above this level. All three of these Q3 applications were approved and paid:

| Q3 application | Requested | Approval |
|---|---:|---:|
| [#51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51): Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability (Taylor Hornby) | $750,000 | 99.99% |
| [#57](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/57): exploit chain across zcashd and Zebra (Alex Sol) | $400,000 | 98.66% |
| [#58](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58): five Critical Zebra consensus divergences (sangsoo) | $425,000 | 96.33% |

The approval figures are ZEC-weighted shares of the non-abstaining votes in the [finalized Q3 tally](https://zvote.zfnd.org/shielded-vote/v1/vote-summary/2cba66eb16c7581a1692cb0b033785da0131059f645a0d2fb4dc2a5131505e01) hosted by the Zcash Foundation.

#58 is the closest match. It priced each sole-reporter Zebra consensus divergence at the $150,000 Core Node Critical base from ZCG's 2026 schedule, priced each shared one at half, and asked for no bonus. I use exactly that method. I have not discounted for "never shipped", for three reasons:

1. **The difference in exposure was timing, not severity.** One of the #58 findings, GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443, was live for about 20 hours. Zebra 4.5.0 shipped it at 01:25 UTC on 29 May, and 4.5.1 fixed it at 21:34 UTC the same day. ZF rated it Critical, and coinholders approved $150,000 for it. I reported mine 21 days before the release that would have carried them.
2. **They would have shipped.** 6.4.0 was the next release after the refactor, and ZF made the fix a blocker for it. The same refactor did ship a vulnerability that was not caught before release: [GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq), rated High, which affected Zebra 6.4.0 to 6.4.2 until 7.0.0 fixed it. ZF's own checklist explains why bugs like these slip through review: "a rule can stop being enforced without any test failing and without any deleted line showing a check being removed. [...] Absence is invisible in a diff, so it has to be hunted deliberately."
3. **A discount pays researchers to wait.** If a consensus bug found before release is worth less than the same bug found after it, the rational move is to sit on it until it ships. Paying the same keeps early reporting the right choice for the researcher as well as for the network.

| Finding | Credit | Reference | Requested |
|---|---|---|---:|
| C-01: `nExpiryHeight` above the ZIP 203 maximum accepted | Sole reporter | $150,000 Core Node Critical base | $150,000 |
| C-02: coinbase `scriptSig` length rule not enforced | Sole reporter | $150,000 Core Node Critical base | $150,000 |
| **Total** | | | **$300,000** |

No bonus is requested. I use ZCG's schedule as a reference point, not as an entitlement.

#### Researcher background

I am an independent security researcher and publish my work on the [Quorint research blog](https://quorint.xyz/research/). 

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

PR #10461 was merged on 22 August. Zakura v1.3.1 never adopted the refactor, which made it a reference to diff against: any transaction or block that Zakura rejects and Zebra `main` accepts is a consensus divergence.

1. **Old rejections, new homes.** For each consensus rejection the pre-refactor deserializers performed, I looked for where `main` still enforces it. That could be the upstream `zcash_primitives` and `zcash_transparent` crates at the versions pinned in `Cargo.lock`, Zebra's re-added checks, or a later verification step. C-02 had no live home: the check survived only in a helper whose remaining callers were its own tests.
2. **Lossy conversions.** I traced the conversions between upstream types and the values Zebra's consensus checks read, looking for errors collapsed into `None` or a default. That is how C-01 showed up. `.ok()` turned an out-of-range expiry into "no expiry", which every downstream check treats as valid.
3. **Production paths.** For each gap I followed the path a real node uses: P2P and RPC into the mempool, then `getblocktemplate`, then block verification. I did not rely on the helper functions the unit tests call.
4. **Proof.** I wrote deterministic tests showing `main` accepting bytes that Zakura v1.3.1 and Zebra v6.3.0 reject. They are published in the write-up.
5. **Disclosure.** I reported bothr privately to the Zcash Foundation on 2 September, each with the analysis, the tests and a suggested fix.

**Tools:** I used LLM-assisted code review to map the refactor and generate leads, and confirmed both findings by hand with the tests above before reporting.

### Time Period of Work Completion

22 August to 23 September 2026. The review began after PR #10461 merged (22 August). I reported privately on 2 September. The fix was merged on 8 September (PR #11387), and Zebra 6.4.0 shipped with both rules enforced on 23 September.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This is a retroactive request for completed work, not a reimbursement of costs.

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

I have not received funding from the Coinholder Grants Program.

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

I have not received, and do not expect, payment from any other source for these two findings. 

### Success Metrics

**Quantitative**

- 2 Critical consensus vulnerabilities removed before any release carried them, restoring the ZIP 203 expiry maximum and the coinbase `scriptSig` length rule (§7.1.2).
- 0 releases affected and 0 production nodes exposed. Zebra 6.4.0 shipped with both rules enforced, 21 days after my report.
- 1 day from my report to ZF's tracking issue, and 6 days to the merged fix.
- About 2.1 billion invalid `nExpiryHeight` values (2^31 to 2^32−1) that `main` would have accepted from anyone.
- Tests through the production path for both rules, plus pinned tests for the rules the refactor moved to the verifier (PR #11387).
- 1 new permanent Zebra Book chapter, with author and reviewer checklists for consensus-critical refactors.

**Qualitative**

- Consensus held at the point where it was most fragile. With zcashd retired, Zcash depends on Zebra and Zakura agreeing exactly.
- The bugs were fixed at the cheapest possible point: no emergency release, operator upgrades, exchange halts or rollback were needed.
- The process change outlasts the fix. The next refactor of Zebra's consensus parsing has a checklist written from this case.
- The public write-up lets other node implementers check their own refactors for the same two patterns.

### Proof of completion

**Repository/Commit**

- PR #11387, the fix (merged 8 September 2026): https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/11387
- Issue #11383, analysis and credit: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/issues/11383
- PR #10461, the refactor that introduced both vulnerabilities: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10461

**Publication**

- Technical write-up (Quorint research blog): https://quorint.xyz/research/zebra-pre-release-consensus-divergences/
- Zebra Book, Refactoring Consensus-Critical Code: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/main/book/src/dev/consensus-refactors.md
- ZF Engineering Update, 7–20 September 2026 ("Security checks restored before release"): https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zf-engineering-update-7-20-september-2026/57756

**Deployment/Release**

- Zebra 6.4.0, the first release after the refactor, with both rules enforced: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.0
- Zebra 6.3.0, the last release before the refactor: https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.3.0

**Other Evidence**

- My original private reports, reported it privately to the Zcash Foundation on 2 September 2026
- My comment in #11383 (3 September): https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/issues/11383#issuecomment-5527705406
- My reply in ZF's update thread (22 September): https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zf-engineering-update-7-20-september-2026/57756/2
- Severity comparisons, all rated Critical by ZF: GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp, GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 and GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc (links in the Project Description)
- The same refactor's shipped vulnerability, GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq (High): https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq
- Q3 precedent, sangsoo's application: https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58
- ZCG's severity framework and payout schedule: https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

None. I have no employment, contracting or governance relationship with the Zcash Foundation, ZCG, FPF, or any keyholder organization. This round I am also applying separately for two other Zebra advisories, GHSA-jq45-ghw5-v37x and GHSA-3c94-hf7p-g5mf, in [Zebra High and Medium Severity Sync Vulnerabilities (#78)](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/78).

### Community Forum Posting

- [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application. Works directly against the live codebases, reproduces each issue, writes a minimal fix plus regression tests, and submits through the normal pull-request review process of each project.
```team-members.yaml
  Responsibilities: Issue discovery and reproduction, patch authoring, test coverage, and shepherding each pull request through maintainer review to merge.
```

From the Zcash Community Forums Retroactive Grants category and the program's GitHub repository.

$1,690 (reduced from $2,000 on 2026-11-02, see Other Funding Sources)

Infrastructure

Thirteen merged security and correctness fixes to Zcash-ecosystem infrastructure: eleven to the ZecHub Bounty Board backend (ZecHub/zec-bounties), one restoring the ZEC price feed on the Namada metrics dashboard, and one repairing broken documentation links in the ZecHub wiki. Every fix was reviewed and merged by the projects' maintainers.

### Project Description

The ZecHub Bounty Board (`ZecHub/zec-bounties`) is the platform the Zcash community uses to post and claim ecosystem bounties. Over October 2026 I audited and hardened its backend, finding and fixing a series of issues that affected data privacy, authorization, and reliability, and I fixed two further ecosystem tools (the Namada metrics dashboard and the ZecHub wiki). All of this work is complete, public, and merged into the upstream repositories by their maintainers.

Highlights of the bounty-board work:

- **Privacy / data exposure.** Bounty read routes returned every assignee's and creator's email address and payout address to any signed-in account; I restricted these fields to admins only (#354). A related fix keeps private bounties out of the public profile's recent-activity lists (#370).
- **Authorization robustness.** Admin wallet routes ran their logic with null parameters before a wallet was actually connected; I added the guard so they no longer execute in an unauthenticated state (#371), and team deletion no longer leaves members holding a dead copy of the team wallet (#419).
- **Input validation / denial-of-service.** A negative `limit` query parameter bypassed the result cap and crashed list endpoints with a 500; I clamped it (#353). Non-string submission fields returned a 500 instead of a clean 400 (#403). A `%`-containing profile lookup returned a 500 and the route exposed no id/nickname/name (#361).
- **State and data-integrity fixes.** Failed wallet imports left a stuck row so retries 409'd (#376); assignee changes silently cleared the cached assignee list (#379); saving a bounty edit with the reward unchanged was wrongly refused as a paid-field change (#392); the admin staff view sorted by weekday name and never loaded `exportedAt` (#377).

Beyond the bounty board:

- **Namada metrics dashboard (#24):** restored the ZEC price display, which had broken after a CoinGecko API change.
- **ZecHub wiki (#2394):** repointed a dead `zcash-local-net` documentation link.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

For each issue I reproduced the behavior against the project's own test harness or a local run of the service, wrote the minimal fix, and added regression tests where the project's suite supported them. Each change went through the maintainer's normal pull-request review and was merged upstream. The bounty-board fixes are TypeScript/Node against the live `ZecHub/zec-bounties` codebase; the Namada fix restores a CoinGecko price-feed call; the wiki fix is a documentation link repair. No change was self-merged — every merge was performed by a project maintainer (primarily @dismad for the ZecHub repositories).

### Time Period of Work Completion

October 2026 (2026-10-11 to 2026-10-21)

$1,690 (reduced from $2,000 on 2026-11-02, see Other Funding Sources)

```
  - Justification: N/A

  - Justification: N/A
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Other:

  - Justification: N/A
- Total $(USD): 1690
```

No

None received as of 2026-11-02. See Other Funding Sources: a 0.248 ZEC ZecHub board reward for 11 of the 13 PRs is pending.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

Update 2026-11-02: after this application was filed, ZecHub's maintainer created a ZecHub bounty-board reward of 0.248 ZEC (about $310) covering the 11 ZecHub/zec-bounties pull requests listed below (#353, #354, #361, #370, #371, #376, #377, #379, #392, #403, #419). It has been submitted and is awaiting ZecHub's weekly payout. To avoid paying twice for the same work, the amount requested here is reduced by that amount, to $1,690.

### Success Metrics

- 13 pull requests merged upstream by the projects' maintainers (11 in `ZecHub/zec-bounties`, 1 in `ZecHub/Namada`, 1 in `ZecHub/zechub`).
- Removed a standing privacy exposure: assignee/creator email and payout addresses are no longer served to arbitrary signed-in users of the community bounty board.

### Terms and Conditions

- [x] I agree to the [Grant Agreement](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_6ff6db4095fd4c4ba21babec361e927e.pdf) terms if funded

All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.
- [x] I agree that for any new open-source software, I will create a CONTRIBUTING.md file that reflects the high standards of Zcash development, using the [`librustzcash` style guides](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#styleguides) as a primary reference.
- [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@sangsoo-osec

### Organization or Individual Name

sangsoo-osec

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual for my own security research contribution.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through the Zcash Community Forum. I previously received a coinholder-approved retroactive grant in the Q3 2026 round.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

37500

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting $37,500 for GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v, a completed Medium severity disclosure concerning a V4 Sapling transaction parsing mismatch between zcashd and Zebra. This application follows the discussion in my [High severity application #74](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/74) and presents a separate Medium finding as a concrete case for considering how severity ratings and practical impact should inform retroactive security rewards.

### Project Description

#### Shared background with application #74

Thank you again to the coinholders who approved my Q3 proposal and everyone in the community who reviewed, discussed, and supported that work.

My [Q4 High severity application #74](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/74) sets out the shared background: the Q3 approvals for critical vulnerability research, recent published security findings, and the opportunity to discuss how researchers' contributions to Zcash's security should be rewarded. I refer readers to that application for the supporting Q3 references and release data.

This application brings the same discussion to a **Medium severity finding**, displayed as **Moderate** on GitHub. It requests recognition for a separate completed disclosure, with its own technical record, exploitation conditions, and proposed amount.

#### The completed contribution

The finding concerns **GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v**, published by the zcashd maintainers on May 8, 2026, with sangsoo-osec credited as the reporter. See the [official advisory](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/security/advisories/GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v).

For a V4 Sapling transaction with no Sapling spends or outputs, the serialized `valueBalanceSapling` must be zero. The malformed case has:

| Serialized field | Value |
|---|---:|
| `nSpendsSapling` | `0` |
| `nOutputsSapling` | `0` |
| `valueBalanceSapling` | A non-zero in-range value, such as `1` |

In the affected zcashd code, the [V4 read path](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/blob/2c63e9aa08cb170b0feb374161bea94720c3e1f5/src/primitives/transaction.h#L857-L887) used the presence of Sapling actions to decide whether to assemble a bundle. With both action vectors empty, it discarded the non-zero balance and exposed an empty-bundle balance of zero. The later validation check therefore examined an already-normalized object. Zebra's [V4 parser](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/a905fa19e3a91c7b4ead331e2709e6dec5db12cb/zebra-chain/src/transaction/serialize.rs#L874-L910) instead rejected the same encoding with `BadTransactionBalance`.

#### Practical impact and trigger conditions

The advisory documents how this parser disagreement can reach block validation:

1. A miner or custom raw block producer embeds the malformed transaction bytes directly into a block.
2. The block's Merkle root uses the normalized transaction ID that zcashd derives after parsing.
3. zcashd can accept the raw block after normalization, while Zebra rejects those same bytes during deserialization.

The ordinary zcashd transaction relay, mempool, and mining path normalizes the encoding before block production. Submitting the malformed transaction to a stock node's mempool alone therefore does not preserve the divergent trigger. Subsequent zcashd block relay can also reserialize the block in canonical form. These conditions limit the issue's practical reach, as explained in the [advisory's impact analysis](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/security/advisories/GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v).

#### Remediation and completed outcome

The [zcashd v6.12.2 security release](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/releases/tag/v6.12.2), published May 6, 2026, describes this issue and its fix: malformed empty-Sapling encodings with a non-zero balance are now rejected during deserialization, matching Zebra's behavior. The advisory lists versions below v6.12.2 as affected and v6.12.2 as patched.

The completed contribution is the accepted disclosure of this mismatch, with publicly documented reproduction steps, practical constraints, reporter attribution, and remediation.

#### The question for coinholders

As discussed in [application #74](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/74), I see this round as a useful opportunity to consider **what criteria should guide rewards for researchers' contributions to Zcash's security**.

This Medium finding gives that discussion another concrete case. It concerns agreement between node implementations, while its practical trigger is constrained by normalization in the ordinary relay and mining path. Both aspects matter when assessing its value.

- **Severity ratings:** How much weight should the affected project's published severity carry in deciding whether to reward a finding and setting the amount? Should it serve as the main basis for a reward schedule?
- **Practical impact:** How should coinholders weigh realistic exploitation conditions, required attacker capabilities, the scope of exposure, and the potential harm alongside that rating?

I would welcome coinholders' views on how to balance these considerations, whether through severity-based reference amounts, case-by-case assessments, or a combination of the two. This application puts one Medium finding and a specific requested amount before coinholders to help make that discussion concrete.

#### Basis for the requested amount

The former [ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545) included zcashd in the **Core Node** category and published a **$37,500 base payout for Core Node / Medium** findings.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

I used **LLM-assisted differential code review** to map equivalent V4 Sapling transaction parsing and validation paths in zcashd and Zebra. I then traced how each implementation handled a non-zero serialized Sapling balance when both Sapling action vectors were empty, including how normalization affected later validation, transaction IDs, and reserialization.

I validated the parsing mismatch and examined the relay, mempool, and mining paths to determine the conditions needed to preserve the malformed bytes through block validation. The [published advisory](https://github.com/zcash/zcash/security/advisories/GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v) records the code revisions and reproduction steps used in that analysis.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Completed by May 2026. The remediation release, zcashd v6.12.2, was published on May 6, 2026; the advisory was published on May 8, 2026.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This is an outcome-based retroactive award request. No salary, software, hosting, contractor, or other expenses are submitted for reimbursement, so the total expense budget is $0.

### Previous Funding

Yes

### Previous Funding Details

I received **$425,000** through the Q3 2026 Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program for [Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities, application #58](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58). That application covered five other advisories and did not include GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v.

I have also submitted a separate [High severity application, #74](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/74), requesting **$75,000** for GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf. The present request covers only GHSA-3jg6-49c6-q99v. The two applications raise the same questions about reward criteria and concern separate findings.

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

_No response_

### Success Metrics

- One completed disclosure with sangsoo-osec credited as the reporter and a published Medium severity classification.

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@sangsoo-osec

### Organization or Individual Name

sangsoo-osec

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual for my own security research contribution.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through the Zcash Community Forum. I previously received a coinholder-approved retroactive grant in the Q3 2026 round.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

75000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting $75,000 for my initial report of CVE-2026-40880, a completed and publicly documented High severity Zebra vulnerability disclosure. Following Q3's recognition of critical vulnerability research, this application also invites coinholders to discuss whether High, Medium, and Low severity findings merit retroactive rewards and how those contributions should be valued.

### Project Description


#### Thank you to coinholders and the community

First, I would like to thank the Zcash coinholders who approved my Q3 proposal, and everyone in the community who reviewed, discussed, and supported it. I appreciate the recognition of my work and the broader message that responsibly disclosed security findings can receive meaningful support from the people whose network they help protect.

The Q3 round approved several applications recognizing critical vulnerability research:

- [sangsoo-osec — Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities, application #58](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58) — **96.33% Accept**.
- [robustfengbin — Zebra Critical Vulnerability Bug Bounty (CVE-2026-34202), application #54](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/54) — **68.98% Accept**.
- [Alex Sol — Temporary Detectable Unlimited Mint and Sell Exploit, application #57](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/57) — **98.66% Accept**.
- [Taylor Hornby — Orchard Counterfeiting Vulnerability Bug Bounty, application #51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51) — **99.99% Accept**.

These acceptance rates are ZEC-weighted, exclude Abstain, and are rounded to two decimal places. They are calculated as Accept / (Accept + Reject + Reject at a lower amount), using the [finalized Q3 tally hosted by the Zcash Foundation](https://zvote.zfnd.org/shielded-vote/v1/vote-summary/2cba66eb16c7581a1692cb0b033785da0131059f645a0d2fb4dc2a5131505e01).

These applications are listed as funded in the [official Q3 results](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/q3-coinholder-directed-retroactive-grants-program-results/57909). Their approval provided an encouraging signal for security researchers, including those continuing to examine Zcash in the hope that useful discoveries will receive retroactive recognition.

#### The completed contribution

This application covers my initial lock-time report for **CVE-2026-40880 / GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf**, a **High severity** consensus vulnerability involving Zebra's reuse of mempool verification results during block validation.

Zebra used an optimization to avoid repeating transaction verification when the same transaction was already verified in its mempool. In the [pre-fix verifier](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/v4.3.0/zebra-consensus/src/transaction.rs#L404), a cache hit could return a successful block-verification result before reaching the block-specific checks, including lock-time validation. A result obtained in the mempool's context could therefore bypass checks required for the block containing the transaction.

The [public advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf) illustrates the broader failure with an expiry-height example:

1. At chain tip height `H`, a transaction valid for `H+1` enters a target node's mempool.
2. A malicious miner includes it in a block at `H+2`, where it has expired, and sends that block before its parent at `H+1`.
3. Zebra reuses the cached result for the ahead-of-tip block; once the parent arrives, it can commit both blocks. Other nodes reject the expired transaction, creating a consensus split.

This scenario requires a malicious miner and a target with the relevant cached transaction. The advisory identifies network partitioning, service disruption, and potential double-spend attacks as consequences.

The advisory credits my thorough initial submission identifying the lock-time issue. It also acknowledges shieldedonly's subsequent report, received while the team was already working on mine, which identified further implications for transaction validation.

The maintainers removed the optimization. The patched versions are `zebrad` **4.3.1** and `zebra-consensus` **5.0.2**, with the fix shipped in the [Zebra 4.3.1 security release](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.1).

#### Recent security findings in Zebra

The following releases, published from **August 1 through November 2, 2026**, document a continuing flow of vulnerability findings in Zebra:

| GHSA-designated patched release | Tag published (UTC) | Critical | High | Medium | Low | Unique GHSAs |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [v6.3.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.3.0) | 2026-08-10 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 0 | 4 |
| [v6.4.2](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.4.2) | 2026-09-25 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| [v7.0.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v7.0.0) | 2026-10-22 | 0 | 5 | 2 | 0 | 7 |
| **Total** | | **0** | **7** | **7** | **1** | **15** |

These releases show that vulnerabilities continue to be found and fixed in Zebra. This suggests that security researchers may still be hunting for bugs and preparing further disclosures. It would be useful to clarify how coinholders want to recognize such contributions.

#### The question for coinholders

I see this round as a good opportunity for coinholders to discuss **what criteria should guide rewards for researchers' contributions to Zcash's security**. Following Q3's recognition of critical vulnerability research, there are several questions worth considering:

- **Severity ratings:** How much weight should the severity assigned by the Zebra team carry in deciding whether to reward a finding and setting the amount? Should it serve as the main basis for a reward schedule?
- **Practical impact:** How should coinholders weigh the case-specific risk alongside that rating, including realistic exploitation conditions, required attacker capabilities, the number of nodes or users exposed, and the potential harm?

I would welcome coinholders' views on how to balance these considerations, whether through severity-based reference amounts, case-by-case assessments, or a combination of the two. Discussing completed, publicly verifiable contributions in this round gives the community a practical opportunity to work through those choices.

This application puts one High severity finding and a specific requested amount before coinholders as a concrete case for that discussion. Feedback on the criteria behind a decision would help researchers understand how their contributions are valued and what they may reasonably expect from future rounds.


#### Basis for the requested amount

The former [ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545) published a **$75,000 base payout for Core Node / High** findings and included Zebra in the Core Node category. 

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

I used LLM-assisted code review to navigate Zebra's transaction verification logic and develop focused hypotheses about the interaction between cached mempool verification and height-dependent consensus checks. I then traced the relevant code paths, validated the lock-time issue credited in the advisory, and reported it privately to the Zcash Foundation.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Completed by April 2026. The advisory was published on April 17, 2026, with Zebra 4.3.1 identified as the patched release.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This is an outcome-based retroactive award request. No salary, software, hosting, contractor, or other expenses are submitted for reimbursement, so the total expense budget is $0.

### Previous Funding

Yes

### Previous Funding Details

I received **$425,000** through the Q3 2026 Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program for [Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities, application #58](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58).

That application covered five other advisories. GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf was not included in that request. I thank coinholders and the community for their support of that completed work.

### Other Funding Sources

No

_No response_

### Success Metrics

- One accepted, published High severity vulnerability report with explicit credit for my initial lock-time finding.
- A completed remediation documented in the [official advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf).
- Public release evidence in [Zebra 4.3.1](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.1).


### Proof of completion

- [Zebra 4.3.1 release](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.1) — public remediation release.

The following repository-wide inventory supports the background table; the award requested here covers only CVE-2026-40880.

In Nov 2023, to create a sustainable scholarship engine, we secured donors to build a small crypto mining farm. We began phasing to Zcash exclusively, currently operating 7x Z15 + 2x Z15 Pro units while testing LuxOS efficiency for scale. Facility built: 480V service, 200ft 600kcmil copper, 3x 167kVA cans, 500kVA step-down, 120 outlets, 6 breaker boxes, 36" fan, scissor lift. All permitted via CenterPoint Energy. Capacity: 500kVA = 400kW continuous @ 80% derate. 100x Z15 Pro @ +2 3035W = 303.5kW = 76% capacity. Monitoring: LuxOS API (2 units only, since Oct 2026) + ViaBTC dashboard + Fluke power meter for 2 Pro units + miningpoolstats for network data ### Time Period of Work Completion Q4 2023 to Q2 2025 ### Total Budget (USD) $978,600.00 ### Budget Breakdown **A. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

[@shieldedonly](https://github.com/shieldedonly)

## Applicant & Organization

### Organization or Individual Name

shieldedonly (security researcher)
