### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through the [Q4 2026 call for proposals on the Zcash Community Forum](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/q4-coinholder-directed-retroactive-grant-program-call-for-proposals/58598).

## Project Overview

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$150,000 USD

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I'm applying for a $150,000 retroactive grant for discovering and responsibly disclosing CVE-2026-44499, a Critical Zebra vulnerability that allowed a single unauthenticated peer connection to permanently halt a targeted node's block discovery. I privately reported it on April 14, 2026; the maintainers fixed it in Zebra 4.4.0 and published the advisory on May 5.

### Project Description

#### Completed contribution

Zebra is a Rust implementation of a Zcash full node. This application covers my discovery, validation, and private disclosure of a vulnerability in its peer-to-peer block discovery pipeline. The completed research produced a working proof of concept (PoC) and a report, and I submitted the finding on April 14, 2026. The Zebra maintainers implemented and released the remediation.

The requested grant recognizes this completed security finding and disclosure. The supporting research method is described under Technical Approach.

#### Researcher background

I publish as [@shieldedonly on the Zcash Community Forum](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/u/shieldedonly). The Foundation publicly acknowledges my contributions to two other Zebra findings:

- [GHSA-29x4-r6jv-ff4w](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-29x4-r6jv-ff4w): credits me for discovering and reporting an RPC denial-of-service issue.
- [GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf / CVE-2026-40880](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-xvj8-ph7x-65gf): acknowledges my additional advisory, submitted while the team was working on an earlier report, which showed that the issue affected transaction validation beyond the initially reported lock-time case.

These contributions establish research background. This application requests recognition only for CVE-2026-44499.

#### Publicly documented vulnerability

| Item | Public record |
| --- | --- |
| Software | Zebra (`zebrad`) |
| Identifier | CVE-2026-44499 / GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9 |
| Severity | Critical, as classified by the Zebra advisory |
| Affected versions | Earlier than 4.4.0 |
| Fixed version | 4.4.0 |
| Exposure | Remote, unauthenticated peer connection |
| Outcome | Persistent loss of new-block discovery on the targeted node |

The [Zebra security advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9) classifies the issue as **Critical**, citing an attack that requires no authentication, no special privileges, and only one peer connection. Its assessment states:

> The halt is permanent: the node will never recover without operator intervention.

This persistent loss of a core node function is the security impact underlying the request.

#### How the discovery failure developed

Zebra learns about new blocks through peer announcements and periodic synchronization requests. A peer's `inv` announcement identifies a block to download and verify. The syncer separately asks peers for missing block hashes or headers using `FindBlocks` and `FindHeaders`. These complementary mechanisms allow the node to discover the advancing chain.

The vulnerability combined pressure on the announcement-driven download queue with unhelpful responses on the synchronization path. One malicious connection could consume shared gossip-download capacity while keeping the fallback from making useful progress. Honest peers' new-block announcements could then be dropped at the full queue. Technical Approach explains the mechanisms and corresponding source changes.

#### Why the result matters

A node must keep discovering blocks to maintain a current view of the chain. A sustained discovery halt disrupts that function and can affect services relying on the node for current chain data. The research identified a combined failure across cooperating subsystems and gave maintainers a reproducible finding to address through a security release.

#### Disclosure and publication timeline

| Date | Event | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| April 14, 2026 | Private vulnerability submission | Original report `GHSA-28xj-328h-72vm`; the Zcash Foundation/Zebra team can verify the submission. |
| April 15, 2026 | Private report accepted | Acceptance of original report `GHSA-28xj-328h-72vm`; the Zcash Foundation/Zebra team can verify the acceptance date. |
| April 28, 2026 | ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative announced | [Official announcement](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545/1) |
| May 1, 2026 | Block-discovery hardening committed upstream | [Commit 602c8b7](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8), 17:15:21 UTC |
| May 1, 2026 | Zebra 4.4.0 published on GitHub | [Release metadata](https://api.github.com/repos/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tags/v4.4.0), publication timestamp 21:59:05 UTC |
| May 2, 2026 | Zcash Foundation forum announcement of Zebra 4.4.0 | [Release announcement](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zebra-4-4-0-critical-security-fixes/55576) |
| May 5, 2026 | Current GitHub advisory published | [GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9) |
| May 8, 2026 | CVE record published | [CVE metadata](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-44499) |

#### Why apply for a retroactive grant

My April 14 report preceded the April 28 initiative announcement by fourteen days. In its [May 8 clarification](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545/15), ZCG stated that its initiative covered reports submitted after the announcement and did not apply retroactively.

I am asking coinholders to recognize this completed contribution through the Q4 Coinholder-Directed Retroactive Grants Program. The [Q4 call](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/q4-coinholder-directed-retroactive-grant-program-call-for-proposals/58598) provides a route for completed, publicly verifiable work such as this finding and its documented remediation.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

#### How I found it

I built and used a custom AI-assisted vulnerability research tool, organizing the investigation into focused lanes such as consensus and denial of service. The workflow conducted research and validation and generated a working PoC and report. I ran it against a Zebra version that predated the fix.

The finding connected weaknesses in gossip announcements, syncer responses, and block downloads into one persistent availability failure. That interaction matters because the syncer is expected to discover blocks missed through gossip; the reported behavior degraded that recovery path as well as normal announcements.

#### Validation and research outputs

The published security advisory, upstream fix, and Zebra 4.4.0 release document the vulnerability and its remediation. The Zcash Foundation/Zebra team can verify my original private submission and my role as its submitter, using the report reference under Proof of completion.

#### Technical analysis of the vulnerability

The [public advisory](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9) identifies a composite failure involving the gossip, syncer, and download subsystems. The source references below are pinned to the immediate parent of the fix, `85303ea98ee3fce4f9190b6f05ce3f162f8b5ffd`. These references let reviewers inspect the queue limit, caller behavior, and response handling in the implementation immediately before remediation.

##### 1. A shared gossip queue could be monopolized

Incoming block announcements are translated into `AdvertiseBlock` requests and handed to `Downloads::download_and_verify`. That function manages a shared set of pending block downloads and verification tasks. Before the fix, it deduplicated already-queued hashes and enforced a total concurrency limit, but did not allocate capacity by advertising peer or IP. The advisory also identifies the absence of a per-connection rate limit on incoming `inv` messages.

The pre-patch implementation capped the configured concurrency at **30**, with the effective limit depending on configuration. That global bound did not reserve capacity for other peers. Sequential announcements of distinct fabricated hashes could occupy the same slots needed for legitimate new blocks. The advisory reports that the queue could be filled in under a millisecond; that timing comes from the advisory rather than a separate benchmark claimed here. [Pre-patch download manager](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/85303ea98ee3fce4f9190b6f05ce3f162f8b5ffd/zebrad/src/components/inbound/downloads.rs).

##### 2. Queue exhaustion did not trigger recovery at the caller

When the queue reached its limit, `download_and_verify` returned `DownloadAction::FullQueue`. The `AdvertiseBlock` branch in the inbound service called the function without handling that return value, then returned a normal `Nil` response. The download manager's own documentation expected the sync service to discover a skipped block later.

An honest block announcement could therefore be discarded at the capacity boundary, while recovery depended on the syncer. The download manager logged the drop at debug level and incremented a metric, but the inbound caller took no recovery action in response to `FullQueue`. [Pre-patch inbound handler](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/85303ea98ee3fce4f9190b6f05ce3f162f8b5ffd/zebrad/src/components/inbound.rs).

##### 3. The alternative discovery path could also be made unproductive

The syncer periodically queried peers for missing blocks. The reported malicious peer answered `FindBlocks` with empty `inv` responses and block-download requests with `NotFound`. These replies supplied neither useful discovery information nor the requested block bodies, while remaining valid protocol responses that did not incur a misbehavior penalty.

The connection state machine's `FindBlocks` response handler accepted a block-inventory list and converted it to `Response::BlockHashes`; an empty list could satisfy that handler and complete the request without contributing any hashes. This helps explain why a successful protocol exchange did not necessarily mean synchronization progress. [Pre-patch connection handling](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/85303ea98ee3fce4f9190b6f05ce3f162f8b5ffd/zebra-network/src/peer/connection.rs).

As documented in the advisory, `NotFound` denied the requested block without causing the malicious connection to be removed. The peer could continue applying announcement pressure and supplying unproductive discovery responses as individual download attempts completed or failed.

##### 4. The interaction defeated recovery

| Node function | Expected progress | Behavior under the reported attack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gossip announcements | Queue newly announced blocks for download and verification. | Fabricated announcements consume capacity; honest announcements can encounter `FullQueue`. |
| Syncer discovery | Find blocks missed through gossip. | Empty responses provide no new hashes while retaining the unhelpful peer. |
| Block retrieval | Obtain the block bodies needed to advance. | Negative responses deny useful data without removing the malicious connection. |

The combined result was suppression of both discovery paths through one TCP peer connection using multiple announcements and responses. As the external chain advanced, the target's block deficit could keep increasing. The advisory characterizes the halt as permanent without operator intervention.

#### Responsible disclosure

I privately submitted the finding on April 14, 2026, fourteen days before the ZCG initiative was announced. The private report was accepted on April 15, 2026. The advisory became public on May 5. My original private report is identified under Proof of completion; the Zcash Foundation/Zebra team can verify my submission, its acceptance date, and its connection to the published advisory.

#### Remediation outcome

The corresponding implementation is visible in [commit `602c8b7`](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8), committed May 1, 2026. It addresses both discovery paths:

| Component | Implemented change | Source at the fix commit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gossip downloads | Track the advertising peer's IP and permit one in-flight inbound block download per advertising IP, preventing one advertiser from occupying the whole queue. | [Inbound download accounting](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8/zebrad/src/components/inbound/downloads.rs) |
| Syncer peer handling | Classify empty or failed `FindBlocks` / `FindHeaders` responses and disconnect a peer after three consecutive stalls; useful responses reset its counter. | [Peer-set routing](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8/zebra-network/src/peer_set/set.rs) and [stall tracker](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8/zebra-network/src/peer_set/stall_tracker.rs) |
| Tracker tests | Cover the disconnect threshold, reset behavior, and independent counters for different peers. | [Unit tests](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8/zebra-network/src/peer_set/stall_tracker/tests.rs) |

These protections address capacity allocation and discovery progress separately. The advertising-IP limit prevents one source from taking all gossip-download slots. Stall tracking removes persistently unhelpful discovery peers and frees their connections without requiring a misbehavior ban.

The [comparison with v4.4.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/compare/602c8b745c09133a8e8a956fc2ef7abd88b95fe8...v4.4.0) confirms that the fix commit is included in the release, whose [notes](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.4.0) describe the stalled-peer remedy. The linked unit tests cover tracker behavior; the public advisory documents the overall attack and impact.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Q2 2026 - completed by April 14, 2026 (research, PoC, report, and private disclosure).

## Budget & Funding

### Total Budget (USD)

$0 in costs claimed for reimbursement.

No expenses are claimed for reimbursement. The $150,000 grant request recognizes the completed security outcome separately from the costs of producing it.

#### Requested award and valuation

**Requested grant: $150,000 USD**, recognizing the completed finding, validation, PoC, report, and responsible disclosure.

The amount uses a published ecosystem reference: the former [ZCG initiative's payout table](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/zcash/original/3X/2/8/285725957e26a2dc3339b9cfbc4b0ea00f301a93.png) listed a $150,000 base for a Core Node / Critical finding, and its [announcement](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545/1) included Zebra in Core Node. The request uses that base as a valuation reference and includes no discretionary bonus.

##### Basis for the Critical valuation

The [Zebra team's published assessment](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9) explicitly classifies this vulnerability as **Critical**. Its stated rationale combines remote unauthenticated access, no special privileges, a single peer connection, and a permanent block-discovery halt requiring operator intervention. The attack suppressed both normal block announcements and the syncer fallback, preventing the targeted node from recovering through its alternative discovery path. This persistent loss of a core full-node function is the documented impact underlying my request.

The [GitHub Advisory Database](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9) separately lists a **CVSS v4.0 score of 8.7 (High)**, while retaining the description's Critical assessment. My request follows the Zebra team's explicit Critical classification in its repository advisory.

The [historical ZCG framework](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545/1) assigns severity assessment to remediation teams and technical reviewers and describes its examples as non-exhaustive. On that basis, I ask coinholders to recognize this completed contribution at the **$150,000 Core Node / Critical base**, consistent with the remediation team's published assessment and the funded Q3 Zebra availability precedent below. This is the valuation I am requesting for the completed finding and responsible disclosure.

##### Funded Q3 security-research precedents

The [official Q3 2026 results](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/q3-coinholder-directed-retroactive-grants-program-results/57909) list the following five security-related grant proposals as **Funded**. Administrator comments dated October 16, 2026 also record disbursement of the amounts below:

| Funded application | Completed contribution | Retroactive award | Payment record |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| [#54 - Zebra Critical Vulnerability Bug Bounty](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/54) | CVE-2026-34202: Critical remote denial of service in Zebra; the report predated the bounty initiative. | $150,000 | [Disbursement confirmation](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/54#issuecomment-6226295861) |
| [#58 - Five Critical Zebra Consensus Divergence Vulnerabilities](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58) | Five accepted findings; four reports predated the initiative and the fifth followed its closure. | $425,000 net, after deducting a disclosed $100,000 prior payment | [Disbursement confirmation](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/58#issuecomment-6226306005) |
| [#57 - Temporary Detectable Unlimited Mint and Sell Exploit](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/57) | Multiple disclosed vulnerabilities across `zcashd` and Zebra, presented as a combined counterfeiting attack chain. | $400,000 | [Disbursement confirmation](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/57#issuecomment-6226268840) |
| [#51 - Orchard Counterfeiting Vulnerability Bug Bounty](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51) | Orchard circuit vulnerability allowing unlimited, undetectable creation of counterfeit ZEC; discovered and responsibly disclosed by Taylor Hornby, then remediated. | $750,000 | [Disbursement confirmation](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51#issuecomment-6226331319) |
| [#53 - Bonus Grant for Orchard Counterfeiting Vulnerability Bug Bounty](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/53) | Additional award to Taylor Hornby for the same Orchard discovery covered by #51, nominated by Jason McGee. | $750,000 additional | [Disbursement confirmation](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/53#issuecomment-6226342940) |

The Orchard bounty (#51) and bonus (#53) are separate awards for the same discovery, totaling **$1,500,000** to Taylor Hornby.

These five selected awards total **$2,475,000** and demonstrate that coinholders have already used the retroactive program to recognize completed security findings. The closest reference for this request is #54: a Critical Zebra availability finding reported before the bounty initiative, funded at $150,000.

My request follows that same basis: a completed Critical Zebra finding, privately reported before the initiative opened, subsequently documented and fixed. The Q3 decisions provide a concrete precedent for recognizing this contribution at the requested $150,000 level.

No

### Other Funding Sources

These are completed outputs: research artifacts, a private report, a public advisory, and a released mitigation. The source and release links below document the maintainers' work; the original private submission provides the record through which the team can verify my attribution.

- [CVE-2026-44499](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-44499): vulnerability identifier; [machine-readable record](https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-44499) includes publication metadata.

- **Submitter verification:** I am not publicly named in the published advisory's credits. The Zcash Foundation/Zebra team can verify from the original private report that I was its submitter and that it is the report underlying [GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9 / CVE-2026-44499](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-h9hm-m2xj-4rq9).

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

We received a grant in the Q1 2026 round (issue #19).

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$50,000

### Category

Integration

### Project Summary

Maya Protocol runs live cross-chain swaps with transparent and shielded ZEC. This application covers completed work since our Q1 2026 grant: two upstream contributions to librustzcash and Zebra, NU6.2 and NU6.3 (Ironwood) support on Maya mainnet, the move from zcashd to stock Zebra, and hardening of ZEC threshold signing, reorg recovery and shielded scanning.

### Project Description

Our Q1 2026 grant (issue #19) funded shielded ZEC support on Maya, with work completed through February 2026. Since then we kept Maya current with every Zcash network upgrade and put back into upstream the tooling we needed.

This application covers only completed work that is live on Maya mainnet or merged upstream:

1. Upstream public goods. Two pull requests by our team, reviewed and merged by the librustzcash and Zebra maintainers. They were not claimed in issue #19.
2. Network upgrade support. Maya mainnet followed NU6.2 and NU6.3 (Ironwood) on schedule, so ZEC swaps kept working through both upgrades.
3. Zebra migration. With our Zebra pull request merged upstream, Maya moved its nodes to stock Zebra v4.3.1 and retired its own Zebra fork.
4. Fee and upgrade-transition fixes needed to run ZEC reliably on mainnet.
5. Signing and recovery hardening. ZEC on Maya is signed by validators using threshold signatures (TSS), so every validator has to build the same transaction from its own view of the ZEC chain. Validators now sign from a shared historical height with fixed parameters, recover expired transactions instead of retrying them forever, walk back to the common ancestor after a reorg, and broadcast only transactions they have persisted. Shielded memo scans retry without losing deposits, and deposits whose sender UTXO is bare multisig are rejected so they cannot be credited to the wrong sender.

Work from the independent security audit of our Zcash integration, which was funded separately, is excluded from this application.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Maya's Zcash support has three parts: a Rust library built on librustzcash (shielded and transparent transaction building, exposed to Go through an FFI layer), the Bifrost ZEC client that observes and signs ZEC transactions with Maya's threshold signing (TSS), and Zebra as the full node.

Upstream:
- librustzcash#1786 adds OP_RETURN outputs and external signature support to the transparent builder. This lets a threshold-signing system like Maya's build a ZEC transaction, sign it outside the library and apply the signatures, using the standard builder.
- Zebra#10224 adds mempool standardness checks matching zcashd (scriptSig size, push-only, standard script types, bare multisig and dust rejection) and a configurable OP_RETURN policy. Together these let Zebra replace zcashd for applications that use OP_RETURN memos.

Maya mainnet:
- NU6.2: moved the ZEC client to the NU6.2 library stack, including the Orchard circuit soundness fix (mayanode v1.131.0).
- NU6.3 Ironwood: zcash_protocol 0.10.0, ZIP 2006 unified address normalization, height-aware consensus branch id selection, rejection of Orchard-only unified addresses where unsupported, Zebra regtest bump (v1.131.0). A follow-up observes Ironwood inbound transactions and corrects the shielded fee sign (v1.132.2).
- Zebra v4.3.1: replaced the Maya Zebra fork with the official release once our upstream change shipped (v1.129.3), plus updated ZEC TypeScript client bindings (v1.129.0).
- ZIP 317: corrected max-gas and fee calculation for ZEC outbounds (v1.131.0).
- Network upgrade transition: a store migration that reschedules ZEC outbounds left stale by the hard-fork chain split, so no user funds were stuck (v1.131.0).
- Signing, expiry and reorg recovery (mayanode !856, v1.135.0): signing attempts are pinned to a shared historical ZEC height and keep their original parameters across retries, so validators build identical signing candidates. Definitive expiry is an explicit terminal outcome followed by recovery, and lifecycle coverage extends to Maya's transparent and shielded transactions.
- Reorg recovery, input selection and broadcast safety (mayanode !717, v1.133.0): Bifrost walks back to the common ancestor within the configured reorg window, keeps confirmed, pending and unknown status distinct so transient RPC failures are not treated as reorg evidence, narrows input-selection differences between validators, and requires a signed transaction to be persisted before it is broadcast.
- Shielded memo scan retry (v1.135.0): a shielded memo scan that hits its trial-decryption limit retries the same height, and completed trials are persisted so each retry spends its budget on new transactions. Deposits are not skipped and per-block work stays bounded.
- Sender validation (v1.135.0, BTC/DASH/ZEC; ZEC share claimed): a sender UTXO must be single-sig. A bare multisig sender UTXO is rejected, because an RPC node may report it as several addresses and the deposit could be attributed to the wrong one.
- Signing-height seed at activation (mayanode !877, v1.135.0): the v1.135.0 store migration seeds the ZEC signing height correctly on a cache-wrapped store, so an outbound scheduled right after activation is not signed against a stale height.
- Zebra duplicate broadcasts (mayanode !712, v1.128.0): Zebra's "already in mempool" and "committed to the best chain" responses are accepted as non-fatal, which stopped a retry loop after the move from zcashd.
- UTXO solvency and amount handling (mayanode !724, !772, v1.131.0; !698, v1.135.0; ZEC share claimed): simplified UTXO selection for the ZEC signer, native-amount checks on ZEC outputs, and one solvency reporter for all chains including ZEC.
- Maintenance (mayanode !790, !809; ZEC portion claimed): mainnet hotfixes ported back to the development branch, and an unused ZEC mempool wrapper removed.

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml

```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Zcash Community Forum (Retroactive Grants category) and earlier retroactive applications for Zebra vulnerability disclosures.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$75,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I found and privately reported a High-severity denial-of-service in Zebra (GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq): any connected peer could stall a node's verification with one crafted, unsigned transaction, at no cost and without being banned. The Zcash Foundation confirmed it, fixed it in zebrad 7.0.0, and published the advisory crediting me as the reporter.

### Project Description

Zebra's mempool checks coinbase maturity once for every input a transaction spends. After the transaction newtype refactor in zebrad 6.4.0 (PR #10461), each of those checks rebuilt and cloned the transaction's whole output list, so verifying one transaction cost inputs × outputs. A transaction with about 24,000 inputs and 111,000 outputs (around 1.98 MB) took roughly 19 seconds of CPU on a 4-core machine.

The transaction needs no valid signatures and no funds. It spends existing unspent outputs with empty scriptSigs, and the maturity check runs before the standardness check that finally rejects it. That rejection carries a misbehavior score of 0, so the peer is never banned and can send it again, changing one byte to get past the reject cache. One connection can queue five of these at once, which on a 4–5 core node occupies the whole async runtime. Block verification, peer handling and sync stop while the attack runs, and the node recovers when it stops. No consensus rule or funds were at risk; this was a liveness problem.

Every node on zebrad 6.4.0, 6.4.1 and 6.4.2 (the mainnet releases at the time) and 7.0.0-rc.0 was affected in its default configuration, with no workaround.

I reported it privately through a GitHub security advisory with a working reproduction, kept the details private until the fix shipped and operators were notified, and offered to re-test the patch. The Zebra maintainers accepted the report, shipped the fix in zebrad 7.0.0 and published the advisory on 22 October 2026.

I'm applying here because there is no other way to be paid for this work. The Zcash Foundation does not pay for security reports outside a program, and ZCG's Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative closed on 26 May 2026, before this report. ZCG asked researchers to keep reporting through private channels after the closure, and the Foundation has said the published advisory is the public record of the finding that anyone can cite.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

- Reviewed the zcash_primitives transaction newtype refactor (commit 8b91154, PR #10461) and found that Transaction::outputs() went from returning a borrowed slice to allocating a new Vec and copying every output script on each call.
- Traced the callers. coinbase_spend_restriction() always evaluates outputs() (it's the left operand of an ||), and tx_transparent_coinbase_spends_maturity() calls it inside the per-input loop even though the result only depends on the transaction, network and height.
- Confirmed reachability from the P2P path. In MempoolTxVerifier the maturity check runs after the UTXO lookups and before mempool_standard_input_scripts, so a transaction with empty scriptSigs pays the full cost and is then rejected as NonStandardInputs, which maps to misbehavior score 0. The work is synchronous inside the verification task, so the 73-second download timeout can't interrupt it.
- Wrote a Rust test that builds the transaction as real wire bytes and drives the production MempoolTxVerifier with a mock state service. Tested against v6.4.2 (e3eef2f) and main (a0c1f51).
- Used a scaling control to show the cost follows inputs × outputs rather than size. 4,000 × 40,000 took about 1.0 s; 24,000 × 111,000 took about 19 s (roughly 4× the inputs and 2.75× the outputs gave about 17× the time).
- Checked it against shipped advisories: it is not GHSA-4g24-549m-hp75 and not the #11353 fix.
- Proposed the fix: a non-allocating "has transparent outputs" check and hoisting the loop-invariant restriction out of the loop. I also flagged the same per-spend call on the block-commit path.

### Time Period of Work Completion

October 2026 (research and private report filed on 10 October 2026; coordinated disclosure through advisory publication and the zebrad 7.0.0 release on 22 October 2026)

### Total Budget (USD)

$75,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 75,000
  - Justification: Bounty-equivalent compensation for completed security research and coordinated disclosure. This is ZCG's own published base payout for a High-severity Core Node finding ($75,000). Zebra is a Core Node project under that table, and the Zcash Foundation rated this finding High (CVSS 7.5). The table also allowed a discretionary bonus of up to $37,500, which I am not requesting.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: Own hardware and open-source tools.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Total $(USD): 75,000

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

N/A

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

I have not received, and don't expect, payment from any other source for this finding. The Zcash Foundation does not pay for reports outside a program, and ZCG's vulnerability bounty closed on 26 May 2026, before this report.

### Success Metrics

- The vulnerability was fixed before public disclosure: zebrad 7.0.0 (commit 08743d6), with the advisory and upgrade guidance published on 22 October 2026.
- The vulnerable check went from O(inputs × outputs) to O(inputs) per transaction. Before the fix, one ~1.98 MB transaction cost about 19 seconds of CPU on a 4-core machine.
- It protects every node that was on the 6.4.x line or 7.0.0-rc.0, which in default configuration had no workaround.
- The same fix also covered the per-spend pattern on the block-commit path, which my report flagged, and the per-signature SIGHASH_SINGLE check in zebra-script.
- It removed a free, unauthenticated and repeatable way for a single peer to stop a node from following the chain.

### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [Fix commit 08743d6](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/08743d6) - non-allocating transparent input/output checks; coinbase spend restriction computed once per transaction in the mempool and block-commit paths
  - [PR #10461](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10461) - the refactor that introduced the regression in 6.4.0
- Publication:
  - [GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq) - published by the Zcash Foundation on 22 Oct 2026, High (CVSS 3.1 7.5), reporter credit @janneh2000: "Thanks to @janneh2000 for reporting this with a reproduction against the production mempool verifier."
  - CVE: not yet assigned (requested from the Zcash Foundation)
- Deployment/Release:
  - [Zebra v7.0.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v7.0.0) - Security section: "Fixed a quadratic CPU cost in transaction verification"
- Other Evidence:
  - The original report and the reproduction test are in the advisory's private thread; the Zebra maintainers (ZFND Security) can confirm.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

None. I'm an independent security researcher. I'm not employed by or affiliated with the Zcash Foundation, ZCG, FPF, ZODL, Shielded Labs or any keyholder organization. I also co-founded a DeFi security startup, which has no relationship with any Zcash organization or with this grant.

That rejection carries a misbehavior score of 0, so the peer is never banned and can send it again, changing one byte to get past the reject cache. One connection can queue five of these at once, which on a 4–5 core node occupies the whole async runtime. Block verification, peer handling and sync stop while the attack runs, and the node recovers when it stops. No consensus rule or funds were at risk; this was a liveness problem.

Every node on zebrad 6.4.0, 6.4.1 and 6.4.2 (the mainnet releases at the time) and 7.0.0-rc.0 was affected in its default configuration, with no workaround.

I reported it privately through a GitHub security advisory with a working reproduction, kept the details private until the fix shipped and operators were notified, and offered to re-test the patch. The Zebra maintainers accepted the report, shipped the fix in zebrad 7.0.0 and published the advisory on 22 October 2026.

I'm applying here because there is no other way to be paid for this work. The Zcash Foundation does not pay for security reports outside a program, and ZCG's Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative closed on 26 May 2026, before this report. ZCG asked researchers to keep reporting through private channels after the closure, and the Foundation has said the published advisory is the public record of the finding that anyone can cite.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

- Reviewed the zcash_primitives transaction newtype refactor (commit 8b91154, PR #10461) and found that Transaction::outputs() went from returning a borrowed slice to allocating a new Vec and copying every output script on each call.
- Traced the callers. coinbase_spend_restriction() always evaluates outputs() (it's the left operand of an ||), and tx_transparent_coinbase_spends_maturity() calls it inside the per-input loop even though the result only depends on the transaction, network and height.
- Confirmed reachability from the P2P path. In MempoolTxVerifier the maturity check runs after the UTXO lookups and before mempool_standard_input_scripts, so a transaction with empty scriptSigs pays the full cost and is then rejected as NonStandardInputs, which maps to misbehavior score 0. The work is synchronous inside the verification task, so the 73-second download timeout can't interrupt it.
- Wrote a Rust test that builds the transaction as real wire bytes and drives the production MempoolTxVerifier with a mock state service. Tested against v6.4.2 (e3eef2f) and main (a0c1f51).
- Used a scaling control to show the cost follows inputs × outputs rather than size. 4,000 × 40,000 took about 1.0 s; 24,000 × 111,000 took about 19 s (roughly 4× the inputs and 2.75× the outputs gave about 17× the time).
- Checked it against shipped advisories: it is not GHSA-4g24-549m-hp75 and not the #11353 fix.
- Proposed the fix: a non-allocating "has transparent outputs" check and hoisting the loop-invariant restriction out of the loop. I also flagged the same per-spend call on the block-commit path.

### Time Period of Work Completion

October 2026 (research and private report filed on 10 October 2026; coordinated disclosure through advisory publication and the zebrad 7.0.0 release on 22 October 2026)

### Total Budget (USD)

$75,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 75,000
  - Justification: Bounty-equivalent compensation for completed security research and coordinated disclosure. This is ZCG's own published base payout for a High-severity Core Node finding ($75,000). Zebra is a Core Node project under that table, and the Zcash Foundation rated this finding High (CVSS 7.5). The table also allowed a discretionary bonus of up to $37,500, which I am not requesting.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: Own hardware and open-source tools.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Total $(USD): 75,000

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

N/A

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

I have not received, and don't expect, payment from any other source for this finding. The Zcash Foundation does not pay for reports outside a program, and ZCG's vulnerability bounty closed on 26 May 2026, before this report.

### Success Metrics

- The vulnerability was fixed before public disclosure: zebrad 7.0.0 (commit 08743d6), with the advisory and upgrade guidance published on 22 October 2026.
- The vulnerable check went from O(inputs × outputs) to O(inputs) per transaction. Before the fix, one ~1.98 MB transaction cost about 19 seconds of CPU on a 4-core machine.
- It protects every node that was on the 6.4.x line or 7.0.0-rc.0, which in default configuration had no workaround.
- The same fix also covered the per-spend pattern on the block-commit path, which my report flagged, and the per-signature SIGHASH_SINGLE check in zebra-script.
- It removed a free, unauthenticated and repeatable way for a single peer to stop a node from following the chain.

### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [Fix commit 08743d6](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/08743d6) - non-allocating transparent input/output checks; coinbase spend restriction computed once per transaction in the mempool and block-commit paths
  - [PR #10461](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10461) - the refactor that introduced the regression in 6.4.0
- Publication:
  - [GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-7jp4-mq53-4cvq) - published by the Zcash Foundation on 22 Oct 2026, High (CVSS 3.1 7.5), reporter credit @janneh2000: "Thanks to @janneh2000 for reporting this with a reproduction against the production mempool verifier."
  - CVE: not yet assigned (requested from the Zcash Foundation)
- Deployment/Release:
  - [Zebra v7.0.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v7.0.0) - Security section: "Fixed a quadratic CPU cost in transaction verification"
- Other Evidence:
  - The original report and the reproduction test are in the advisory's private thread; the Zebra maintainers (ZFND Security) can confirm.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

None. I'm an independent security researcher. I'm not employed by or affiliated with the Zcash Foundation, ZCG, FPF, ZODL, Shielded Labs or any keyholder organization. I also co-founded a DeFi security startup, which has no relationship with any Zcash organization or with this grant.

### Community Forum Posting

I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application. Github - @chainapsis / Org - KPLR

```team-members.yaml

  Role: Quality assurance, testing, and product management
  Background: Solutions architect and primary QA testing
  Responsibilities: Desktop, mobile, Keystone, and migration QA
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Recommended by Dev Ojha

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

360000

### Category

Wallets

### Project Summary

Vizor is an Apache-2.0 self-custody Zcash wallet delivered across macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, with shielded transactions, multi-account support, transparent-fund shielding, air-gapped Keystone signing, Pay, swaps, coinholder voting, and current Zcash protocol support. Its clearest measurable impact came at Ironwood activation, when CipherScan identified Vizor as the first end-user wallet with full ZIP-318 migration compliance.

### Project Description

KPLR requests $360,000 retroactively for the complete Vizor wallet delivered from mid-March through August 7, 2026. This application does not request funding for a future roadmap. The wallet, releases, hardware-signing path, and Apache-2.0 source code are already public and available for review.

### Complete self-custody wallet

Vizor gives users a modern, non-custodial interface for Zcash. Users can create or restore a wallet, receive through Unified Addresses or transparent addresses, shield transparent funds, send shielded ZEC, attach encrypted memos, review transaction history, and manage multiple accounts without giving a hosted service control of their keys.

The wallet includes configurable lightwalletd endpoints, sync and balance states, an app password, privacy mode, transparent-address rotation, ZIP-317 fees, ZIP-320 TEX addresses, the June 3 Orchard circuit update, and signed or notarized releases. The same modified Rust core based on librustzcash supports Flutter interfaces across macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android.

### Hardware security and wallet utility

Vizor supports air-gapped Keystone accounts through animated-QR PCZT exchange. Users prepare a transaction in Vizor, authorize it on Keystone, and return the signed result without connecting the signing device by USB or network. The hardware path supports ordinary transfers, shielding, swaps, voting, and multi-transaction Ironwood migration.

Vizor also expands how holders can use shielded ZEC:

- **Pay:** recipient entry and scanning, recent recipients, address-book support, amount review, encrypted memos, and activity status.
- **Cross-chain swaps:** NEAR Intents quotes, ZEC deposit preparation, external settlement tracking, recovery states, and Keystone authorization.
- **Coinholder voting:** proposal discovery, vote commitments and shares, submission tracking, interrupted-session recovery, and software or Keystone signing.
- **Account and activity UX:** unified transfer and swap history, recipient labels, progress and failure states, and responsive desktop and mobile layouts.

### Ironwood as proof of product impact

Ironwood required every part of the wallet—sync, account state, transaction construction, proofs, signing, background execution, recovery, release operations, and user communication—to work together under a fixed mainnet deadline.

After the activation height was confirmed on July 10, Vizor shipped its production migration implementation when Ironwood activated on July 28. The completed system includes canonical 1-2-5 denominations, boundary-aligned anchors, shared expiry buckets, randomized scheduling, large-holder denominations, diversified submission endpoints, and fail-closed broadcast checks.

Users can choose between a staged private migration and an explicit immediate migration, see the schedule, stop or switch modes, resume interrupted work, and recover expired transfers. Mobile builds use iOS BGProcessingTask and Android WorkManager to broadcast prepared transactions in the background. Keystone users can authorize batches of up to 35 migration transactions through one QR session with idempotent recovery.

Mainnet operation also produced improvements across the wallet. KPLR and Valar Group eliminated 92% of hot-path wallet-summary calls, fixed a 3.5× sync regression, made account switching about 10× faster, and measured 30–50% faster migration phases. Five stabilization releases followed activation through August 3.

Vizor's mainnet observations also informed the open [[ZIP-318 timing proposal](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343)](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343). [[librustzcash #2855](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855)](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855) adopted the resulting constants, including a reduction in the transfer-delay mean from 144 to 66 blocks.

### Why retroactive funding is appropriate

KPLR funded Vizor without Zcash ecosystem funding or pre-arranged compensation. Coinholders are evaluating a completed product with public releases, open code, app listings, a working hardware path, and observable mainnet impact rather than a staffing plan or forecast. Ironwood is the strongest evidence of the wallet's impact, but the funded output is the complete Vizor product and its contribution to Zcash's wallet ecosystem.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Vizor uses Flutter and Dart for its multi-platform interface and orchestration layer over a modified Rust core based on librustzcash, connected through `flutter_rust_bridge`. Rust owns the security- and protocol-sensitive path: account state, chain sync, note selection, transaction construction, proof generation, signing state, and ZIP-318 scheduling. SQLite persists wallet, activity, and migration state so long-running or interrupted operations can resume instead of restarting.

The wallet connects to lightwalletd over gRPC. Users select a preset or custom endpoint before account creation. Migration submission is diversified across endpoints to reduce dependence on one broadcaster. Mobile background execution uses iOS BGProcessingTask and Android WorkManager to submit transactions that have already been prepared and signed.

Keystone integration uses animated QR codes and PCZTs instead of USB or a network connection. Vizor prepares and proves transactions, Keystone authorizes them, and Vizor imports the signed result into the same persistent workflow used by software accounts. Ironwood extended this design to resumable batches of migration transactions.

Pay, swaps, and voting build on the same wallet state rather than moving users into separate custodial systems. Pay composes standard Zcash transactions with recipient, memo, and activity UX. Swaps obtain a NEAR Intents route, prepare a ZEC deposit, track external settlement, and retain a recoverable activity record. Voting derives eligibility from wallet state and supports commitment, share, submission, and recovery flows with software or Keystone signing.

CI covers Flutter, Rust, and regtest migration simulations. Test paths cover preparation, scheduled transfer, expiry, retry, interruption, and completion. Distribution uses signed or notarized desktop builds, platform-native update channels, the Apple App Store, and Google Play. The repository includes build and release-verification instructions so reviewers can inspect the code behind the published applications.

### Time Period of Work Completion

March 2026 – August 7, 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

360000

### Budget Breakdown

- **Compensation**
  - **Amount:** $340,000
  - **Justification:** Completed engineering, product, design, QA, release, and operational work for the Vizor wallet.
- **Technology/Software**
  - **Amount:** $0
  - **Justification:** No separate amount requested; core dependencies and development tooling are open source or included in compensation.
- **Infrastructure/Hosting**
  - **Amount:** $10,000
  - **Justification:** CI/CD, code signing and notarization, lightwalletd infrastructure, and validator operation.
- **Services/Contractors**
  - **Amount:** $10,000
  - **Justification:** Test devices, Keystone units, legal policies, and app-store compliance.
- **Other**
  - **Amount:** $0
  - **Justification:** None.
- **Total:** **$360,000**

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

KPLR and Vizor have not received funding from the Zcash Coinholder Grants Program or another Zcash ecosystem grant program.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

KPLR raised venture financing for Keplr Wallet and funded Vizor internally from company resources. No Zcash ecosystem funding or pre-arranged compensation funded the completed work covered by this application.

### Success Metrics

### Shipped product

- A complete self-custody wallet spanning account creation and recovery, shielded receive and send, transparent-fund shielding, memos, multi-account management, activity history, and privacy controls.
- Distribution across macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android from one Flutter/Rust architecture.
- Air-gapped Keystone support for ordinary transactions, shielding, swaps, voting, and Ironwood migration.
- Shipped Pay, cross-chain swaps, coinholder voting, ZIP-317 fees, ZIP-320 TEX addresses, transparent-address rotation, and the June 3 Orchard circuit update.
- Apache-2.0 source, signed or notarized releases, verification instructions, and regtest coverage.

### Observable Ironwood impact

CipherScan's August 6 snapshot—before later compliant wallet integrations were listed—contained 5,666 Orchard-to-Ironwood transactions. Its classifier grouped **1,521 transactions moving 854,446.52 ZEC** into the current-SDK family. Of those, **1,500 transactions moving 831,943.52 ZEC** passed all three full-compliance checks: standard denomination, expected Orchard/Ironwood action structure, and a boundary-aligned anchor.

The corresponding network overview reported 1,194,271 ZEC moving from Orchard into Ironwood. The fully compliant current-SDK footprint represented roughly **70% of observed Orchard-to-Ironwood value** at that snapshot. CipherScan then listed Vizor and the reference implementation as the fully compliant entries; because the reference implementation was not an end-user wallet, this is the best available public estimate of migration through Vizor during that period.

This attribution is based on timing and transaction fingerprints, not a cryptographic wallet identifier. The estimate excludes transactions that only partially matched ZIP-318 or belonged to separately identified implementation families.

### Ecosystem impact

- Vizor was the first end-user wallet CipherScan identified as fully ZIP-318 compliant.
- Mainnet observations informed [[zcash/zips #1343](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343)](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343), and [[librustzcash #2855](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855)](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855) adopted the resulting timing constants.
- Mainnet stabilization eliminated 92% of hot-path wallet-summary calls, fixed a 3.5× sync regression, made account switching about 10× faster, and improved measured migration phases by 30–50%.
- The public Flutter/Rust implementation gives other Zcash teams a production reference for wallet UX, hardware signing, background execution, recovery, and ZIP-318 integration.

### Proof of completion

### Repository and code

- [[Vizor repository](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet)](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet) — Apache-2.0 Flutter/Rust wallet source, tests, release tooling, and verification instructions.
- [[Keystone integration PR #6](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/6)](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/6) — air-gapped PCZT signing.
- **Required before submission:** add and link `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### Deployments and releases

- [[Desktop activation release v0.0.39](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/releases/tag/release/v0.0.39)](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/releases/tag/release/v0.0.39) — Ironwood activation release.
- [[Vizor releases](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/releases)](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/releases) — published desktop releases and stabilization history.
- [[Vizor on the Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/vizor-wallet/id6776591245)](https://apps.apple.com/app/vizor-wallet/id6776591245) — production iOS listing.
- [[Vizor on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.keplr.vizor)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.keplr.vizor) — production Android listing.

### External and upstream evidence

- [[CipherScan Ironwood tracker](https://cipherscan.app/ironwood)](https://cipherscan.app/ironwood) — migration totals, transaction analysis, and wallet-readiness classification.
- [[CipherScan migration privacy dataset](https://api.mainnet.cipherscan.app/api/migration/scatter)](https://api.mainnet.cipherscan.app/api/migration/scatter) — transaction-family and full-compliance data.
- [[CipherScan migration overview](https://api.mainnet.cipherscan.app/api/migration/overview)](https://api.mainnet.cipherscan.app/api/migration/overview) — Orchard inflow and network totals.
- [[ZIP-318 timing proposal](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343)](https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1343) — credits Vizor's measurements and recommendations.
- [[librustzcash #2855](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855)](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/pull/2855) — adoption of the resulting timing constants.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

## Conflict of Interest Disclosure

- **Swap fees:** KPLR receives a share of the NEAR Intents route fee on swaps executed through Vizor. Current revenue does not cover Vizor's operating costs.
- **Company funding:** KPLR funded Vizor from company resources originally raised for its broader wallet business. Vizor received no Zcash ecosystem funding for the completed work in this application.
- **Validator:** KPLR operates a coinholder-voting-chain validator and may receive at-cost infrastructure compensation.
- **Collaborations:** KPLR worked with Valar Group on ZIP-318, sync, and usability improvements, and with Keystone on Ironwood-ready firmware. This request covers only KPLR's work.
- **Organizational roles:** No KPLR personnel hold roles at FPF, ZCG, Zcash Foundation, or Shielded Labs.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

### Organization or Individual Name

Valargroup

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
- name: Adam Tucker
  github: czarcas7ic
  role: Protocol Engineer
  responsibilities: Continuous end-to-end integration and testing across the
    Ironwood stack, including consensus rules, librustzcash, Orchard, Zebra,
    Vizor, transaction test vectors, PCZT, and Keystone hardware signing;
    follow-on response with wallet teams and users after activation
- name: Roman Ackhtariev
  github: p0mvn
  role: Protocol Engineer
  responsibilities: Five and one-third weeks of Ironwood work on zcashd
    deprecation and
    compatibility, wallet hardening, security review of the consensus rules,
    and peer-to-peer security, including follow-on response with wallet teams

- name: Evan Forbes
  github: evan-forbes
  role: Protocol Engineer
  responsibilities: Peer-to-peer security, mining and reorganization testing,
    network hardening, and review of the Ironwood consensus rules; only one-third
    of his time during the period is allocated to this application
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Background knowledge as an active Zcash community member and protocol contributor.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

1203000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

This application requests retroactive compensation for Valargroup's emergency
development, integration, testing, infrastructure, and activation work for
Ironwood (NU6.3). The work connected the upgrade's consensus rules to a
production full node, wallet and migration tooling, transaction hashing and
hardware signing, miner compatibility, public test infrastructure, and
mainnet operations on an under-two-month emergency schedule.

### Project Description


#### Background and impact

On May 29, 2026, a critical soundness vulnerability was discovered in Orchard.
NU6.2 closed the vulnerable circuit, but Orchard's privacy made it impossible
to inspect the pool or determine whether counterfeit ZEC had already been
created. Ironwood resolved that uncertainty without sacrificing user privacy.
It sealed Orchard to new value, moved future shielded activity into a corrected
pool, and required all value leaving Orchard to pass through the turnstile. No
more value could exit than had legitimately entered. [Shielded Labs explains
the threat and Ironwood's effect here](https://shieldedlabs.net/ironwood/).

Only 52 days separated the [June 6 public
plan](https://tachyon.z.cash/blog/auditing-orchard-supply/) from July 28 mainnet
activation, making Ironwood Zcash's fastest planned network upgrade. The
circuit, consensus rules, transaction hashing, nodes, mining, lightwallet
services, wallets, hardware signing, test infrastructure, and exchange
operations all had to mature in parallel. Within three days, Valargroup had an
end-to-end stack crossing the upgrade boundary; a public integration testnet
followed. We kept that path current as the specifications, ZIPs, and audit
findings evolved. We continually updated these, and co-designed ZIPs take into
account all security and user needs.

We also addressed operational frictions that could have prevented users from
making it through the upgrade. `zcashd` was scheduled to reach its
End-of-Support halt on July 18 while exchanges, mining pools, and other
production systems still depended on it. While ZODL and Zec.rocks worked on
Rust CLI wallet paths, Valargroup built and operated a `zcashd` compatibility
bridge for organizations that could move consensus to Zebra or Zakura but
could not yet replace their wallet infrastructure. We put the integration
testnet online before official support, added Keystone migration signing, and
tested miners with real ASICs. During activation week, we supplied recovery
tooling and network support. After activation, we continued hardening wallet
migration and supporting integrators and users.

[Shielded Labs credits
Valargroup](https://shieldedlabs.net/ironwood/), Project Tachyon, and ZODL with
helping define Ironwood's architecture, implement its consensus rules, and
carry out the wider formal-verification effort. Valargroup maintained an
executable path across the node, `librustzcash`, `lightwalletd`, and wallet as
the design changed, giving upstream teams early integration feedback.

Ironwood activated after its node, wallet, migration, signing, mining, testnet,
and compatibility paths had been exercised together. This application claims
only Valargroup's documented share of the wider ecosystem effort. In
particular, Valargroup built and operated the `zcashd` compatibility bridge;
the Zcash Foundation later ported its production design into upstream Zebra.

Valargroup also mobilized twice, bringing every team member whose visa allowed
travel first to Denver and later to Prague. Co-location shortened design,
review, integration, and incident-response loops. All associated travel and
mobilization expenses are included in the fixed compensation request.

#### Completed work and timeline

**June 2: NU6.2 recovery.** Immediately after the NU6.2 activation,
Valargroup helped operators recover nodes that had missed the emergency patch.
Almost no non-mining operators had installed an updated binary before the
activation height, so many could not reconnect without operational help. We:

- productionized full-node chain-state snapshots, now published as [Zakura
  snapshots](https://zakura.com/snapshots/), so operators could bootstrap from
  a known recent state instead of resynchronizing from genesis; and
- built rewind and recovery tooling so affected nodes could return to the
  valid chain without a complete resync.

**June 7–July 22: preserve exchange continuity with Valargroup's `zcashd`
compatibility bridge.** Roman led the implementation, with contributions from
Dev, Evan, and Adam. An Ironwood-capable Zebra or Zakura node remained
authoritative for network consensus, while a restricted local `zcashd` sidecar
served the wallet RPCs, real-time notifications, and operational interfaces
expected by legacy exchange and custody systems. Mining RPCs were removed so
misconfigured operators failed closed.

The implementation progressed from supervised compatibility mode and RPC tests
to a minimal P2P sidecar. We validated existing mainnet datadirs without
reindexing, a single locked local peer, wallet and transparent transaction
flows, restarts, supervision, and deep reorganizations; delivery included
pinned binaries, installers, Docker support, health checks, TLS, and operator
documentation.

The bridge remained necessary despite Zallet's progress. [Zallet
v0.1.0-alpha.4 was tagged June
25](https://github.com/zcash/zallet/releases/tag/v0.1.0-alpha.4), only 23 days
before the `zcashd` halt, with substantial `wallet.dat` migration work.
[Zallet v0.1.0-beta.1 followed July
12](https://github.com/zcash/zallet/releases/tag/v0.1.0-beta.1), six days before
the halt. Exchanges could not necessarily replace mature wallet and operational
integrations that quickly. The bridge separated consensus-node migration from
wallet integration and carried legacy systems across both the July 18 halt and
July 28 activation.

ZODL [reported the work on June 12 for organizations unable to migrate directly to
Z3](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcash-z3-updates-formerly-zcashd-deprecation/48965?page=8).
Its Ironwood announcement [described the wrapper as the continuity path for
`zcashd` wallet
users](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/ironwood-verifying-the-soundness-of-zcash-s-circulating-supply/56044/2).
The Zcash Foundation [ported the production Zakura design into upstream
Zebra](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10952), and Zebra 6.2.0's
[release notes](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.2.0)
credit Zakura's authors for the major part of the implementation. On July 22,
[Zakura 1.0.3](https://zakura.com/announcements/zakura-1-0-3/) marked
the mode stable and Ironwood-ready after partner and upgrade testing.

**June 6–11: build the end-to-end Ironwood steel thread.** Within a day of the
[June 6 public commitment to
Ironwood](https://tachyon.z.cash/blog/auditing-orchard-supply/), Valargroup had
working branches spanning Vizor migration, `librustzcash`, Zebra, and
`lightwalletd`. Within nine days of NU6.2 activation, the integrated stack was
crossing an upgrade boundary with every consensus rule known at that time. The
early result is recorded in [this public status
update](https://x.com/ebfull/status/2065289918604283991?s=20).

These branches directly de-risked upstream delivery. Merged
[lightwallet-protocol
#29](https://github.com/zcash/lightwallet-protocol/pull/29) explicitly says its
Ironwood changes were taken from Valargroup's integration branch "for
steel-threading full stack integration." During development, [Zebra
commit](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/29eba9cd4e3ca6b1b9472f3303298f9514fc78b0),
the Zcash Foundation pinned `librustzcash` and Orchard to Valargroup's matching
v6 branches while adding and testing its NU6.3 verification path. Zebra later
[replaced those pins with published
releases](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/commit/ee5c0e5e98e01e9e2895606cad0f907c158a388e).
Official [Ironwood support in
`lightwalletd`](https://github.com/zcash/lightwalletd/pull/567) then imported
the protocol release containing Valargroup's changes. This live path made
cross-layer decisions testable while they could still change.

**Protocol and consensus delivery during June and July.** Across the Ironwood
ZIPs, Valargroup contributed design work, review, test vectors, implementation
feedback, and production code. This work covered the v6 transaction format,
pool restrictions, quantum recoverability, value-pool accounting, shielded
coinbase behavior, deployment parameters, wallet requirements, and
Orchard-to-Ironwood migration. The team helped make consensus-rule decisions
and maintained a second working implementation in our Zebra fork, which became
Zakura.

This included:

- implementing the Ironwood bundle, state, value-pool, chain-history, RPC,
  mining, and activation rules in the node stack;
- implementing and reviewing the v6 transaction ID, signature digest, test
  vectors, and related hashing needed to pre-authorize migration transactions;
- carrying our pre-existing Quantum Recoverability implementation into the
  Ironwood release, which made it practical to include quantum recoverability
  in the emergency upgrade;
- continuously testing the full stack across `librustzcash`, Orchard,
  Zebra/Zakura, our Vizor and `lightwalletd` forks, transaction test vectors,
  and real wallets
- maintaining a deployable independent implementation of the complete
  consensus scope that received external security review. The external-review
  fees themselves are not included in this application.
- coordinating with auditors for these updates.

**Migration and hardware signing.** Ironwood required users to move Orchard
funds through a public turnstile. Naive migrations could disclose balances,
and hardware wallets could not efficiently approve a large series of
transactions. Vizor's reference implementation supported software and Keystone
accounts, durable split planning, background execution, pre-signing, and safe
recovery across restarts and reorganizations. As the final ecosystem design
converged, we integrated the shared migration backend, canonical randomized
denominations, custom privacy controls, and additional scheduling, recovery,
and privacy hardening.

Below the wallet, we implemented storage, scanning, policy, v6 PCZT,
signer-only parsing, redaction, and anchor updates. Our Keystone firmware and
SDK contributions covered account binding, batch/result UR types,
memory-constrained signing, compact responses, recovery, performance, and
resource limits. Cypherpunk firmware 3.0.2 shipped July 27 with Ironwood and
batch-PCZT support, letting users review and sign migration batches instead of
approving transactions individually. [Adam's explanation of the Keystone
integration](https://x.com/czarcas7ic/status/2081842368412885141?s=20) covers how
Valargroup made Ironwood migration signing practical on constrained hardware,
and it was [recognized as the automated migration
path](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/ironwood-verifying-the-soundness-of-zcash-s-circulating-supply/56044/56).

We also made a critical Keystone security fix: firmware now rejects PCZTs that
reuse a randomized validating key (`rk`) across actions ([Keystone
#2216](https://github.com/KeystoneHQ/keystone3-firmware/pull/2216), refined in
[#2218](https://github.com/KeystoneHQ/keystone3-firmware/pull/2218)). Actions
within the same pool share a transaction-wide shielded sighash, so if two had
the same `rk`, a signature for one would also validate for the other. A
malicious software wallet could potentially exploit this to reuse a
hardware-wallet authorization and steal funds. Keystone now rejects the PCZT
before signing and retains a defensive duplicate check across Orchard and
Ironwood.

Valargroup also identified and helped fix privacy and UX issues that emerged as
the migration path reached users: reusing each PCZT circuit's cached Orchard
proving key instead of rebuilding it for every proof ([Vizor
#341](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/341)); preventing the
privacy timer from interrupting an active Keystone signing session while
preserving background-timeout protection ([Vizor
#368](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/368)); and deriving the
migration payload-encryption key once per read rather than once per row ([Vizor
#437](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/437)), reducing its
representative benchmark from 1.49 seconds to 24 milliseconds while keeping key
material operation-scoped.

**Miner migration and consensus testing.** We repeatedly rehearsed migration
from `zcashd` to both the compatibility service and Zallet. Using real ASICs on
testnet and mainnet, we tested block-template, coinbase, and reorganization
behavior under meaningful hashrate; ASIC tests had previously triggered
reorganizations hundreds of blocks deep.

**June 15 onward: put a wallet-integration network online before official
testnet support.** Our [Ironwood public
testnet](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-testnet) had Zebra and
`lightwalletd` [crossing NU6.3 within hours of repository
creation](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-testnet/commit/33efce28e32e1f4348245b23882ef4b7753b23c0).
The following day we added a [faucet and pre-funded Orchard migration
wallets](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-testnet/commit/1062e03831f786be7a188b586b3d34a87f24845b)
and a [public integrator configuration and
guide](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-testnet/commit/28ddc52625e56555d079af4115b3ed8d7a5b7bee).
This provided external integrators an always-on post-activation chain,
bootstrap tooling, and a shadow-fork path. ZODL [recorded the early testnet
progress](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcash-z3-updates-formerly-zcashd-deprecation/48965?page=8),
[NozyWallet validated its migration
loop](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/nozywallet-ironwood-nu6-3-migration-case-breakdown-and-v2-4-0-cli-release/56568)
against the Valargroup stack, and [Zec.rocks deployed
`lightwalletd`](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/ironwood-is-active-on-testnet-zec-rocks/56557)
from our branch. Our Vizor and `lightwalletd` forks provided the early
end-to-end wallet path.

**June through activation week: expand mainnet and testnet monitoring.** We ran
more than ten monitored nodes across both networks, tracking their chain and
fork status, block-arrival times, peer counts, and other liveness indicators.
This instrumentation was instrumental in debugging testnet upgrade issues and
gave meaningful assurance that mainnet nodes remained on the expected chain
and received blocks normally during activation. Peer counts were especially
useful for confirming that mainnet connectivity remained stable. Testnet was
substantially less stable; the general P2P work that later improved it is
outside this application, while the Ironwood-specific monitoring and diagnosis
are included.

**July 28 and activation week: mainnet activation and recovery.** We handled an
upgrade-boundary edge case in which affected nodes repopulated peers only after
a new discovery event. We coordinated patches with the Zcash Foundation and
deployed an 18-node mainnet recovery fleet to restore connectivity.

**July 29–August 5: follow-on migration hardening and user response.** Roman and
Adam [removed head-of-line scheduling
races](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/404), [shortened dense
migration schedules](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/425),
[randomized denominations
recursively](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/427), [recovered due
Keystone broadcasts](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/456), and
[kept migration broadcasts alive while the desktop application was
hidden](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/465). Dev, Adam, and
Roman also supported wallet teams and users through post-activation response
and triage; this time is included in their Ironwood allocations.

**Through August 14:** We completed activation-specific follow-up, preserved
the compatibility and snapshot paths for operators, and assembled the public
and private evidence needed to verify the work and its costs.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)


- **End-to-end executable integration.** We kept a live path from consensus
  primitives through nodes and services to wallet construction, signing, and
  visible behavior, exposing cross-layer defects early.
- **Independent consensus implementation.** We implemented the Ironwood
  consensus surface in the Zebra fork that became Zakura and cross-checked it
  against the specification, vectors, libraries, and upstream Zebra.
- **Repeated mixed-node and real-hardware rehearsals.** We repeatedly ran
  [testnets with four Zebra and four Zakura
  nodes](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-upgrade-observatory) through the
  upgrade height, validating cross-implementation agreement and a broad range
  of mempool behavior. We also exercised regtest, public testnet, and mainnet
  with real ASICs, Zallet, and the compatibility route.
- **Backwards-compatible transition.** The compatibility service isolated a
  restricted `zcashd` wallet behind an Ironwood-capable node, preserving legacy
  interfaces without treating `zcashd` as a post-NU6.3 validator.
- **Pre-authorized, updateable migrations.** The v6 digest and PCZT work made
  effects authorizable before proofs and anchors were final. Updater roles,
  redaction, compact responses, aggregate review, and batch signing made this
  practical on Keystone hardware.
- **Operational recovery infrastructure.** Published snapshots, rewind tools,
  monitoring across more than ten mainnet and testnet nodes, bootstrap nodes,
  faucets, and the recovery fleet improved visibility and shortened recovery.
- **Defense in depth.** Consensus review was performed across separate code
  paths and external audit; P2P and reorganization behavior was tested under
  real network and mining conditions.
- **Emergency in-person mobilization.** We mobilized the team twice, bringing
  every member whose visa allowed travel first to Denver and then Prague,
  reducing coordination latency. The expenses are included in compensation.
