- Keystone also merged the critical [duplicate-`rk`
  rejection](https://github.com/KeystoneHQ/keystone3-firmware/pull/2216) and its
  [follow-up](https://github.com/KeystoneHQ/keystone3-firmware/pull/2218),
  preventing signature reuse across same-pool actions and retaining a
  defensive cross-pool check.
- Vizor merged [one-session batched Keystone migration
  signing](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/357) on July 27 and
  moved to the [released Ironwood crate
  family](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/369) before activation
  on July 28. User-facing privacy, UX, and performance hardening included
  cached circuit-specific proving keys in
  [#341](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/341), Keystone signing
  and privacy-lock lifecycle fixes in
  [#368](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/368), and reuse of a
  derived migration payload key in
  [#437](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/437). After activation,
  Roman and Adam also merged migration hardening in
  [#404](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/404),
  [#425](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/425),
  [#427](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/427),
  [#456](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/456), and
  [#465](https://github.com/chainapsis/vizor-wallet/pull/465).

#### Compatibility, test, and operational infrastructure

- The compatibility bridge progressed through supervised mode in [Valargroup
  Zebra #20](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/20), the initial complete
  implementation in [#25](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/25), and the
  second-generation implementation in
  [#54](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/54). Large-batch response
  validation, TLS, and the operator guide are in
  [#55](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/55),
  [#59](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/59), and
  [#64](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/64).
- [Integration tests #1](https://github.com/valargroup/integration-tests/pull/1)
  adds the `zcashd`-compatible RPC profile;
  [#4](https://github.com/valargroup/integration-tests/pull/4) and
  [#5](https://github.com/valargroup/integration-tests/pull/5) add benchmark and
  Zebra/`zcashd` compatibility coverage.
- The production sidecar design moved block ingestion to minimal P2P in [Zakura
  #19](https://github.com/zakura-core/zakura/pull/19). The dedicated
  [`zcashd` build](https://github.com/valargroup/zcashd/pull/4) removed mining
  RPCs and bypassed the End-of-Support halt, then [locked itself to one local
  peer](https://github.com/valargroup/zcashd/pull/10) and [kept header sync live
  against that peer](https://github.com/valargroup/zcashd/pull/15). Zakura
  [maintained the sidecar
  connection](https://github.com/zakura-core/zakura/pull/76), [added it to the
  production fleet](https://github.com/zakura-core/zakura/pull/78), and
  [preserved wallet RPCs used by legacy
  integrations](https://github.com/zakura-core/zakura/pull/278).
- The Zcash Foundation's upstream [Zebra compatibility
  PR](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10952) identifies the
  Zakura implementation as the production origin it ported. [Zebra
  6.2.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v6.2.0) credits
  Zakura's authors for the major part of the implementation, and [Zakura
  1.0.3](https://zakura.com/announcements/zakura-1-0-3/) records production
  readiness after partner testing.
- [Ironwood public
  testnet](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-testnet) contains the faucet,
  seeded wallets, bootstrap tooling, and upgrade-test infrastructure.
- The [Ironwood Upgrade
  Observatory](https://github.com/valargroup/ironwood-upgrade-observatory)
  records the repeated four-Zebra/four-Zakura upgrade-height rehearsals used to
  validate cross-implementation agreement and mempool behavior.
- Fleet telemetry from more than ten mainnet and testnet nodes tracked fork
  status, block-arrival times, peer counts, and liveness through activation.
  Deployment records and monitoring output can be provided privately to FPF.
- [Zakura snapshots](https://zakura.com/snapshots/) publishes current,
  historical, pruned, archive, and `zcashd`-compatibility snapshots; the
  underlying [Zakura](https://github.com/valargroup/zakura-snapshots) and
  [`zcashd` compatibility](https://github.com/valargroup/zcashd-snapshots)
  services are public.
- [Zakura #462](https://github.com/zakura-core/zakura/pull/462) replenishes
  depleted outbound peers; the related upstream [Zebra
  #11073](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/11073) fixes the first
  peer-cache write. Fleet deployment records and activation logs for the
  18-node activation-week response can be provided privately.
- [Valargroup Zebra #365](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/365) carries
  the Ironwood commitment root and action count through header sync, while
  [#447](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/447) and
  [#458](https://github.com/valargroup/zebra/pull/458) verify commitment roots
  before fast-synced state is persisted. This is cited as integrity hardening;
  generic Zakura sync-performance work remains excluded.
- [Zcash Foundation's Zakura and NU6.3
  statement](https://zfnd.org/zebra-zakura-and-the-road-through-nu6-3/) and
  [Shielded Labs' Ironwood page](https://shieldedlabs.net/ironwood/) provide
  independent acceptance and attribution.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure


These disclosures are ordered by what we consider the most significant actual,
potential, or perceived conflicts.

- **Dev Ojha is a small angel investor in v12.** v12, a Zellic product, was
  used during the broader Ironwood response. No v12 expense is included in
  this development application. Paid v12 credits and external audit expenses
  appear only in the separate audit reimbursement application, where the same
  investment is disclosed.
- **Valargroup co-develops Zakura with Project Tachyon.** Project Tachyon is a
  close collaborator and co-author of the June 6 Ironwood statement. Tachyon
  has submitted its own application for circuit and formal-verification work.
  This application excludes that work and every Tachyon expense. The teams'
  shared interest in Zakura's adoption creates a reputational and potential
  future commercial benefit, which we disclose even though Zakura-only
  development is excluded from the requested amount.
- **A separate Valargroup audit application is pending.** The $599,000 audit
  reimbursement application concerns third-party invoices and AI credits. This
  application concerns Valargroup labor and infrastructure. No cost appears in
  both requests, but the applications relate to the same emergency response
  and should be reviewed together for scope clarity.
- **The work was collaborative.** Valargroup worked closely with Project
  Tachyon, ZODL, the Zcash Foundation, Shielded Labs, Keystone, exchanges, and
  miners. Their contributions are acknowledged and excluded where independently
  produced. Review, coordination, or acceptance by those organizations should
  not be understood as independent validation of our requested dollar amount.
- **Prior and ongoing ecosystem roles.** Dev Ojha and the other team members
  are established Zcash protocol contributors. Valargroup continues to develop
  Zcash infrastructure and may benefit reputationally or commercially from a
  successful network and from adoption of software it maintains.
- **Keyholder organizations.** Valargroup has no financial, contractual, or
  governance relationship with the Zcash Foundation, Shielded Labs, or the
  Financial Privacy Foundation beyond the public inter-organizational
  coordination described here and ordinary participation in ecosystem grant
  processes.

### Community Forum Posting

- [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application. Note: If you are unable to post on the forum (for example, due to new user restrictions), please leave a comment below, and we will adjust your posting permissions.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@Zk-nd3r

### Organization or Individual Name

Frontier Compute LLC

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am submitting this through Frontier Compute LLC.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Zcash Community Forum and Frontier Compute's existing participation in the Coinholder Retroactive Grants process.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$136,250

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I found concrete security failures in Zcash infrastructure and wallet code, disclosed them responsibly, stayed with the work through remediation, and verified what merged and shipped. This application claims only accepted, public, merged or released outcomes. Private, open, rejected, disputed, and partially unresolved work is excluded.

### Project Description

I am Skander, founder of Frontier Compute. This was not a drive-by bug report. The operating loop was: define the security property, find and validate the failure path, report it privately, help make the required control precise, track remediation through review and merge, verify release ancestry, and re-read the fixed code for residual risk.

I am applying for one completed security-remediation pack because the work was run as one operation across infrastructure and wallet surfaces.

#### 1. Accepted and shipped lightwalletd work - $56,250

- [GHSA-9p9r-mggr-8q9g](https://github.com/zcash/lightwalletd/security/advisories/GHSA-9p9r-mggr-8q9g): a slow or non-reading `GetMempoolTx` client could hold the shared mempool mutex across streaming sends and block concurrent calls. I am the sole accepted reporter. The advisory is public and the fix shipped in lightwalletd 0.5.2. I submitted it on 5 May 2026. Valuation: $18,750, the base Supporting Infrastructure Medium schedule then in force.
- [GHSA-x4m7-3gpp-xc36](https://github.com/zcash/lightwalletd/security/advisories/GHSA-x4m7-3gpp-xc36): unauthenticated transparent-address RPC paths could force resource exhaustion. I authored and maintained the Frontier Compute report and preserve every additional public credit. This application claims only the two accepted paths fixed and released in lightwalletd 0.5.0. The remaining materialize-before-filter residual is expressly excluded. I submitted it on 28 April 2026, after the VDI launch. Valuation: $37,500, the base Supporting Infrastructure High schedule then in force.

I use the applicable bountyzcash-to-VDI process and the base VDI price grid in force on each disclosure date. I do not prorate an accepted severity band by fixed path count, and I do not claim the discretionary 50 percent uplift. These figures are valuation benchmarks only, not evidence of an existing award.

#### 2. Accepted and merged ZODL mobile-wallet remediation - $80,000

I delivered coordinated security reports covering transaction-review integrity, account and session binding, secret-export surfaces, and swap validation. ZODL maintainers independently implemented and reviewed the fixes. I am claiming my research, responsible disclosure, control specification, adversarial verification, and fix-to-release tracking, not authorship of their patches.

This application relies only on the following public, approved, merged work and public release evidence:

- [zodl-android #2299 - Swap Security Hardening](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-android/pull/2299), approved and merged 9 June 2026.
- [zodl-android #2317 - Security hardening](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-android/pull/2317), approved and merged 12 June 2026.
- [zodl-ios #1825 - remove hidden debug seed export without authentication](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-ios/pull/1825), approved and merged 16 June 2026.
- [zodl-ios #1849 - fail closed on multi-recipient ZIP-321 payment requests](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-ios/pull/1849), approved and merged 26 June 2026.
- [zodl-ios #1851 - enforce account/signing boundaries and end stale Flexa sessions](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-ios/pull/1851), approved and merged 26 June 2026.
- [zodl-android 3.8.1-2027](https://github.com/zodl-inc/zodl-android/releases/tag/3.8.1-2027), public release evidence for the relevant Android merge ancestry.

I ask ZODL, as the intended user and remediation owner, to confirm the report-to-fix linkage during review. Any item ZODL does not confirm must be removed from the funded scope rather than inferred in my favour.

#### Explicit exclusions

- No private advisory identifier, exploit detail, unreleased report, or confidential inventory is included.
- No open, draft, rejected, disputed, or unmerged work is valued.
- The unfixed `x4m7` residual is excluded.
- I do not claim maintainer-authored patches as my code.
- I do not claim an award, receivable, or payment that does not exist.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

1. Define the property that must not fail: fund safety, review-to-signing equivalence, account binding, secret handling, availability, or bounded resource use.
2. Trace attacker-controlled inputs through validation, proposal, signing, streaming, and backend-RPC paths.
3. Reproduce locally or create regression-shaped evidence without stressing public services.
4. Disclose through controlled maintainer channels.
5. Map accepted work to exact public pull requests, review state, merge state, tests, and release ancestry.
6. Re-read the post-fix code and exclude every unresolved residual from the completed claim.

AI-assisted source analysis was part of the workflow. Human judgment controlled target selection, validation, severity restraint, disclosure, evidence admission, and remediation verification. Model output was never treated as proof by itself.

### Time Period of Work Completion

April 2026 through July 2026.

### Total Budget (USD)

$136,250

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation: $136,250 - retroactive, outcome-based valuation of completed security research, responsible disclosure, control specification, regression evidence, and release verification.
- Technology/Software: $0 separately claimed.
- Infrastructure/Hosting: $0 separately claimed.
- Services/Contractors: $0 separately claimed.
- Other: $0.
- Total: $136,250.

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

Frontier Compute has not received Coinholder Retroactive Grants funding for this work. The separate ZAP1 application concerns unrelated attestation protocol and verification tooling.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

Some public lightwalletd findings entered the former ZCG vulnerability process and may still be reviewed there. As of submission, I have no primary evidence of an award, receivable, or payment for any work claimed here.

I will not double collect. Any later ZCG bounty or other payment attributable to the same finding will be disclosed and deducted dollar-for-dollar before disbursement. If another route fully compensates an item, I will withdraw that item. This filing does not waive existing bounty eligibility.

### Success Metrics

- Two public lightwalletd advisories with accepted Frontier Compute reporter credit.
- Sole accepted reporter credit and a released 0.5.2 fix for GHSA-9p9r-mggr-8q9g.
- Only the two released `x4m7` paths claimed; the live residual excluded.
- Five approved and merged public ZODL security-hardening pull requests.
- Public Android release evidence.
- Zero private finding identifiers or unpublished exploit details disclosed.
- Dollar-for-dollar deduction or withdrawal prevents double recovery.

issues.body:
### Terms and Conditions

- [x] I agree to the [Grant Agreement](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_6ff6db4095fd4c4ba21babec361e927e.pdf) terms if funded

- [x] I understand that this grant program is only eligible for completed work, as it is a retroactive grant program. Applications for planned or partially completed work will not be considered. All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.
- [x] I agree that for any new open-source software, I will create a CONTRIBUTING.md file that reflects the high standards of Zcash development, using the [`librustzcash` style guides](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#styleguides) as a primary reference.
- [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@BitFalco21

### Organization or Individual Name

ShieldedScan

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

By being active on X with the Zcash community

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

4060

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

ShieldedScan is a free, no-tracker, cypherpunk-styled Zcash block explorer. It lets users explore blocks and transactions, including cross-chain transfers, as well as shielded pools and network analytics through charts, tables and visualisations such as Sankey diagrams. The explorer also offers a free, keyless API.

### Project Description

ShieldedScan is a Zcash block explorer built to give the community a different way to look at the chain, with an interface that fits Zcash's cypherpunk atmosphere rather than the generic explorer look. It goes beyond browsing blocks and transactions: it adds analytics that help users make sense of transaction fees, shielded activity and the Ironwood migration, for example. Rather than seeing the chain only as UTXOs for transparent transactions and encrypted data for shielded pools, the aim is a global view of what is happening on Zcash and how it is evolving. I also put particular emphasis on cross-chain flows.

_What is on the site today:_

- **Chain browsing:** blocks and block detail, transactions and transaction detail, address pages with full history, the mempool, and universal search over heights, hashes and addresses.

- **Shielded pools:** all four pools including Ironwood, pool balances, shielding and unshielding volumes, and the Ironwood migration since activation.

- **Analytics:** an analytics overview plus 11 dedicated charts; shielded supply, pool balances, shielding flow, transactions by type, median fee, fee totals, difficulty, block size, price, Ironwood balance and cross-chain volume.

- **Cross-chain:** a transfer list with filters, per-transfer detail, and a flows view with Sankey diagrams and per-chain trends, covering NEAR Intents and Maya Protocol.

- **Reference pages:** transparent rich list with balance-band distribution, supply accounting by value pool, a halving countdown, a market-cap comparison, and an observed reorg log.

- **API:** a free, keyless public API with 26 documented endpoints, each with a pinned example and an in-browser playground at /api-docs.

- **Testnet:** a second full deployment at testnet.shieldedscan.xyz, with its own node, database and API.

I run my own Zcash archive node (Zakura) with a derived Postgres index, on a single server, so there is no dependency on a third-party data provider. That covers all four shielded pools including Ironwood, per-transaction fees across the whole chain, address history, the transparent rich list, supply accounting by value pool, a halving countdown, and cross-chain ZEC movement collected from public swap protocols. The analytics are limited to what the chain actually publishes: counts, fees, net pool flows and shielding versus unshielding volume.

There are no trackers, no cookies and no request logging, and the API is free and keyless.

Some things are deliberately absent: no viewing-key field, no privacy score, no transaction linkability analysis. My focus is on aggregate views of the chain rather than analytics aimed at individual addresses. That said, all of it is public data, so if the community asks for a given metric I see no reason not to build it.

The end goal is a Zcash explorer that users enjoy, with selected analytics giving a more global view of the chain. Please note I launched the explorer less than two weeks ago, so it is very recent, but I am putting my heart into improving it.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

**Architecture:** The site is Next.js and TypeScript in strict mode, deployed on Netlify. Chain data comes from my own Zcash archive node with a derived Postgres index, both on a single server. The frontend reaches them only through a read-only API on that machine; Postgres and node RPC are never publicly exposed. The data types mirror Zcash's own semantics rather than what happens to be convenient for the interface, and the UI has no knowledge of where its data comes from, so the source can change without touching a page.

**Building the index:** A follower service walks blocks from the node into Postgres. The full transaction backfill ran from genesis to the tip and completed on 2026-07-31, and I verified it before trusting it: no blocks missing transactions, transaction counts reconciling against the blocks' own totals, and addresses checked against the node. Per-transaction fees were derived across the whole chain on 2026-08-01, with coverage stated on the page wherever it isn't complete. A gap in historical difficulty, caused by adding a column after part of the chain had already been ingested, was found and repaired on 2026-08-08. Aggregations that would otherwise scan millions of rows are materialised and refreshed on timers, and chain list pages use keyset pagination rather than offsets, so paging cost doesn't grow with the chain.

**Node:** Zakura in archive mode, currently v1.1.0, upgraded from v1.0.5 on 2026-08-06. Zakura releases carry an end-of-support height at which the node halts, so a cron job alerts on new releases and approaching deadlines. Ironwood (NU6.3) activated on mainnet on 2026-07-28, adding a fourth shielded pool, which required changes to fee derivation and pool accounting.

**Correctness process:** Two rules did most of the work. Anything the chain doesn't state directly, like a block's miner or a transaction's fee, is computed in one place and used everywhere, so the index and the page can't disagree. And nothing counts as verified until it's checked against something independent: the node, an outside source, or the deployed site itself. Reading configuration or passing tests proved unreliable often enough that curling production became routine.

**Testing:** CI runs formatting, type checking, linting, unit tests and a production build on every push. A Playwright suite then checks properties rather than known values: that no page overflows on a phone, that pagination never duplicates or skips a row, that a list row and its detail page agree, that shielded values never render as numbers, and that every text colour is readable against its background by the WCAG AA standard.

**Deployments:** Two independent ones, mainnet and testnet, sharing one codebase with separate nodes, databases and credentials, so testnet figures can't render as mainnet. Testnet went live 2026-08-05, and the public API launched 2026-08-01.

### Time Period of Work Completion

July 2026 - August 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

4060

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 4000
  - Justification: Covers frontend, indexer and API development, node and database operations, design and product decisions. This is time already spent building and launching the explorer, not a forecast.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: The stack is entirely open source (Next.js, TypeScript, Postgres,
    Zakura, Hono, Playwright). No licences or paid tooling.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 45
  - Justification: Costs already incurred and self-funded: the server hosting the
    Zakura archive node, Postgres and the API from late July, block storage added in
    early August, and Netlify frontend hosting. Partial months, hence the small figure.
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: All development and operations handled by me. No contractors,
    agencies or paid data providers. Chain data comes from the node I run, and
    cross-chain and price data from free public APIs.
- Other:
  - $(USD): 15
  - Justification: Domain registration, paid for the current term.
- Total $(USD): 4060


### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

_No response_

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

I accept shielded ZEC donations on the site, but they have brought in very little so far and are unlikely to cover infrastructure costs.

### Success Metrics

An honest limitation first: the explorer has no trackers, no cookies and no request logging, so I have no visitor counts or per-user statistics to report. What I can evidence is what exists and that it works.

**Quantitative**

- A complete index of Zcash mainnet from genesis to the tip and in sync, covering every block and transaction with transparent inputs and outputs resolved and per-transaction fees derived.
- A free, keyless public API with 26 documented endpoints, each with a working example and an in-browser playground.
- A second full deployment for testnet, with its own node, database and API.
- All four shielded pools supported, including Ironwood from the day it activated.
- Cross-chain ZEC transfers collected from two public swap venues, shown as flows and as individual transfers.
- 22 end-to-end test suites alongside unit and component tests, checking properties across every page rather than known values.
- No user data collected: no cookies on any route, no request logs, no client-side storage.

**Qualitative**

- Zcash has another independent explorer, with its own node, index and API, so the ecosystem's public view of the chain does not run through a single provider.
- Analytics that cover shielded pools, cross-chain flows and network activity.
- An API anyone can use with no account, no key and no identification.
- A design built for Zcash, with a cypherpunk-styled interface.

I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1) @emersonian ### Organization or Individual Name Zec.rocks ### Additional Team Members ```team-members.yaml N/A ``` ### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program? Signal group chats, and attending in-person Zcash events ### Requested Grant Amount (USD) $584,992 ### Category Infrastructure ### Project Summary Zec.rocks ran the infrastructure powering 16 months of uptime for every major Zcash wallet. Great infrastructure is invisible: wallets operated smoothly as we were on-call monitoring global edge locations, supporting core teams with testing new software at scale, and deploying critical updates including the careful Orchard security response before it was published. ### Project Description If you use Zcash, you probably use [Zec.rocks](https://zec.rocks/). When you open a wallet, it connects to the Zcash network through a “light wallet server.” Zec.rocks is the default server in Zashi, Zodl, Zingo, Ywallet, Zkool, and the secondary in Cake Wallet. That’s because we’re obsessive about providing the fastest possible sync experience, by deploying our servers as close to users as possible. We host Zcash at “the edge.” Zec.rocks hosts 37 edge routers in 11 cities around the world today. When your wallet connects to Zec.rocks, a technology called anycast directs you to our closest router. Then, you are connected to our closest backend cluster, which is running multiple full Zcash nodes and light wallet servers - enabling us to update Zcash software without downtime. We host backend clusters in 9 cities around the world: NYC, Houston, Los Angeles, São Paulo, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Singapore, Sydney, and Johannesburg. Zec.rocks uses dedicated hardware in the majority of regions for increased autonomy, with the occasional use of hyperscalers when we need to scale quickly in an unexpected place. It’s best that Zcashers host Zcash infrastructure, because we are privacy fanatics: we maintain a strict no IP logging policy, and minimize all logging across our stack wherever possible. We are also advocates of all wallets moving to Tor and Nym, so that we can deprecate our public internet some day. Zec.rocks has hosted Tor hidden services (.onion) for light wallet connections since 2024. Zec.rocks served 240 million requests in July 2026 alone, powering every major Zcash wallet’s ability to sync and broadcast transactions. ### Technical Approach (how you did it) **Reproducible, Open Source Infrastructure** Our entire stack is transparent and can be deployed by anyone technical. We publish the open source code that we use to run our global infrastructure. It uses haproxy at the edge, and Kubernetes for our Zcash nodes. It's called [zcash-stack](https://artifacthub.io/packages/helm/zcash/zcash-stack), and [we keep it updated](https://github.com/zecrocks/zcash-stack/commits/main/) as we deploy the latest Zcash software. Over-provisioned capacity allows us to handle unusual peaks without degrading sync times. Extra capacity also gives us more options to localize and mitigate DDOS attacks. Great infrastructure is invisible to end-users. We are on-call 24/7 responding to unexpected peaks and DDOS attacks. We are also typically the first to deploy new software built by Zcash core teams, providing feedback and code improvements informed by our experience with operating Zcash at scale. **Hosh: Observability of all light wallet servers** We built an open source utility to help all ecosystem server operators monitor their light wallet servers: [Hosh](https://hosh.zec.rocks). [(source code)](https://github.com/zecrocks/hosh/) Also, we built a utility to help operators quickly ping servers to see which are responding properly, and which are the closest to them: [zecping](http://github.com/zecrocks/zecping). **Training more light wallet operators** Empowering more people to host more light wallet servers, further decentralizing the network, is a passion - so we hosted a node workshop which rewarded participants a total of $72,427 (from a private donor) over the span of six months. ### Time Period of Work Completion April 2025 - August 2026 (16 months) ### Total Budget (USD) $584,992 ### Budget Breakdown - Infrastructure/Hosting: - $72,427: Dedicated Hosting Providers - $27,041: Cloud Hosting Providers - $2,170: Github Actions - Compensation: - $483,354: Engineering, payroll, benefits (Senior Site Reliability Engineer, 14 months) - Total: $584,992 ### Previous Funding Yes ### Previous Funding Details We received $45,000 from ZCG on April 1st, 2024 for one year of hosting. The Zcash network has grown substantially since then and has become much more costly to host. ### Other Funding Sources Yes ### Other Funding Sources Details We intend to apply for future grants for software development expenses unrelated to operating the Zec.rocks infrastructure. ### Success Metrics Zec.rocks is the default server powering every major Zcash wallet today. **Metrics from the past 14 months** Below are graphs of the limited data that we do log, including our monthly hosting expenses, and the amount of wallet requests served. A note regarding metrics: We do not log requests. True wallet traffic is underreported, as most Zcash wallets use long-lived streaming connections. If a user is connected to a streaming endpoint, receiving realtime data which otherwise would have resulted in dozens of requests, that is only counted once. ### Proof of completion - [zcash-stack](http://github.com/zecrocks/zcash-stack) - The open infrastructure we use to power Zec.rocks - [hosh](http://github.com/zecrocks/hosh) - Uptime monitoring for light wallet servers ### Conflict of Interest Disclosure I am the founder of an early-stage tech startup that has raised funding from private investors. I have used a portion of that funding to cover these costs, and intend to reimburse my company for the expenses if this retroactive grant is approved. ### Community Forum Posting - [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. Responsibilities: technical consultation on best use of Zcash technology, technical product management so that the end product gets shipped timely and with good quality.

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Background knowledge of Zcash ecosystem

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

6000

### Category

Non-Wallet Applications

### Project Summary

The proposal is made by [zcashlabs](https://zcashlabs.org/) for the project [zcashto.cash](https://zcashto.cash), which is a team that we have supported from ideation, to helping them with technical product management, to giving them a kickstart grant of $5000.

zcashto.cash allows anyone to easily get fiat in exchange for ZEC in their favorite fiat apps, across  100+ geographies and 6 fiat apps which for now include: Cash APP, Chime, Monoz, Revolut, Venmo, Zelle.

The service is provided by leveraging [peer](https://peer.xyz/) protocol under the hood, hence it is non-custodial, and secure by peer’s design, where the escrow is only completed when the order taker gives a proof that they indeed sent fiat.

This project was funded by the new ZcashLabs program [announced recently](https://zcashlabs.org/blog/announcing-zcash-labs), which proactively manages and pays for projects deemed appropriate for Coinholder Retroactive Grants.

### Project Description

[zcashto.cash](https://zcashto.cash) solves one of the most pressing problems for ZEC holders, of being able to use their zec easily in their day to day life, most places still accept fiat, and there isn’t a way to directly get fiat for you ZEC without going through a middleman, or trusted services.

This is the exact problem zcashto.cash solves, it is built on top of the [peer](https://peer.xyz/) protocol, where you can exchange your crypto assets for fiat in your favorite app, without security and custody.

Exchanges on peer are p2p and are verified on-chain, where the escrow in only completed when the order taker provides a proof that they indeed sent the fiat to the requested id on the fiat app of the user’s choice.

Zcashto.cash leverages the existing technology and order book of peer, benefiting from its robust infrastructure and its already existing liquidity.

As we speak, there are users actively using the service to exchange their ZEC for fiat in their favorite apps, this activity can be tracked [here](https://zcashto.cash/activity), and has resulted in over $1300 in cashout requests in the first 2 days since launch.

Zcash Labs, helped identify the problem statement, and was involved with technical product management and integration help from day 0 to the launch with the zcashto.cash team, we also provided them an upfront payment of $5000 to kick start the build out of this idea.

The Zcash Labs business model is giving capital upfront to projects that are promising for zcash and then applying for Coinholder-Directed Retroactive Grants with a 20% markup, to help justify the operational costs and capital risk we take while supporting these projects. Hence with a 20% markup for grant we allocated and time we spent to get this into real life, our grant application is for $6000.

Zcashto.cash team is actively working on making sure that this infra is robust and keeps on improving in terms of UX, service and coverage.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Zcashtocash is built on top of peer, and each cashout follows the following lifecycle:


1. You get a one time zec address where you send your funds
2. The near API is leveraged to convert your zec to USDC
3. With the converted USDC and new order is opened on Peer on base
4. A peer taker pays you on your fiat app of choice, and creates a proof for the peer protocol of proof of payment, and takes away the USDC
5. You have now received your fiat, in case there is no taker available for any reason, you can at all point cancel the order and get your USDC back.

The app uses already existing infrastructure to build on top of like peer, near intents, privy, making it architecturally very simple, while offering very high value to the users. 

### Time Period of Work Completion

July 2026 - August 2027

### Total Budget (USD)

6000

  - Justification: project management
- Services/Contractors:
  - $5000

- Total $(USD): 6000

No

_No response_

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

zcashto.cash has received no funding for the project prior to the Zcash Labs payment.

Zcash Labs is self funded.

### Success Metrics

Zcashto.cash although being new is already processing orders to through it, which can be tracked [here](https://zcashto.cash/how-it-works), the orderflow flowing through it has been increasing day by day and so are the number of people using it. Over $1300 in cash out volume recorded in the first 2 days of launch.

The project is live, with all the promised value proposition it aims to provide, get fiat for your zcash without having to trust centralized middleman, or loosing custody of your assets, and post launch it already has real usage from zcashers cashing out fiat from their ZEC.

I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1) @tzarebczan ### Organization or Individual Name Thomas Zarebczan ### Additional Team Members N/A Solo ### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program? Zcash Community Forum, and Zcash discussion on X. ### Requested Grant Amount (USD) $10,000 ### Category Non-Wallet Applications ### Project Summary CyphZec is a free site (no account required!) at https://cyphzec.com for watching ZEC and CYPH: live prices, shielding and Ironwood, treasury, network stats, and an on-device portfolio. You have both information that's auto updating at a glance, and can drill in deeper when required. ### Project Description I got tired of jumping between explorers, market APIs, and company pages to follow ZEC and CYPH. I wanted one place I could leave open and glance at. On desktop the dashboard updates itself. On a phone it can sit in a small pop-out overlay so you can keep watching while you do something else. I built and designed CyphZec so that is one single resource, with information at a glance, and ability to drill in further. It is a dashboard, not an explorer or indexer. Pool and migration numbers come from CipherScan's public APIs, and other Zcash related stats from zecstats.com (thanks to both for allowing anyone to use their APIs!). There are many customization options for users on both desktop and mobile, such as what bottom buttons/top nav are shown, so users get to see what's important to them. Also a few display and theme options are available. What's live today: 1. **Dashboard.** Live ZEC, BTC, and CYPH prices, including CYPH extended hours and overnight Blue Ocean ATS. Market cap, volume, supply, rank, CYPH/ZEC and ZEC/BTC, charts, and a ticker strip (BTC, ETH, indices, gold, VIX, etc.). CYPH session state accounts for US market holidays. 2. **Network and shielding.** Supply and emission, tx counts, per-pool balances, hourly and daily flows, and a beta unshielding view that classifies what happens after ZEC lands on transparent addresses. 3. **Ironwood.** Live NU6.3 tracker: progress, tx count and value, velocity, inflow sources, privacy cohorts, pool accounting, supply check. 4. **Cypherpunk treasury.** Disclosed ZEC holdings and buys, NAV per share, diluted NAV, published mNAV, discount/premium, share volume vs the 7-day average. 5. **Tools.** CYPH estimator at a ZEC target. What-if market-capture table (BTC price or market-cap basis). BTC/ZEC relative performance. BTC and ZEC rainbow charts. On-device CYPH/ZEC portfolio with cost basis. Orchard-risk page (Polymarket signal). 6. **App shell.** Works on phone and desktop. PWA install. Pop-out price widget: real floating window on desktop Chrome, small overlay on Android/iOS (mini / compact / full). Custom header, bottom nav, and dashboard tiles. Theme, font, density, glow, motion. Share images for X. Stale-data fallbacks so a dead upstream does not blank the page. No account. Portfolio and cost basis never leave the device. Aggregate chain stats are worded so they do not pretend to identify a person, exchange, or sale. Everything above is live at https://cyphzec.com. I am not asking for future work or ongoing hosting. ### Technical Approach (how you did it) Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript. Runs on Cloudflare Workers via OpenNext. KV holds shared cache and stale snapshots. A Worker cron fires every minute for jobs that should not wait for a visitor. 16 pages, 30 API routes (25 JSON, 5 Open Graph images). Each upstream has its own cache lifetime. CipherScan for pools and Ironwood. Kraken for ZEC. Yahoo for CYPH and the ticker. CoinPaprika / CoinGecko as market fallbacks. zecstats.com for daily tx counts. Cypherpunk’s public site for treasury history and mNAV. Grateful those feeds are public. The client polls with SWR and refreshes when you come back to the tab. Unshielding history is classified once by a scheduled worker and cached, not rebuilt per page load. Ironwood refresh follows block timing. Charts are Recharts plus custom SVG. Share images are generated on the server and only emit once the numbers have actually loaded. The pop-out is a second live price surface. Desktop Chrome uses Document Picture-in-Picture (a real window, same React UI). On phones, where that API is flaky, the widget is drawn to a canvas, turned into a video stream, and popped out with the regular video PiP API so it still floats over other apps. I started with a CYPH/ZEC price page on May 3 and kept shipping. 277 commits through August 14, 2026. About 40,000 lines in 110 app TypeScript files, not counting a 57-file shadcn kit. Diff from the first commit: +46,835 / -2,696. I used AI tools to write faster. I chose what to build, checked the sources, tested it, and deployed it. ### Time Period of Work Completion May 2026 - August 2026 ### Total Budget (USD) $10,000 ### Budget Breakdown - Compensation: - $(USD): 10,000 - Justification: Three months of solo product and engineering work, roughly 100 hours. This is at a rate of $100/hour. - Technology/Software: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: None separate. - Infrastructure/Hosting: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: Domain and Cloudflare were self-funded. Not in this ask. - Services/Contractors: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: No contractors. - Other: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: None. - Total $(USD): 10,000 ### Previous Funding No ### Previous Funding Details N/A ### Other Funding Sources No ### Other Funding Sources Details N/A ### Success Metrics ### Shipped - Live at https://cyphzec.com. No account, no paywall. Checked August 14, 2026: all 16 routes returned HTTP 200 (`/`, `/ironwood`, `/shielding`, `/shielding/unshieldings`, `/stats`, `/bitcoin`, `/holdings`, `/what-if`, `/estimator`, `/portfolio`, `/exchanges`, `/updates`, `/about`, `/settings`, `/more`, `/orchard-risk`). - 277 commits, May 3 to August 14, 2026. - 16 pages, 30 API routes, ~40k lines of application TypeScript. - In-app `/updates` lists the major feature groups as they shipped. - Cloudflare HTTP Traffic, August 14, 2026: **last 7 days 217.98k requests;** **last 30 days 1.22M requests, 10.37k unique visitors (1.08k max / 227 min per day);** last-month strip 1,196,464 SSL requests. Requests include API polling and bots. Uniques are Cloudflare estimates, not lifetime people. - Other people have posted the site since May. A few examples: [Will McEvoy](https://x.com/will__mcevoy/status/2058750921253773473) (May 25, quoted `/what-if`: "Epic"), [Ben / @TheBookofBen](https://x.com/TheBookofBen/status/2057534979672768930) (May 21), [Slow_n_Steady / @seams5s](https://x.com/seams5s/status/2075488807005360606) (July 10, Ironwood), [same, BTC/ZEC](https://x.com/seams5s/status/2075556615068271067), [unshieldings](https://x.com/seams5s/status/2065072656899252309), [Link Marine](https://x.com/linkmarine/status/2074661844086882361) (July 8), [Tom Howard](https://x.com/_TomHoward/status/2076188528753643913) (July 12, Ironwood tracker), [The Market Tunnel](https://x.com/TheMarketTunnel/status/2052033054764372479) (May 6). ### Why it is useful - One place to watch pool balances and flows without an explorer account. - A dedicated Ironwood view for people who are not living in CipherScan. - ZEC price, supply, exchanges, and Cypherpunk treasury on a phone. - Labels that say what NAV / diluted NAV / mNAV / unshielding outcomes actually are. - Portfolio stays on-device. - Pop-out widget if you want the prices while you do something else. - I shipped changes people asked for (what-if BTC toggle, mobile layout, sharing, Ironwood). ### Proof of completion - Deployment/Release: - [Dashboard](https://cyphzec.com/) - including the POP-OUT widget - [Settings](https://cyphzec.com/settings) - [Ironwood](https://cyphzec.com/ironwood) - [Shielding](https://cyphzec.com/shielding) - [Unshieldings](https://cyphzec.com/shielding/unshieldings) - beta - [Stats](https://cyphzec.com/stats) - [Bitcoin / ZEC](https://cyphzec.com/bitcoin) - [Treasury](https://cyphzec.com/holdings) - [What-if](https://cyphzec.com/what-if) - [Estimator](https://cyphzec.com/estimator) - [Portfolio](https://cyphzec.com/portfolio) - [Exchanges](https://cyphzec.com/exchanges) - [Updates](https://cyphzec.com/updates) - Repository/Commit: - [Source](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker) - public, MIT - [First dashboard](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/58e675c) - [Shielding](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/c2b8959) - [Portfolio](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/9871383) - [Bitcoin / ZEC](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/aceffd4) - [Ironwood](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/6990170) - [Last product commit](https://github.com/tzarebczan/zec-cyph-tracker/commit/e6b079f) - Other: - Cloudflare traffic screenshots from August 14, 2026 - X posts listed under Success Metrics A few screenshots: ### Conflict of Interest Disclosure I hold ZEC and CYPH, so better public data helps me too. - [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@sangsoo-osec

### Organization or Individual Name

sangsoo-osec

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual for my own security-research contributions.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

I saw it on the Zcash Community Forum

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

425000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting a net retroactive security award for five responsibly disclosed Zebra vulnerabilities, each published by the Zcash Foundation as Critical, that could make Zebra and `zcashd` disagree on transaction or block validity. I used an LLM-assisted differential review to locate the mismatched consensus logic, then validated the findings against concrete code paths and reported them privately. Four reports predated the ZCG vulnerability bounty program; the fifth concerned a regression released after that program had closed. All five were accepted, remediated, and publicly disclosed. I received no payment through the official ZCG bounty framework; I disclose and fully deduct a separate $100,000 payment from a third-party organization from this request.

### Project Description

### The completed work

Zcash relies on independent node implementations reaching exactly the same answer about whether every transaction and block is valid. A disagreement between Zebra and `zcashd` can cause the implementations to follow different chains. I reviewed equivalent consensus-critical paths in the two implementations, found five distinct divergence conditions, validated their reachability, and reported them through the Zcash Foundation's coordinated disclosure process.

The five completed and published findings covered three separate consensus surfaces:

| Advisory | Public classification | Consensus mismatch | Remediation record |
|---|---|---|---|
| [GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj / CVE-2026-41583](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj) | Critical | Zebra failed to reject undefined V5 transparent sighash types and canonicalized V4 hash-type bytes where `zcashd` used the raw byte. Depending on the transaction version, one implementation could accept a transaction the other rejected. | Published and fixed in [Zebra 4.3.1](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.1). |
| [GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc / CVE-2026-44498](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc) | Critical | Zebra undercounted coinbase legacy sigops and omitted aggregate P2SH sigops from block validation. A miner could construct a block Zebra accepted but `zcashd` rejected for exceeding the 20,000-sigop limit. | Published with Zebra 4.4.0 listed as the patched version. |
| [GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp) | Critical; no CVE assigned | For V5 transparent `SIGHASH_SINGLE`, Zebra computed a digest when an input had no corresponding output, while `zcashd` failed validation under ZIP 244. The advisory documents a Zebra mempool → `getblocktemplate` → external-miner path to a block-validity split. | Published with Zebra 4.4.0 listed as the patched version; the same area received additional follow-up hardening in 4.4.1. |
| [GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv / CVE-2026-44497](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv) | Critical | The fix for the first sighash issue returned failure without overwriting an FFI output buffer. A valid signature check could prime the buffer, after which an undefined hash type reused the stale digest: Zebra accepted the spend and `zcashd` rejected it. | Fixed by [PR #10524](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10524) and released in [Zebra 4.4.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.4.0). |
| [GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443) | Critical; no CVE assigned | Zebra 4.5.0's P2SH sigop fix used legacy counting instead of `zcashd`'s accurate P2SH mode. Low-threshold multisig was counted as 20 sigops rather than its actual 1–16, so Zebra could reject a valid block whose true total remained below 20,000 while `zcashd` accepted it. No malicious miner was required: broadcasting enough valid P2SH spends was sufficient once an ordinary miner included them. | Patched in [Zebra 4.5.1](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.5.1); published 1 June 2026. |


### Why the outcome mattered

A consensus node's primary security property is that it enforces the protocol identically to the rest of the network. These defects crossed that boundary:

- malicious transactions or blocks could be accepted by Zebra and rejected by `zcashd`, or in the V4 hash-type case rejected by Zebra and accepted by `zcashd`;
- miners and block-template pipelines relying on Zebra could build on a chain that `zcashd` nodes would not accept;
- a materialized split could partition the node population, disrupt services, and create double-spend risk against parties following different chains; and
- immediate security releases and regression-oriented fixes were required to restore agreement.

I am not claiming that any of these bugs was exploited on mainnet or that a permanent split actually occurred. Prevention is the completed security outcome. The advisories also note an important mitigating fact: most miners were using `zcashd`, which reduced the practical likelihood that an offending Zebra-accepted block would become the dominant chain.

### Why this is a retroactive-grant request

The first four reports were submitted before the ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative was announced on 28 April 2026. ZCG later stated explicitly that its framework [does not apply retroactively and covers only reports submitted after that announcement](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545/15). 

The fifth finding fell into the gap at the other end of the program. ZCG [closed the vulnerability bounty program on 26 May 2026](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/closing-the-zcg-vulnerability-bounty-program/55855), stating that reports already submitted before closure would retain their existing terms. GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 affected Zebra 4.5.0, was fixed in 4.5.1, and was published on 1 June—after the program had closed. It therefore had no active bounty channel when the vulnerable version and my finding existed.

The five findings were not considered and rejected on their technical merits under the official ZCG bounty framework. The first four preceded the framework, and the fifth followed its closure. I received a separate $100,000 payment from another organization whose identity is not public, and I deduct that amount in full from this application to avoid double compensation. I received no ZCG or Zcash Foundation bounty for these findings. The Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program is the available mechanism for coinholders to recognize the remaining uncompensated value of these completed, accepted, and publicly verifiable security outcomes.


### Basis for the $425,000 request

The amount is based solely on the public payout schedule of the official ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative, a program that operated only briefly in 2026. I use that short-lived program as a convenient, ecosystem-specific reference point because it supplied a published value for a Core Node / Critical finding; I do not suggest that its terms bind this separate retroactive-grant process.

That schedule set a $150,000 base payout for a Core Node / Critical finding. Zebra was expressly listed as a Core Node repository, and each of the five advisories in this application is publicly labeled Critical by the Zcash Foundation. I have voluntarily divided that base equally wherever the public record identifies two researchers, rather than asking for the full base for myself.

| Advisory | Credit basis used here | Amount requested before third-party deduction |
|---|---|---:|
| GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj | Two publicly acknowledged researchers: Alex “Scalar” Sol and `sangsoo-osec` | $75,000 |
| GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc | Two structured reporter credits: `sangsoo-osec` and `defuse` | $75,000 |
| GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp | Two structured reporter credits: `sangsoo-osec` and `defuse` | $75,000 |
| GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv | Sole reporter: `sangsoo-osec` | $150,000 |
| GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443 | Sole reporter: `sangsoo-osec` | $150,000 |
| **Gross amount based on reporter allocation** |  | **$525,000** |
| **Less another organization payment already received** |  | **-$100,000** |
| **Net requested grant** |  | **$425,000** |

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

### LLM-assisted differential consensus review

The core method was semantic differential analysis between `zcashd`, the established C++ implementation, and Zebra, the independent Rust implementation. Rather than asking an LLM to generate unverified bug reports, I used it to accelerate code navigation, map conceptually equivalent validation paths across two large codebases, and generate focused hypotheses about places where the implementations might encode the same consensus rule differently.

For each hypothesis, I then traced the actual production path and checked the consensus outcome on both sides:

1. **Identify the invariant.** I started from rules where exact agreement is mandatory: permitted signature hash types, sighash-preimage construction, the block-wide sigop ceiling, and ZIP-244's `SIGHASH_SINGLE` failure conditions.
2. **Map both implementations.** I followed `zcashd`'s C++ validation and Zebra's Rust/C++ FFI path to find where each implementation parsed, normalized, counted, or rejected the same data.
3. **Compare behavior, not syntax.** The relevant bugs were not simple identical-code matches. They included a rule lost across a refactor, raw-versus-canonical byte semantics, a per-transaction count omitted from a block-wide aggregate, a library returning an empty-output hash where the caller expected failure, and a failure signal lost at an FFI boundary.
4. **Validate exploitability.** I reduced each difference to a concrete transaction, script, or block condition and checked which implementation accepted and which rejected it. For the `SIGHASH_SINGLE` report, the public advisory records the pinned Zebra and `zcashd` revisions, the exact missing-output construction, and the ordinary Zebra mempool-to-block-template path.
5. **Report privately and reproducibly.** I submitted the issues through Zebra's private GitHub Security Advisory process with the relevant code paths, expected and actual behavior, impact analysis, and reproduction logic, allowing maintainers to triage and remediate before public disclosure.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Q2 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - USD: $0 in reimbursable costs
  - Justification: This request is for the value of five completed, accepted security outcomes, not reimbursement of salary or hours.
- Technology/Software:
  - USD: $0 claimed

- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - USD: $0 claimed

  - Justification: No other costs are claimed.
- **Total costs: $0**


### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

_No response_

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

1. I received $100,000 from another organization. I disclose that payment here and deduct it in full from the $525,000 gross reporter-adjusted valuation, leaving a net request of $425,000. 

2. I received bounties from [ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcg-security-vulnerability-disclosure-initiative/55545) for bugs I didn’t mention here. details: [Zcash Community Grants Coinholder Grants Dashboard](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FQ28rDCyRW0TiNxrm3rgD8ai2KGUsXAjPieQmI1kKKg/edit?gid=2043949055#gid=2043949055)


### Success Metrics

### Quantitative evidence

- **5** accepted and published GitHub Security Advisories, all labeled **Critical** by the affected project's remediation team.
- **3** assigned CVEs: CVE-2026-41583, CVE-2026-44498, and CVE-2026-44497; two advisories state that no CVE is known.
- **5** distinct consensus failures: V4/V5 hash-type handling, coinbase and aggregate P2SH block sigop undercounting, V5 `SIGHASH_SINGLE` missing-output handling, stale-buffer reuse across a Rust/C++ FFI callback, and P2SH multisig sigop overcounting in Zebra 4.5.0.
- **3** security releases directly carrying the listed remediations: Zebra 4.3.1, Zebra 4.4.0, and Zebra 4.5.1, plus subsequent `SIGHASH_SINGLE` follow-up hardening in 4.4.1.
- Affected-version records covering all supported Zebra versions before 4.3.1 for the first finding, all versions before 4.4.0 for the earlier sigop and `SIGHASH_SINGLE` advisories, the short-lived 4.3.1 code path for the stale-buffer regression, and Zebra 4.5.0 for the later P2SH overcount.
- Public structured credits naming `sangsoo-osec` as a reporter on every advisory in this application.

### Qualitative evidence

- **Consensus safety:** The work removed cases where two Zcash full-node implementations could disagree on transaction or block validity—the boundary a multi-implementation network most needs to protect.
- **Mining-path safety:** The findings covered both direct block validation and Zebra's mempool/block-template path, reducing the chance that a Zebra-backed miner would build an incompatible block.
- **Depth rather than scanner volume:** The defects required reasoning across languages, repositories, consensus specifications, aggregation layers, and an FFI error contract. Each report led to an accepted advisory rather than an unverified ticket.
- **Responsible disclosure:** The findings were reported privately, giving maintainers time to reproduce, fix, release, and notify operators before full technical publication.


### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [Zebra PR #10524 — fix stale sighash issue](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10524) — merged 1 May 2026; the PR body states that it fixes GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv.
  - [Zebra changelog](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) — records the 4.3.1, 4.4.0, and 4.5.1 security releases and links the relevant advisories.
- Publication:
  - [GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj / CVE-2026-41583](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj) — Critical; credits `sangsoo-osec` as reporter.
  - [GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc / CVE-2026-44498](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-jv4h-j224-23cc) — Critical; credits `sangsoo-osec` as reporter.
  - [GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-cwfq-rfcr-8hmp) — Critical; credits `sangsoo-osec` as reporter and contains pinned revisions and a public reproduction path.
  - [GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv / CVE-2026-44497](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-gq4h-3grw-2rhv) — Critical; lists `sangsoo-osec` as the sole reporter.
  - [GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-2prc-cj5x-4443) — Critical; lists `sangsoo-osec` as the sole reporter and documents the no-mining-capability trigger and Zebra 4.5.1 patch.
- Deployment/Release:
  - [Zebra 4.3.1](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.1) — security release containing the hash-type consensus fix.
  - [Zebra 4.4.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.4.0) — security release containing the sigop and stale-buffer remediations and other consensus fixes.
  - [Zebra 4.5.1](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.5.1) — hotfix that corrected P2SH sigop counting to match `zcashd` and thanks `sangsoo-osec` for reporting the issue.
  - [Zcash Foundation: Zebra 4.3.1 Critical Security Fixes](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zebra-4-3-1-critical-security-fixes-dockerized-mining-and-ci-hardening/55389) — describes both directions of the sighash divergence and thanks me for the independent report.

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Following discussions with Shielded Labs about compensation for these findings, and ZCG's decision on additional funding, Shielded Labs suggested that this retroactive grants program was the right venue to bring the question to the community.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$400,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I'm requesting a retroactive bounty for multiple vulnerabilities I found and responsibly disclosed across Zcash's two node implementations, `zcashd` and `zebra` nodes

The Sprout proof-verification bypass (live since 2020) lets a miner slip invalid Sprout spends past `zcashd`. The duplicate-header bug disables ZIP 209 turnstile enforcement. And the consensus-divergence and node-crash findings take Zebra.. Composed, is an exploit to temporary **detectable** unlimited mint-and-sell of counterfeit ZEC (likely few hours windows)

### Project Description

At the end of February 2026 I began auditing several privacy coin protocols, looking for critical vulnerabilities and mainly for inflation bugs. 

That work turned up findings in Grin, in Litecoin's MWEB (found independently, a few hours after the LTC devs), and in a few other projects that were quietly patched and never disclosed to their community.

Then I decided to take a shot at Zcash :shield:

Between March and April, I found and privately disclosed multiple vulnerabilities to Shielded Labs

**zcashd**

| Finding | Impact |
|---|---|
| [Sprout proof verification skipped](https://zodl.com/zcashd-sprout-verification-vulnerability) | Invalid Sprout spends accepted; present since July 2020 |
| Identity `rk` in Orchard actions | Crashes zcashd during proof verification |
| Identity `epk` | Spec requires a non-identity point; Zebra enforced it, zcashd did not. Consensus split |
| Duplicate block header | Silently resets pool balance tracking, disabling ZIP 209 turnstile enforcement |

The Sprout bug came first; the other followed in the same codebase over the following days.

**Zebra**

| Advisory | CVE |
|---|---|
| [Consensus Failure via Crafted V5 Authorization Data](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-3vmh-33xr-9cqh) | CVE-2026-34377 | 
| [Consensus Divergence in Transparent Sighash Hash-Type Handling](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-8m29-fpq5-89jj) (credit to @sangsoo-osec) | CVE-2026-41583 |
| [rk Identity Point Panic in Transaction Verification](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-452v-w3gx-72wg) | CVE-2026-41584 |


Composed together, this leads to a chained critical exploits: 
- split consensus between Zebra and zcashd
- use the identity `rk` panic to knock out Zebra nodes
-cspray duplicate headers to disable turnstile enforcement
- use the sprout verification bypass to temporary mint and withdraw from the sprout pool unlimited zec and sell it and hypothetically coul have lasted during few hours before the network could respond


**On the requested amount.** My benchmark is the worst case these findings put on the table: temporary unlimited mint-and-sell of counterfeit ZEC. And hypothetically +10m to +100m in damage. We will never know, defender got it first!


### Technical Approach (how you did it)


Manual code review, backed by heavy testing and assisted by AI. The target was the critical consensus path:

- **Proof verification**: the checks that a shielded spend is actually valid.
- **Sighash construction**: how the signed message is computed, where a small difference between implementations becomes a consensus split.
- **Pool balance accounting**: the ZIP 209 turnstiles, which are the only supply-visibility a shielded chain has left.
- **Shared cryptographic libraries**: `librustzcash` and the primitives underneath both nodes, where one bug reaches zcashd and Zebra at once.

Also prompt such as: 
> (claude) find inflations bug, make no mistakes


### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Background knowledge as an active community member

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$599,000

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

This application seeks retroactive reimbursement for $599,000 of external security review costs incurred during the Ironwood incident response. Immediately after the soundness vulnerability was disclosed, we engaged leading cryptography and blockchain auditors and state-of-the-art AI tools to ensure no second soundness bug existed.

This does not include any margin to Valargroup, or costs to any Valargroup team member.

### Project Description

The work began rapidly, right after the NU6_2 soundness bug was found. 
This is when uncertainty and concern across the ecosystem were at their highest. 
This was emergency security work. The cost is higher than normally scheduled
audits because the firms were asked to change their priority queues and assign their best
auditors on short notice, away from their existing engagements.

The response included:

- **Zellic:** Audits looking for latent soundness bugs across the Ironwood
  changes in Orchard, `librustzcash`, and the Ironwood scope in Zakura, along
  with a separate completed audit of Sapling.
- **OtterSec:** A review of Halo 2, Orchard, and Zebra/Zakura focused on
  soundness vulnerabilities. This work identified numerous bugs in the
  Zebra peer-to-peer stack and optimizations for Halo 2 verification.
- **v12:** $100,000 in https://v12.sh credits used to audit Zcash repositories and Ironwood
  development with frontier AI models.
- **Additional outreach:** We also attempted to engage other firms to obtain
  further access to frontier models and expand the independent review surface.

The v12 credits were consumed during the Ironwood incident response. 
Project Tachyon team-members also shared these credits, expressly working on
Ironwood and ensuring no second bug with them as well.

Waiting for a normal grant cycle and normal audit scheduling would have delayed the response at precisely
the moment when speed mattered most, and uncertainty of a second bug was highest. 
We funded the work immediately so that independent experts and AI-assisted review
could begin while the vulnerability was fresh and the risk of an undiscovered 
related flaw was the community's most urgent concern.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

The response combined independent manual review by specialist cryptographic
auditors and AI-assisted review of Zcash repositories and Ironwood
development. Audit scopes included the protocol and proof-system components
most relevant to soundness, as well as implementation review across Orchard,
Sapling, Halo 2, `librustzcash`, and Zebra/Zakura.

Using independent firms and separate frontier-model review efforts increased
coverage and reduced the risk that a single methodology, reviewer, or tool
would miss a related vulnerability. Findings were reported to the appropriate
developers for validation and remediation.

The firms detail their methodology in their audit reports.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Day before NU6_2 hard fork to August 14th

### Total Budget (USD)

$599,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: null
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 100,000
  - Justification: Using state of the art AI auditing tools, built on a corpus of all blockchain vulnerabilities.
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 499,000
  - Justification: Audits as needed

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

_No response_

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

Valargroup currently operates on donations and retroactive grants.

### Success Metrics

The work expanded independent security coverage during a high-risk period for
Zcash. Its outputs include:

- independent soundness-focused review of critical protocol and implementation
  components;
- completed independent audit coverage of Sapling;
- identification of numerous bugs in the Zebra peer-to-peer stack; Many seen and
  patched as GHSA's in Zebra and Zakura.
- identification of optimizations for Halo 2 verification; and
- repository-wide review using multiple frontier AI systems, along with myriads of
  v12.sh PR comments.

These were additionally the only audits covering the Ironwood scope, so Ironwood could
not have shipped without these, per the ZIP-0 requirements for audits.

The intended users and relevant maintainers can validate the audit scopes,
findings, and value of the completed work. Public reports and findings will be
linked or disclosed where doing so is safe, contractually permitted, and
consistent with responsible vulnerability disclosure.

The Zellic reports can be found here: https://github.com/Zellic/publications/pull/245
The current Ottersec audit report draft can be found here: https://zakura.com/audits/ottersec/ottersec-zcash-stack-2026-07-v1.pdf
The current Sapling audit report draft can be found here: https://zakura.com/audits/zellic/Zcash-sapling.pdf

All expenses have an associated invoice, aside from one $28,000 expected expense to be invoiced in August.
