I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1) @Connaugh ### Organization or Individual Name Connaugh ### Additional Team Members ```team-members.yaml My Background Six years in tech marketing across biotech, AI and crypto, the last two and a half in zero-knowledge cryptography at Mina Foundation and o1Labs. There I built the ecosystem content programme and ran it at a consistent cadence for over a year, the first time that had been sustained in that ecosystem. It held because of process rather than effort: a repeatable pipeline built around the constraints of the crypto industry. I produced many different types of videos including: thought leadership, Ecosystem highlights, protocol upgrades, whiteboard sessions, fundraising announcements, whitepaper announcements and more. I do research, scripting, editing, graphic design and distribution myself. That removes the handoffs that normally set the ceiling on how often a small team can publish, and it is the reason the cost per film and speed of delivery in this application is what it is. My Responsibilities - Sourcing and archiving video from across the Zcash ecosystem: co-founders, engineers, the ecosystem organisations, external advocates, and the institutional cohort - Editorial. Finding the story inside each source, and threading claims across separate videos so speakers corroborate one another - Verifying technical claims against primary sources - Scripting and voiceover - Editing, graphic design, sound design and packaging - Publishing and distribution - Series architecture and publishing cadence ``` ### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program? Through conversations with the Cypherpunk Technologies team, who directed me to the Zcash Community Grants team. ### Requested Grant Amount (USD) $22,000 ### Category Media ### Project Summary Zcash produces more high-quality video than almost any ecosystem its size, scattered across founders, engineers, the ecosystem organisations, external advocates and its institutional backers. I cut that footage and re-architect it into short, single-argument films designed for audiences who will never sit through a two-hour podcast: five films published between 28 July and 12 August 2026, reaching 45,811 impressions and 9,931 views from a standing start. 31 days total work including research, editing and publishing. ### Project Description - Overview Zcash has huge potential with its current video output. Every month the ecosystem produces a serious volume of video: protocol engineers explaining upgrades, co-founders on podcasts, the organisations building on Zcash, advocates from other ecosystems, and the institutional cohort that has arrived over the past year. The material is excellent. It is also long, spread across a dozen channels, and mostly reaching people who are already convinced. I want to pull all the content into one place and re-edit it to tell the Zcash story with less friction. Each film pulls clips from across the ecosystem and threads them into a single argument, so that people who were recorded months apart, in different places, end up corroborating each other on camera. The technical claims stay in the mouths of the people who built the protocol. My job is the through-line. - Origin The work started with Ironwood. The upgrade was significant, and the explanation of it was scattered, with different aspects covered by different people in different places. Nothing assembled them. I built the first film to do that and shipped it within a week. - Why the films are short Each film carries one or two points, told once, properly. Three things follow. The archive compounds. Crypto content dates fast, whether through protocol changes or shifts in the political situation. A long film dies as a whole when one section goes stale. A short film making a single point stays publishable, which means every film I make adds to a library I can keep drawing on instead of a back catalogue that decays. Fragmenting the case widens the reach. Zcash is not one story. It is an institutional story, an apolitical money story, a cypherpunk story, a technical story about what the protocol does, the people, etc. Different stories and viewpoints are critical for reaching different audiences. Cutting to the point level lets each audience find the argument aimed at them, and lets advocates share the exact claim they care about instead of a film that is three-quarters about something else. The format is what distribution rewards. Short, fast-paced explainer video is the dominant form outside crypto and thinly served inside it, where most output is either long-form conversation or low-effort promotion. The video direction of travel is visible: Ethereum has committed to an in-house media team, and a16z's video output over the past six months has moved towards short documentary work at a production standard the rest of the industry has not matched. - Why this is worth funding Having one person with a specialist background to run the entire video process will dramatically reduce costs and time. I want to commit to a cadence of 2 videos a week to really help grow the Zcash momentum. Because research, script, edit, design and distribution all sit with one person, these cost $3,000 each and ship published. It multiplies work the ecosystem has already paid for. Every film is built from footage that already exists. This does not compete with the podcasts, talks, and engineering explainers being made across Zcash. It extends their reach to people who were never going to watch them in full. It is already working. Five films, 16 days, no existing Zcash audience, and the numbers are set out below. ### Technical Approach (how you did it) - Process Every film runs the same five stages. Research. I gather source material from across the ecosystem: podcast appearances, conference talks, engineering explainers, interviews. Each clip is logged against the claim it supports. Editorial. I build the narrative before I open the timeline. Claims are threaded so that speakers recorded independently corroborate one another. Anything technical is checked against primary sources. Scripting. I write voiceover into the gaps only. Source clips carry the mechanism, voiceover carries the consequence, which keeps the technical claims with the people who built the protocol and keeps me out of the way of them. Production. Editing, sound design, and music in Adobe Premiere Pro. Motion and graphic design in Figma. Distribution. Published to X, packaged and hooked for that feed specifically. - Tooling and position on AI Premiere Pro for editing. Figma for design. Claude for research synthesis and script structure. ElevenLabs for generated video assets, including a generated likeness of myself used as an on-screen presenter. All narration is my own recorded voice. There is no voice cloning and no synthetic narration anywhere in this work. I use AI at the edges and keep it out of the center. The edit is done by hand in professional software, deliberately. Template-driven AI video tools produce output that is recognisable on sight, and in an ecosystem whose entire value proposition is credibility, content that looks automatically generated damages the argument it is making. That is an editorial decision before it is a technical one. - Equipment Recording and production hardware, including a Shure SM7dB and mixing desk, is mine and self-funded. It is not claimed here. ### Time Period of Work Completion 13 July 2026 to 12 August 2026 (31 days) working full time, weekends and evenings. Five films published over 16 days (publishing period only). ### Total Budget (USD) $22,000 ### Budget Breakdown
Line | Amount | Justification -- | -- | -- Compensation | $22,000 | Time only, priced per film + initial research week ($4,000). Launch film $6,000, covering the longer build and the research base it established. Four subsequent films at $3,000 each. Technology / Software | $0 | Adobe, Figma and AI tooling subscriptions self-funded. Not claimed. Infrastructure / Hosting | $0 | None incurred. Services / Contractors | $0 | Sole producer. No third parties engaged. Other | $0 | Recording and production equipment owned and self-funded. Not claimed. Total | $22,000 |  
### Previous Funding No ### Previous Funding Details _No response_ ### Other Funding Sources Yes ### Other Funding Sources Details I have received no funding for this work from any source. I intend to explore different funding options within the Zcash ecosystem for future work. I believe I can dramatically scale video content and reach in the Zcash ecosystem. ### Success Metrics

The account carried no Zcash audience when this started. Every figure below was built from a standing start. Snapshot taken 14 August 2026, 14:29 BST.

Film | Impressions | Views | Likes | Reposts | Replies -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- Ironwood launch | 5,479 | 1,483 | 87 | 17 | 8 Scaling Zcash to Visa levels | 3,322 | 713 | 45 | 9 | 2 Zcash never upgraded its privacy | 8,018 | 2,679 | 123 | 27 | 4 You don't have a right to a bank account | 16,578 | 2,486 | 68 | 15 | 1 Zcash is much better than Bitcoin | 12,414 | 2,570 | 133 | 37 | 10 Total | 45,811 | 9,931 | 456 | 105 | 25
Reach grew across the run. Each of the three most recent films reached more people than either of the first two, and the strongest took roughly three times the impressions of the opener. Views tracked the same curve. Films three and five drew the heaviest engagement of the set. Film four reached the largest audience by some margin on lighter engagement. The full set is reported here, including the weakest performer. Five films is an early signal rather than a proven programme, and the figures are presented as such. ### Proof of completion All five films published on X at @zkmarketer. - Ironwood launch: https://x.com/zkmarketer/status/2082103793253335140 - Scaling Zcash to Visa levels: https://x.com/zkmarketer/status/2082880148924190798 - Zcash has never upgraded its privacy: https://x.com/zkmarketer/status/2084651572529627618 - You don't have a right to a bank account: https://x.com/zkmarketer/status/2085691623367696612 - Zcash is much better than Bitcoin. Satoshi would agree: https://x.com/zkmarketer/status/2087188128561795464 Analytics snapshot for each film, taken 14 August 2026, 14:29 BST. ### Conflict of Interest Disclosure N/A ### Community Forum Posting - [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. - [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@robustfengbin

### Organization or Individual Name

robustfengbin (independent security researcher)

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. I am applying as an individual, and I am the sole credited reporter on this advisory.

For context on the public record: my ZCG #234 grant proposal describes that fuzzing programme in the first person plural, because that engineering grant has a co-proposer. This application concerns the vulnerability finding only — on which the advisory credits me alone — and I am applying for it as an individual.

Remediation was carried out by the Zcash Foundation's Zebra team — @arya2 and @upbqdn (remediation developers), @conradoplg (remediation reviewer), @mpguerra (coordinator), @alchemydc (analyst), per the advisory's structured credits. The fix shipped within days of the report. This application requests nothing on their behalf.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

From the Zcash Community Forum, following the Q3 2026 call for proposals and the ongoing discussion about how the ecosystem should compensate security research in the absence of an active bug bounty programme.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$150000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting a bug bounty for CVE-2026-34202, a Critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2) vulnerability that let any unauthenticated peer crash any Zebra node with a single P2P message. I found it through coverage-guided fuzzing while my ZCG grant application for that fuzzing work was still under committee review and unfunded, reported it privately through the Zcash Foundation's coordinated disclosure process, and supported remediation. It shipped fixed in Zebra 4.3.0. No bounty was ever paid for it, and none can be: ZCG's vulnerability bounty programme launched 32 days later and does not apply retroactively.

### Project Description

On 27 March 2026 the Zcash Foundation published GHSA-qp6f-w4r3-h8wg (CVE-2026-34202), "Remote Denial of Service via Crafted V5 Transactions", rated Critical with a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2. I am the sole credited reporter. The advisory reads: "Thanks to robustfengbin who discovered this issue and reported it via our coordinated disclosure process."

WHAT THE BUG WAS

Zebra lazily validated transaction fields that librustzcash validates eagerly. A malformed V5 transaction passed Zebra's network codec cleanly, and then panicked the node when Zebra converted it to compute the transaction ID — a conversion the code assumed could not fail. Per the advisory, an attacker could "trigger this crash by sending a single crafted tx message to a Zebra node's public P2P port", and the same path was reachable through the sendrawtransaction RPC. Scope, in the Foundation's words: "Any node with an open P2P port (default 8233) or exposed RPC interface is vulnerable."

Remote. Unauthenticated. No user interaction, no special configuration, no privileged position. One message, one dead node — and the same message worked against every reachable Zebra node below 4.3.0.

WHAT THE FOUNDATION DID WITH IT

Zebra 4.3.0 shipped on 26 March 2026 with the fix, under the headline "Critical Security Fixes", telling operators that "all node operators are strongly encouraged to upgrade immediately". The Foundation's Q1 2026 report records it in full: "Zebra 4.3.0 was a critical security release addressing two responsibly disclosed vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-34202 (CVSS 9.2), a remote DoS via crafted V5 transactions that could crash a node, and CVE-2026-34377 (CVSS 8.4), a consensus logic error that could allow a malicious miner to induce a chain split. Both were patched, disclosed publicly, and test generators were updated to provide broader coverage against regressions."

The remediation was structural rather than local. The advisory states the fix "ensures that any transaction that would fail TxID calculation is rejected during the initial deserialization phase, and replaces internal panics with graceful error handling" — it removed a category of failure, not one instance of it (PR #10426). The Foundation paired it with regression coverage in the V5 transaction generator and NU5 branch ID strategy (PR #10429), listed in the release post under "Improved Test Coverage".

WHERE THIS SITS IN ZEBRA'S RECORD

Zebra's public GitHub security-advisory record currently contains 39 published advisories. The earliest publication date in that record is 27 March 2026, when exactly two were published: CVE-2026-34377 (High, 8.4) and this one (Critical, 9.2). This is therefore the first Critical in Zebra's public GitHub security-advisory record. The next Critical in that record appears three weeks later, on 17 April 2026.

I state that with the qualifier "in Zebra's public GitHub security-advisory record" deliberately. It is a claim about that record, not about the whole history of the project — Zebra's network layer had been fuzzed before, by Ziggurat, and real vulnerabilities were found and fixed then too. The claim I am making is narrow, and it can be checked in a single unauthenticated API call.

I should also say plainly that I was not the only external researcher involved in that release. The Foundation's release post also thanks alexs-scalar, for a separate issue fixed in the same release — the V5 transaction proof verification bypass (PR #10425). I am not claiming to have been the only person helping Zebra that month, and this application says nothing about anyone else's work.

WHY I AM ASKING COINHOLDERS RATHER THAN ZCG

ZCG launched its $1,000,000 Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative on 28 April 2026 — 32 days after this advisory was published. Asked directly on the announcement thread whether earlier reports qualified, ZCG answered: "No, the program does not apply retroactively. Only security issues submitted after the official announcement of the ZCG Security & Vulnerability Disclosure Initiative (April 28, 2026) are eligible for payouts under this specific framework."

The programme also states that "ZCG, under the administration of FPF, does not accept payout requests directly from researchers"; a payment request comes from the remediation team after triage, not from the researcher.

I want to be precise about what that adds up to, because it is the whole basis of this application. This finding was not judged and rejected. It was not weighed and found wanting. It fell outside a framework that did not exist when it was made, and there is no mechanism inside that framework through which it could ever be considered. ZCG's own wording — "under this specific framework" — leaves the question of recognition to some other mechanism. This programme is that other mechanism.

So for a vulnerability disclosed in March 2026 there is no bounty channel at all. Not a channel I was refused — a channel that did not exist. As Jason McGee wrote in application #53 this round: "The retroactive grants program is currently the only mechanism that can pay a researcher for a catastrophic finding."

This is the same gap Taylor Hornby describes in application #51, seen from the other side: his bug was found days after ZCG's programme closed, mine 32 days before it opened.

For context, and without drawing any comparison to my own case: ZCG's launch announcement for that programme also contained a retroactive act — "we've matched the awards previously given to Alex Sol — 200 ZEC for his first disclosure and 100 ZEC for his second — bringing his total compensation to 600 ZEC in recognition of his contributions." Those were separate disclosures on a separate timeline, and I make no claim of equivalence to them. I mention it only because it shows that recognising work done before the programme existed is not a novel idea in this ecosystem.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

The finding came out of a multi-layer fuzzing harness, and I described the method publicly on 24 March 2026 — three days before the advisory was published, while the disclosure was still embargoed — in the forum thread for ZCG grant application #234. What follows is that same account, and it can be checked against the record rather than taken on trust.

THE METHOD

Standard fuzzing of a node's deserialization path asks one question: does this input deserialize without panicking? I had run exactly that against Zebra — 95.6 million iterations across six targets, seeded with real mainnet data (1,565 transactions and 473 blocks pulled from a fully-synced Zebra node), distributed across a 2-core GCP instance and an 8-core dedicated server for roughly 52x scaling.

It found nothing. Zero crashes in 95.6 million iterations.

The methodological contribution was to stop treating successful deserialization as the end of the test. The multi-layer harness takes the object that deserialized cleanly and keeps going: property access, hash computation, consensus checks, fee calculation. That is where the interesting failures live, because that is where code assumes an object which parsed must also be well-formed enough for everything downstream.

That harness found a reportable issue within minutes of deployment — the first day it ran.

This detail is independently checkable against the vulnerability itself. The advisory describes a transaction that "passes initial deserialization but fails during transaction ID calculation". Layer-1 deserialize-only fuzzing is structurally incapable of finding that class of bug, which is precisely why 95.6 million iterations of it found nothing. The contemporaneous account of the method and the technical description of the defect corroborate each other.

TRIAGE AND DISCLOSURE

The crash-handling process I described in that same post, and had just executed end to end on this finding:

1. Discovery — the fuzzer flags a crash and the triggering input is preserved automatically.
2. Reproduction — minimise the test case with `cargo fuzz tmin`, confirm stable reproduction.
3. Classification — assign severity and, critically, analyse reachability: can this be triggered remotely, over P2P, over RPC? This is the step that separates a local assertion failure from a network-exposed vulnerability, and in this case it established that a single unauthenticated `tx` message to the default P2P port was sufficient.
4. Reporting — Critical and High findings go privately to the Zcash Foundation security team within 24 hours via GitHub Security Advisory per Zebra's SECURITY.md. Medium and Low go to public issues.
5. Documentation — each report carries the minimised input, stack trace, impact analysis, reachability assessment and a suggested fix.
6. Fix assistance and verification.
7. A 90-day responsible disclosure window.

I followed that process here rather than filing a public issue, and stayed inside the embargo even while a grant reviewer was publicly questioning whether I could do this work — on 24 March I told the committee a finding existed and declined to describe it.

The Foundation's release post records the outcome: "Thanks to robustfengbin for responsibly disclosing the vulnerability and working with us to quickly reproduce and remediate it." The fix merged as PR #10426 on 25 March 2026, with regression coverage in PR #10429 the same evening, and shipped in Zebra 4.3.0 on 26 March.

TOOLING DISCLOSURE

I use AI assistants as part of my development workflow, and said so publicly in that same forum thread when a reviewer raised it. They accelerate fuzzing-harness design and code-path analysis. The security judgement, the methodology design, the reachability analysis and the disclosure process were human-driven. I mention it because it is already on the public record and because this ecosystem is, rightly, paying attention to the difference between AI-assisted research and AI-generated noise.

CONTEXT ON THE PROPOSAL'S FRAMING

My #234 proposal argued that Zebra lacked in-tree fuzzing infrastructure. That characterisation was partly corrected on the forum by a community member who pointed out that Ziggurat had previously fuzzed Zebra's network layer and found real vulnerabilities. The accurate, narrower statement is that the repository carried no cargo-fuzz configuration, no in-tree fuzz targets and no OSS-Fuzz registration. I would rather restate it correctly here than repeat a claim that has already been publicly qualified.

The relationship between this finding and grant #234 is set out in full under Other Funding Sources. I have not left it for reviewers to discover.

### Time Period of Work Completion

March 2026 — discovery, coordinated disclosure and remediation support; fix shipped in Zebra 4.3.0 on 26 March 2026; advisory published 27 March 2026.

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

This application claims no costs, so the budget total above is zero. The finding cost me machine time on hardware I already had; the fuzzing programme's compute is covered under ZCG #234, disclosed below and not claimed here. The requested amount is not a reimbursement for expenses — it is a bounty for a specific accepted, remediated and publicly disclosed Critical vulnerability, and it should be judged on the value of that outcome rather than on what it cost to produce.

Where the $150,000 figure comes from:

ZCG's published payout schedule sets a base payout of $150,000 for a Core Node / Critical finding, with a discretionary bonus of up to $75,000 on top, and states that Core Node "is the only category eligible for a Critical rating". Zebra is a Core Node repository. The Zcash Foundation rated this finding Critical.

I offer that schedule to coinholders as a reference point for valuing the finding, not as an entitlement. The programme it belongs to does not apply to this disclosure, and I set out the argument against using its Critical tier here under Success Metrics, alongside my answer to it.

I am expressly NOT requesting the $75,000 bonus. ZCG describes that bonus as "awarded at the full discretion of the remediation team", and it is not mine to ask coinholders to exercise on their behalf.

### Previous Funding

Yes

### Previous Funding Details

I have not received previous funding from the Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program.

I do hold two grants from Zcash Community Grants, which is a separate programme. Both are milestone-based engineering grants and neither pays for vulnerability findings. They are set out in full under Other Funding Sources, together with the timeline of how one of them relates to this finding.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

I hold two grants from Zcash Community Grants (ZCG), a separate programme from this one. Both are milestone-based engineering grants; neither pays for vulnerability findings.

- ZCG #234, "Zebra Coverage-Guided Fuzzing Infrastructure" — $30,000 over six months. Approved by ZCG vote on 30 March 2026, three days after this advisory was published. Milestone 1 ($9,000) paid 1 June 2026; Milestone 2 ($9,000) paid 19 June 2026. Deliverables to date include five fuzz targets with published per-target coverage figures, CI integration, and OSS-Fuzz submission work.
- ZCG #332, "Batch-vs-Single Verification Equivalence: Continuous Soundness Verification" — approved 29 June 2026; Milestone 1 complete 27 July 2026.

CVE-2026-34202 does not appear as a deliverable, acceptance criterion, or payment justification in either grant.

The first of those grants has a genuine complication attached to it, and I would rather put it in front of coinholders myself, in full, than have it surface during the review period.

1) THE RELATIONSHIP TO ZCG GRANT #234

The fuzzing work that found this bug is the work described in ZCG grant application #234. I am not going to describe this finding as unrelated to that grant, because it is not.

What I will say is that when the finding was made, that grant did not exist as a funded engagement. The whole sequence is on the public record, in the grant's own forum thread and in GitHub:

  16 March 2026 — I submit ZCG #234. Status: awaiting committee review.
  23 March 2026 — A ZCG committee member posts a direct objection: "Proposer credibility gap on fuzzing specifically... I found no public evidence of fuzzing work. No fuzz targets, no crash triage, no OSS-Fuzz contributions."
  24 March 2026 — I reply, disclosing the existence of the finding but not its details: "we've continued our PoC work and our deep fuzzing methodology has already uncovered a security issue that we've reported to the Zcash Foundation through Zebra's official responsible disclosure process... We can't share details until the disclosure process completes."
  25 March 2026 — Fix PRs #10426 and #10429 merged.
  26 March 2026 — Zebra 4.3.0 released with the fix.
  26 March 2026 — The same committee member confirms independently: "I can confirm that the bug that you found and reported responsibly in Zebra was 1) serious and 2) remotely exploitable. Indeed this validates your approach, methodology and triage capabilities. Bravo!"
  27 March 2026 — Advisory GHSA-qp6f-w4r3-h8wg published.
  30 March 2026 — ZCG votes to approve #234. Milestone 1's first month runs 30 March to 30 April.

So the discovery, the private report, the remediation, the release and the public disclosure were all complete before ZCG approved the grant. The work was unfunded and uncontracted at the time, and there was no bounty programme in existence to claim from. ZCG's later exclusion for "defects surfaced through... an active ZCG grant" turns on the word active, and on 24 March 2026 that grant was not active — it was being argued about.

I would put the causality the honest way round rather than the flattering way round: I cannot claim this finding caused the grant to be approved, because I cannot know why each committee member voted as they did. What the public record does show is that the finding was raised by the committee's own reviewer as validation of the methodology and triage capability he had just questioned, and that approval followed four days after the confirmation quoted above. It materially strengthened the case for approval.

Separately from timing: #234 is a $30,000 six-month engineering grant whose deliverables are fuzz targets, CI integration and OSS-Fuzz onboarding, accepted and paid against milestones. No milestone is conditioned on finding vulnerabilities. That grant bought capability. It did not price this outcome, and it could not have — the milestones would have been paid identically had the fuzzing found nothing.

Jason McGee made the same distinction in application #53 this round, about Taylor Hornby's contracting relationship with Shielded Labs: "We paid for auditing effort at a standard consulting rate. We did not, and could not, pay for the outcome... His rate did not include a discovery premium, and no bounty program in the world nets out salary before paying an award."

If coinholders nonetheless conclude that a later engineering grant should absorb the value of a finding made before it was approved, that is a legitimate view, and I would rather they reach it with the whole record in front of them.

2) NO PAYMENT HAS EVER BEEN MADE FOR THIS VULNERABILITY

CVE-2026-34202 has never received any bounty, award, gift or payment of any kind, from any source. It is not the subject of any pending bounty request, and it cannot be: ZCG's programme does not apply retroactively, and ZCG does not accept payout requests from researchers directly.

This application covers CVE-2026-34202 and nothing else. It requests nothing in respect of any other advisory, and cannot overlap with any other payment, because no other payment exists.

### Success Metrics

QUANTITATIVE

- Severity as assigned by the remediation team: Critical. CWE-248. CVSS v4.0 base score 9.2 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:H) in the advisory; NVD separately assigned CVSS v3.1 7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H). Both are on the record and I address the difference below.
- Cost to exploit: one unauthenticated P2P message per node. No authentication, no user interaction, no non-default configuration.
- Population at risk before the fix: per the advisory, "All Zebra versions supporting V5 transactions (Network Upgrade 5 and later) prior to version 4.3.0" — that is, every reachable Zebra node running a default configuration.
- Time from report to shipped fix: days. Zebra 4.3.0 shipped 26 March 2026.
- Position in the record: the first Critical in Zebra's public GitHub security-advisory record (39 advisories; earliest publication date 27 March 2026). The next Critical in that record appears three weeks later.
- Downstream engineering: PR #10426 moved rejection of undeserializable transactions into the deserialization phase and replaced internal panics with graceful error handling; PR #10429 broadened the V5 transaction generator and NU5 branch ID strategy against regressions.

QUALITATIVE

- Availability of the node layer is not a peripheral property for Zcash. Zebra is one of the network's consensus node implementations, and a crash reachable from any peer at will is an attack on the network's ability to keep running — exchanges, wallet backends and block explorers running Zebra were all in scope.
- The disclosure was handled the way this ecosystem asks researchers to handle disclosures: privately, through the project's own process, with reproduction and remediation support instead of a public issue. When a grant reviewer asked me about it on the forum on 24 March, the advisory was still embargoed and I declined to give details. The Foundation's own summary: "working with us to quickly reproduce and remediate it."
- The finding was made with no funding, no contract and no bounty programme in existence. Whatever coinholders decide here, that is the behaviour the ecosystem presumably wants to see repeated.

ON THE ARGUMENTS AGAINST THIS APPLICATION'S FIGURE

There are two, and I would rather make them myself than have them made for me.

THE FIRST: NVD SCORES THIS 7.5, NOT 9.2

The advisory carries a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.2. NVD's own analysis, recorded as the Primary metric for this CVE, assigns CVSS v3.1 7.5 — High, not Critical. Anyone checking this CVE will see both numbers, so here is the reason they differ.

They are not two assessments of the facts. The two vectors agree completely on the attack: network-reachable, low complexity, no privileges required, no user interaction, high availability impact. What differs is what each version of CVSS can express. CVSS 3.1 has no dimension for impact that extends beyond the compromised host; its scope flag is set Unchanged here, and confidentiality and integrity impacts are None, which structurally caps any pure remote denial-of-service at 7.5. CVSS 4.0 added subsequent-system impact metrics, and this finding's vector sets Subsequent System Availability to High — the observation that crashing a consensus node degrades something beyond that one machine.

I am not going to overreach on that point: SA:H explains the arithmetic difference between 7.5 and 9.2. It does not by itself establish a threat to finalization, and I am not claiming one. What matters for this application is not either number but the severity label the remediation team assigned, which was Critical.

THE SECOND: ZCG'S LATER FRAMEWORK LISTS NODE DoS UNDER HIGH

ZCG's severity framework, published on 28 April 2026, lists under High: "Non-distributed denial of service against an individual node or wallet." A reviewer can reasonably read that and argue this finding belongs at High ($75,000 base), not Critical ($150,000 base). Four responses, and then it is coinholders' call.

First, severity here was not self-assessed. ZCG's own framework says "Severity is assigned by the remediation team and/or technical reviewers after a disclosure has been categorized." For this finding the remediation team was the Zcash Foundation, and they assigned Critical, CVSS v4.0 9.2 — recorded in the advisory, in the release announcement, and in their Q1 2026 report. I am citing their rating, not proposing my own.

Second, that framework describes its own bullets as "illustrative, not exhaustive", and says "the remediation team evaluates each disclosure on its own merits against the core tenets and the harms above."

Third, the High tier is defined as harm "only for specific users at limited scale", and the framework explains that "'Limited scale' here means the practical reach of the defect is narrow — for example, it only manifests under a specific hardware configuration, operating system version, or less common combinations of configuration options." This defect had none of those limits. It reached every Zebra node below 4.3.0 running a default configuration on the default port, from any peer, with no per-target condition. Its reach was the opposite of narrow.

Fourth, the Foundation assigned that rating on 27 March 2026, thirty-two days before the framework existed.

Having said all of that, I am not asking anyone to treat the Foundation's rating as beyond question. I am asking that it be the starting point, because the people who fixed the bug are the people ZCG's own framework says should assign its severity.

Having said all of that: I am not claiming this finding put funds at risk, and I am not pricing it as a share of value at risk the way application #51 reasonably does for the Orchard counterfeiting bug. That bug threatened the supply; this one threatened availability, and the CVSS vector says so plainly — confidentiality none, integrity none, availability high. I am asking coinholders to value an accepted Critical in a Core Node repository at the figure the ecosystem itself has published for that tier, and I have given them the argument for paying less.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING

I am not claiming this report caused ZCG to create its bounty programme; that announcement cites other disclosures, and I have no evidence for the claim. I am not claiming it caused the Foundation to change its disclosure practice. I am not claiming it was the reason ZCG approved grant #234. Each of those would be more flattering than the record supports.

### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [PR #10426](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10426) — merged 25 March 2026; identified as the fix in the Foundation's release post. Note that the commit title carries a `fix(test):` prefix, but the change is to production serialization code: the single file touched is `zebra-chain/src/transaction/serialize.rs` (+25/-3), which is where the advisory's "rejected during the initial deserialization phase" behaviour lives.
  - [PR #10429](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/pull/10429) — "Add NU5 branch ID strategy and update V5 transaction generator", merged 25 March 2026; listed under "Improved Test Coverage" in the release post. Touches `zebra-chain/src/parameters/arbitrary.rs` and `zebra-chain/src/transaction/arbitrary.rs` — the proptest generators, i.e. the regression coverage.
- Publication:
  - [GHSA-qp6f-w4r3-h8wg / CVE-2026-34202](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/security/advisories/GHSA-qp6f-w4r3-h8wg) — published 27 March 2026, Critical, CVSS v4.0 9.2; structured credits list robustfengbin as an accepted reporter.
  - [Zcash Foundation — "Zebra 4.3.0: Critical Security Fixes, ZIP-235 Support, and Performance Improvements"](https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-3-0-critical-security-fixes-zip-235-support-and-performance-improvements/) — "Thanks to robustfengbin for responsibly disclosing the vulnerability and working with us to quickly reproduce and remediate it."
  - [Zcash Foundation Q1 2026 report](https://zfnd.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Zcash-Foundation-Q1-2026.pdf), "Key Zebra Developments" — "Zebra 4.3.0 was a critical security release addressing two responsibly disclosed vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-34202 (CVSS 9.2), a remote DoS via crafted V5 transactions that could crash a node, and CVE-2026-34377 (CVSS 8.4), a consensus logic error that could allow a malicious miner to induce a chain split."
- Deployment/Release:
  - [Zebra v4.3.0](https://github.com/ZcashFoundation/zebra/releases/tag/v4.3.0) — released 26 March 2026; patched versions zebrad 4.3.0 and zebra-chain 6.0.1.
- Other Evidence:
  - [ZCG #234 forum thread](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zebra-coverage-guided-fuzzing-infrastructure/54972) — the full timeline quoted under Other Funding Sources, including the reviewer's objection of 23 March, my embargoed disclosure of 24 March, his confirmation of 26 March, and ZCG's approval of 30 March.


### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

1. I hold two grants from Zcash Community Grants — #234 (Zebra fuzzing infrastructure) and #332 (batch-vs-single verification equivalence). The relationship between #234 and this finding is the material disclosure in this application; it is set out in full under Other Funding Sources and I have not minimised it.
2. I have no employment, contracting or governance relationship with any of the keyholder organisations, and no role in administering this grants programme.

### Community Forum Posting

- [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application. Note: If you are unable to post on the forum (for example, due to new user restrictions), please leave a comment below, and we will adjust your posting permissions.

issues.title: Taylor Hornby - Bonus Grant for Orchard Counterfeiting Vulnerability Bug Bounty
issues.body:
### Terms and Conditions

- [x] I agree to the [Grant Agreement](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_6ff6db4095fd4c4ba21babec361e927e.pdf) terms if funded
- [x] I agree to [Provide KYC information](https://9ba4718c-5c73-47c3-a024-4fc4e5278803.usrfiles.com/ugd/9ba471_7d9e73d16b584a61bae92282b208efc4.pdf) if funded above $50,000 USD
- [x] I agree to disclose conflicts of interest
- [x] I understand that this grant program is only eligible for completed work, as it is a retroactive grant program. Applications for planned or partially completed work will not be considered. All completed work will be verified and accepted by its intended users or their representatives, who will confirm that the outputs meet the required quality, functionality, and usability before the work is listed as an option for Coinholder voting.
- [x] I agree that for any new open-source software, I will create a CONTRIBUTING.md file that reflects the high standards of Zcash development, using the [`librustzcash` style guides](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#styleguides) as a primary reference.
- [x] I understand when contributing to existing Zcash code, I am required to adhere to the project specific contribution guidelines, paying close attention to any [merge](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#merge-workflow), [branch](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#branch-history), [pull request](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-review), and [commit](https://github.com/zcash/librustzcash/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages) guidelines as exemplified in the librustzcash repository.
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@aquietinvestor

### Organization or Individual Name

Jason McGee. I am recommending coinholders approve a bonus grant to Taylor Hornby, the sole recipient, in addition to the bug bounty he requested in application #51. I am submitting this in my personal capacity as a coinholder; no funds go to me or to Shielded Labs, where I serve as Executive Director.

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None. Taylor did not request this nomination and had no role in preparing it.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

I helped create the Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program and helped administer its first rounds, and Shielded Labs is one of the keyholder organizations. This nomination was prompted by reading application #51 and concluding that Taylor asked for too little.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$750000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

This is a bonus grant nomination, not a standard application. Taylor Hornby applied for a $750,000 bug bounty in [application #51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51) for finding and responsibly disclosing the Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability, a bug that put roughly $2.3B of ZEC at risk. His ask is far below industry norms for a finding of this severity. This application adds $750,000, bringing the total to $1,500,000.

### Project Description

This application was inspired by [Zooko's forum post](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/retroactive-grant-application-give-bigger-grants-to-taylor-and-tachyon/57012) suggesting we should be able to nominate people for retroactive grants rather than waiting for them to apply, and that Taylor deserved to receive more. I agree, and this application acts on it. Frank Braun also reached out to me separately to advocate for a bonus grant for both applicants, having come to the same conclusion on his own. 

The work itself is described in [application #51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51) and I won't restate it here. In short: Taylor found an undetectable counterfeiting vulnerability that had sat in the Orchard circuit for four years through every audit, reported it immediately, built the proofs of concept that established it was real and exploitable, and then spent weeks helping ZODL and the Zcash Foundation review and test the patches. Every ZEC holder benefited from that disclosure.

The reason for this application is the number. Taylor's own table makes the case better than I can: the smallest bounty-to-funds-at-risk ratio among the precedents he cites is 0.24%, and most are far higher. His request works out to 0.033%. Even with this bonus, the total of $1,500,000 is about 0.066% of the funds at risk, still roughly a quarter of the smallest precedent. He deliberately asked below industry norms. That restraint speaks well of him, but coinholders do not have to accept the discount, and there is a good reason not to.

The reason is incentives. Zcash has no formal bug bounty program; ZCG's closed days before Taylor found this bug. The retroactive grants program is currently the only mechanism that can pay a researcher for a catastrophic finding. What we pay here sets the reference point for the next person who finds a counterfeiting bug and weighs disclosure against the alternatives. A bounty that rounds up to industry norms, rather than down, is cheap insurance for a protocol whose entire value rests on the integrity of its supply.

One more point, because I am well placed to make it: Shielded Labs hired Taylor as a contractor to do AI-assisted security auditing, and that engagement is how the bug was found. Some might argue his consulting pay covers the discovery. I run Shielded Labs and I disagree. We paid for auditing effort at a standard consulting rate. We did not, and could not, pay for the outcome of preventing a multi-billion-dollar counterfeiting event. Bounties exist precisely because the value of a critical finding bears no relationship to the hourly cost of looking for it. His rate did not include a discovery premium, and no bounty program in the world nets out salary before paying an award.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Not applicable. This application adds no new work. The technical approach is documented in [application #51 ](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51)and in Shielded Labs' published account of the vulnerability.

### Time Period of Work Completion

May 2026 - June 2026 (the same period as application #51)

### Total Budget (USD)

$750000

### Budget Breakdown

Other: $750,000. Justification: a bonus to Taylor Hornby in recognition that his requested bounty sits far below the industry precedents cited in his own application. The figure is set so that the total bounty for the disclosure equals $1,500,000, which is about 0.066% of the funds at risk, still well under the lowest comparable ratio.

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

Not applicable 

### Other Funding Sources

No

### Other Funding Sources Details

No funding source covers this bonus. Taylor's own funding history, including his Shielded Labs consulting engagement and the gifts he received after disclosure, is disclosed in [application #51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51).

### Success Metrics

The success metrics for the underlying work are in [application #51](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/51): the vulnerability was disclosed responsibly, patched without exploitation, and led directly to the formally verified Ironwood pool.

The success metric for this application is different: that coinholders establish, on the record, that a researcher who hands Zcash back billions of dollars of protected value will be paid at a level that makes honest disclosure the obvious choice next time.

### Proof of completion

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

I helped create the Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program and helped administer its first rounds, and Shielded Labs is one of the keyholder organizations. This nomination was prompted by reading application #50 and concluding that Tachyon asked for too little.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$261,058

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

This is a bonus grant nomination, not a standard application. Tachyon Foundation applied for $738,942 in [application #50](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/50) for leading the formal verification of the Ironwood zk-SNARK. That application deliberately excludes real costs they absorbed and prices their emergency work at the bottom of the market band. I believe coinholders should recognize the full value of what they did. This application adds $261,058, bringing the total recognition for the Ironwood formal verification to an even $1,000,000.

### Project Description

This application was inspired by [Zooko's forum post](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/retroactive-grant-application-give-bigger-grants-to-taylor-and-tachyon/57012) suggesting we should be able to nominate people for retroactive grants rather than waiting for them to apply, and that Tachyon and Taylor both deserved to receive more. I agree, and this application acts on it. Frank Braun also reached out to me separately to advocate for a bonus grant for both applicants, having come to the same conclusion on his own

The work itself is described in [application #50](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/50) and I won't restate it here. In short: after the Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability was disclosed in June 2026, Tachyon dropped everything, implemented the Ironwood circuit changes, funded two independent verification firms out of their own audit budget, and delivered a machine-checked Lean formalization of the Ironwood zk-SNARK verifier on the day of mainnet activation. Formal verification of a deployed cryptographic protocol is normally measured in years. They did it in under two months, against a fixed deadline, because the ecosystem needed it.

The reason for this application is what #50 leaves out. By their own accounting, Tachyon claims nothing for the two-month stall of their own roadmap, nothing for the burden on team members who carried Project Tachyon with reduced support during the pivot, no mobilization fee, and billing at the bottom of the emergency-response band. Those are real costs. They chose not to price them, which speaks well of them, but the community does not have to accept that discount.

There is also a strategic reason. The people who can do this work are rare. Zcash was lucky that a team with the right expertise, including a principal author of halo2, existed and was willing to act immediately with no guarantee of payment. Retroactive grants are the mechanism we have for making sure that kind of decisive action is rewarded, so that the people capable of it stay in this ecosystem and act just as decisively next time. Paying exactly cost for emergency work teaches the wrong lesson.

The amount is chosen simply: $738,942 plus $261,058 equals $1,000,000. I think a million dollars is a fair round number for work that resolved an existential question about the ZEC supply.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Not applicable. This application adds no new work. The technical approach is documented in [application #50](https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/50) and in Tachyon's publications.

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@DefuseSec

### Organization or Individual Name

Taylor Hornby

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
I am requesting this bounty as an individual, however my work was made possible thanks to Shielded Labs funding my LLM-assisted auditing research as well as the audit that found this bug. ZODL's and Zcash Foundation's teams and leadership deserve an immense amount of credit for patching the vulnerability in an unprecedented security response (really the best I have ever seen in my career!).
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

I was around when the program grew out of discussions here on the forums!

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$750,000

### Category

Research & Development

### Project Summary

I am requesting a bug bounty for responsibly disclosing the Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability, which likely prevented the loss of $2.3B USD worth of ZEC. Funding this bounty supports Zcash's long-term security: it sends a message to security researchers that they can report potentially-devastating counterfeiting vulnerabilities and have a good chance of getting paid legitimately, reducing the incentive to exploit counterfeiting vulnerabilities maliciously.

### Project Description

I am applying for a bug bounty as a result of finding and responsibly disclosing the recent Orchard counterfeiting vulnerability. I found the bug while developing AI-assisted security auditing tools and performing Zcash security audits as a contractor for Shielded Labs, though I am applying for the grant as an individual.

If the vulnerability had been exploited, it would have allowed an unlimited amount of ZEC to be minted within the Orchard pool. If an attacker exploited the bug, they could have effectively "stolen" all of the funds in the Orchard pool. At the time, Orchard contained around 4.2M ZEC, worth $2.3B USD. Without my timely disclosure, the bug could have been found and exploited by a malicious actor using AI tools.

Funding this bounty is important for Zcash's long-term security. It sends a message to security researchers: if you find a catastrophic counterfeiting bug in Zcash, you can report it honestly, request a bounty through a retroactive grant (even though there isn't a formal bug bounty program), and have a good chance of getting paid legitimately.

*Funding this bounty reduces the incentive to attack Zcash.* This is especially important as a fallback in the absence of a formal bug bounty program; ZCG's bounty program was [closed](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/closing-the-zcg-vulnerability-bounty-program/55855) just days before I discovered the bug! Hopefully this was the last counterfeiting vulnerability Zcash will ever have, but just in case it isn't, this precedent will help encourage future bug-discoverers to do the right thing.

Asking for $750,000 is a lot, so it's important to justify that number. The bounty programs of several major projects suggest an award of [10% of the affected funds](https://immunefi.com/blog/industry-trends/a-defi-security-standard-the-scaling-bug-bounty/) up to maximums of around $1M-$2M (e.g. [1](https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/compoundfinance/information/), [2](https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/optimism/information/)):

> "Critical bug bounty payouts should be priced as a percentage of the economic damage they would have caused, so that even blackhats are incentivized to review code and disclose vulnerabilities, thereby reducing malicious exploits. For most DeFi projects, that’s 10% of TVL at risk." — Immunefi

I'd rather keep my ask below industry norms, and I've already received some gifts, so I am asking for an amount that's reasonable in proportion to the harms that were prevented, and which will help me continue to expand the ways I can contribute to Zcash. The following table will help you compare my ask to a sampling of similar cases:

| Precedent | Vulnerability / impact | Funds at risk (approx.) | Bounty | Ratio (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Wormhole, 2022 — satya0x](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/wormhole-uninitialized-proxy-bugfix-review/) | Uninitialized implementation contract allowed an attacker-controlled Guardian set and SELFDESTRUCT of the implementation, bricking the Ethereum bridge and locking its assets | $1.8B in the contract at time of submission | $10,000,000 | 0.56% |
| [Aurora, 2022 — pwning.eth](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/aurora-inflation-spend-bugfix-review-6m-payout/) | "Infinite spend" allowing repeated balance doubling; effectively infinite ETH creation in the Aurora Engine | 70,000 ETH ($204M) plus $200M in other assets | $6,000,000 | 1.48% |
| [Optimism, 2022 — Jay Freeman (saurik)](https://medium.com/immunefi/optimism-infinite-money-duplication-bugfix-review-daa6597146a0) | Unlimited creation of OETH; counterfeit OETH could drain DEXes and bridged assets | $322.5M TVL | $2,000,042 | 0.62% |
| [Polygon, 2021 — Gerhard Wagner](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/polygon-double-spend-bugfix-review-2m-bounty/) | Plasma Bridge replay/double-spend allowing one burn transaction to be exited up to 223 times | $850M | $2,000,000 | 0.24% |
| [Belt Finance, 2021 — Alexander Schlindwein](https://medium.com/immunefi/belt-finance-logic-error-bug-fix-postmortem-39308a158291) | Logic error produced excess shares; repeatable until the contract was drained | $60M (single iteration $10M) | $1,050,000 total ($1M Belt + $50k BSC match) | 1.75% |
| **My request**| **Unlimited, undetectable creation of counterfeit ZEC within Orchard** | **$2.29B (4.2M ZEC at $545)** | **$750,000** | **0.033%** |

Comparing funds-at-risk to bounty reward ratios, the reward ratio I am asking for is 1/7th of the smallest ratio in the table above.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

In September of 2025, I started developing tools for security auditing using LLMs. My intention was to automate as much of my manual security audit process as possible. The models that existed at the time weren't that smart, so this took a lot of prompt engineering, but it worked.

I continued developing the tools throughout 2026 and started running them against Zcash-adjacent software like the Keystone hardware wallet and found some bugs. I've open-sourced this general-purpose AI auditing framework on GitHub: [defuse/auditician](https://github.com/defuse/auditician) (this is not a deliverable for this grant).

Later on, Shielded Labs hired me as a contractor to continue this work and audit more Zcash-related software. I ended up developing a new set of agents specifically for auditing Zcash. Using those agents to audit Orchard's balance integrity properties, with Opus 4.8 the day after it was released, was what ultimately found this bug.

In brief, the agent framework that found the bug is based on the principle that a bug becomes transparent to an LLM when it has everything it needs to spot the bug right there in its context window: the security property that's violated, good ideas for how that security property can be attacked, and all of the relevant code and specification text. To make that happen, the tool:

1. First helps you clearly define the security property you're trying to attack (in this case, Orchard balance integrity).
2. Then it enumerates all relevant statements in the protocol specification and ZIPs, all relevant security sub-properties, all possible failure modes (attack ideas), and all relevant code locations. This requires running several rounds of expansion to find everything.
3. Then it passes small batches of the enumerated items to agents designed for specific auditing purposes: A design-auditor checks if the specification itself contains any vulnerabilities, a failure-mode-auditor checks if any of the attack ideas actually work, a code-auditor spends time looking for vulnerabilities in a region of code, and a security-property-auditor exhaustively checks whether a claimed security property is true or false.
4. Finally, an issue validator agent then validates and tries to expand on all of the security issues that come out of this process.

The day after Opus 4.8 was released, I set this framework running to audit Orchard's balance integrity. A few hours later it found the vulnerability, which had been missed by all of my prior AI-assisted (and manual) audits of Orchard.

At first I couldn't believe the bug was real, but Claude's explanation sounded correct. I used Claude to help me develop a series of proof of concepts, starting by writing a small circuit that just used the vulnerable component, which proved to me that a critical circuit constraint was actually missing. 

I immediately reported the issue to ZODL, then, working overnight, I had Claude develop a full proof of concept as an RPC test within `zcashd`. The RPC test proved the issue was exploitable by creating millions of "regtest" ZEC on my local node (regtest is `zcashd`'s testing mode, none of this ever hit a live chain). Having the ability to create infinite ZEC right in front of me was honestly the craziest emotional experience of my life; while I'd like to think that I'd do the right thing in any case, my shared history with and love for the Zcash engineers, who pretty much raised me intellectually and morally, and the possibility of applying for this grant, made it a lot easier to make the right choice.

I spent the next weeks helping the ZODL and ZF engineers by reviewing and testing the patches that temporarily disabled the Orchard pool to close off the vulnerability, as well as the changes that eventually re-enabled a secure Orchard pool.

The full details can be found in [Shielded Labs' blog post](https://shieldedlabs.net/the-orchard-counterfeiting-vulnerability/) and my [work log](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SVK41y-ip3Vw9eB69E9QRy-Qn3idTOwV/view).

### Time Period of Work Completion

May 2026 - June 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

0

### Budget Breakdown

The bug was discovered at little financial cost (aside from self-funding my own research prior to being hired by Shielded Labs) thanks to judicious use of Claude's Max plan. The amount requested is based on the harm to ZEC holders that was prevented and to set a reasonable precedent that makes Zcash safer, not a reimbursement for expenses.

### Previous Funding

No

### Previous Funding Details

I have not received any prior funding from the Zcash Coinholder Grants Program. In 2022-2023, I received funding from ZCG for my [Zcash Ecosystem Security Lead](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcash-ecosystem-security-lead/42090) grant.

### Other Funding Sources

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

I received one substantial gift as well as some smaller ones in response to [this tweet](https://x.com/DefuseSec/status/2062927120775750029?s=20). Shielded Labs paid me at my regular consulting rate for the Zcash-specific research and auditing work. I have chosen to request an amount below the industry norms cited above.

### Success Metrics

Assuming the bug was not exploited during the four-year period of vulnerability (it looks like it wasn't), this work prevented unbounded inflation within the Orchard pool, possibly resulting in the loss of all Orchard ZEC. This would have been devastating not only to everyone who held Orchard ZEC but also to Zcash's reputation as a safe, private store of value.

The discovery of this bug also led the community to develop and deploy the formally-verified Ironwood pool, which aims to mathematically close off the possibility of similar bugs being found in that pool as well as the current Orchard pool. (I did not contribute to Ironwood's development, aside from some security review.)

### Proof of completion

A full writeup, as well as my work log, is available in [Shielded Labs' blog post](https://shieldedlabs.net/the-orchard-counterfeiting-vulnerability/). 

See also [ZODL's post](https://zodl.com/orchard-vulnerability-successfully-remediated/) and [Zcash Foundation's post](https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/) about the vulnerability.

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

I'm a board member of the Zcash Foundation, I am an independent contractor doing work for Shielded Labs, and I own various stocks and cryptocurrencies, including ZEC. The Zcash Foundation is one of the keyholders for the disbursement of funds from this grant program, as is Shielded Labs, so I will recuse myself from any discussion around supporting/vetoing/funding grants in this round, as well as anything else related to coinholder grants voting. I will not vote for my proposal with my own coins. I've reviewed ZIP-1016 and I believe I am eligible to apply for this grant as an individual.

I understand this is required in order for the community to discuss and vote on this grant application.
