After ZecKit’s Milestone 3 was reviewed, approved, and paid under the original ZCG grant, we completed additional work focused on documentation, onboarding, installation, stabilization, and maintenance. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@gilmorre

### Organization or Individual Name

Gleyo

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None, solo project.
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Through LOWO (LEONINE DAO / Nozy Wallet), an active ecosystem collaborator, who pointed me to this round after seeing Gleyo's production usage of Nozy.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$9,081.20

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

Gleyo is a Zcash-native community growth platform that enables any online community to reward contributors directly in shielded ZEC, making Zcash onboarding a natural outcome of community participation rather than a prerequisite.

### Project Description

Gleyo lets project owners fund a community wallet with ZEC (or USDT/USDC, auto-converted to ZEC via NEAR Intents/Defuse Protocol), create quests with XP and/or ZEC rewards, and review member submissions, while giving owners real retention analytics (7d/30d/90d active members, dropoff percentage, growth signals) instead of the vanity social metrics offered by platforms like Zealy.

The core design decision that separates Gleyo from every other quest platform is who it's built for: not the Zcash-native user, but the newcomer. Community members can earn ZEC without ever connecting a wallet upfront, removing the single biggest barrier to entry for newcomers unfamiliar with Zcash or shielded transactions. This means a person's first experience with Zcash can be "I completed a task and received private money," rather than "I need to learn what a shielded transaction is before I can participate." That is a fundamentally different, and lower, on-ramp than anything else currently serving the ecosystem.

Since launching during ZecHub Hackathon 2026 (July 14, 2026), Gleyo has grown to 38 weekly active users in closed beta, processed real mainnet ZEC deposits and withdrawals, redesigned its withdrawal architecture into a queued system to safely support concurrent multi-community activity, shipped multi-token (USDT/USDC) funding following a suggestion from ZecHub PR reviewer @zksquirrel, and successfully verified full end-to-end compatibility with the July 28, 2026 Ironwood network upgrade across both direct shielded-wallet deposits and stablecoin-to-ZEC swap deposits.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

Gleyo's production infrastructure is intentionally split across multiple services to isolate responsibilities and reduce risk. Cloudflare fronts the application, providing DNS, TLS termination, caching, and DDoS protection before traffic reaches the Flask backend running on AWS EC2. The application uses Flask with SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL on AWS RDS for persistent data, Redis as the server-side session store (with automatic filesystem fallback if unavailable), and Supabase for object storage.

All shielded ZEC functionality is isolated from the application tier. The Flask backend communicates with the Nozy Wallet API (developed by LEONINE DAO), which runs on a separate Contabo VPS alongside a self-hosted Zebra full node. This separation keeps wallet infrastructure independent from the web application while providing direct access to the Zcash network without relying on third-party lightwalletd services.

Wallet authentication uses a shielded micro-transaction containing a session code in the memo field, while deposits, balance synchronization, and withdrawals are handled entirely through Nozy. Withdrawals are routed exclusively to Unified (u1) addresses through Nozy's transaction API.

Security is layered throughout the deployment. The Nozy API is not publicly exposed to the internet; UFW firewall rules restrict access exclusively to Gleyo's EC2 instance, with authenticated API requests providing an additional security layer. Nozy communicates with Zebra over RPC for balance synchronization, deposit verification, and shielded transaction broadcasting, while Zebra maintains its own peer-to-peer connection to the Zcash mainnet. External integrations, including GitHub, Discord, Telegram, YouTube, email delivery (Resend/SMTP), and NEAR Intents (Defuse Protocol) for USDT/USDC-to-ZEC funding, operate as independent outbound services, ensuring failures in third-party providers do not interrupt Gleyo's core platform.

During Ironwood migration testing (July 28, 2026 network upgrade), this dependency on Nozy surfaced a production-breaking Axum routing incompatibility. I diagnosed and fixed the issue, merging the fix upstream to LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet (PR #180), restoring Ironwood pool deposit compatibility for Gleyo and every other project depending on Nozy's API layer.

Separately, in the course of operating Gleyo's withdrawal pipeline, I diagnosed a pending-transaction reconciliation issue in Nozy where certain withdrawal attempts would surface as failed on the client side despite the underlying transaction later confirming, caused by a balance/state sync gap between Nozy and Gleyo's polling logic. I traced this to its root cause and worked with the Nozy team on a fix, improving reconciliation reliability for Gleyo and any other project consuming Nozy's transaction status API.

Beyond Nozy, testing and building Gleyo has surfaced real issues on other Zcash ecosystem projects as well. While testing Dizzy, I reported a validation bug where Orchard-only Unified Addresses were incorrectly rejected as invalid despite passing correct Bech32/Bech32m checksum validation; the dismad team confirmed and worked with the developer on a fix. While testing LiveZEC (zec.live), a private ZEC donations platform for streamers, I reported two UX issues: an account-deletion 2FA requirement that lacked explanatory context, and a "Set up your Viewing Key" modal that kept re-triggering on page navigation; both were addressed by the LiveZEC team following the reports.

**Note on Nozy-related contributions:** This application is entirely separate from the retroactive grant application already submitted by LEONINE DAO/Nozy Wallet for their own work. The Nozy PR #180 and reconciliation fix referenced above are unpaid contributions I made to Nozy specifically because Gleyo depends on its API, and are cited here only as evidence of technical skill and ecosystem impact. My requested compensation covers hours spent building Gleyo itself; it does not claim any hours tied to Nozy's own development, and there is no overlap between this request and Nozy's separately submitted application.

### Time Period of Work Completion

November 2025 - August 2026

### Total Budget (USD)

$9,081.20

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 9000
  - Justification: ~9 months of solo full-stack development, infrastructure management, and ecosystem contributions (Nozy PR #180, Nozy reconciliation fix, Dizzy and LiveZEC bug reports), averaging ~23 hours/week over ~39 weeks (900 hours), priced at $10/hour, well below typical freelance blockchain development rates ($50–150+/hour), reflecting a deliberate choice to keep this ask modest and grounded in actual time invested rather than to extract maximum value from a retroactive claim.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: All third-party services used to date (Supabase, Resend, Cloudflare, AWS) remain within free tier limits with no costs incurred.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 81.20
  - Justification: Contabo VPS (Zebra + Nozy) hosting, $16.80/month, covering June through September 2026 (4 months, including the upcoming September renewal) = $67.20, plus domain registration ($14). All other infrastructure (Cloudflare, Supabase, Resend, AWS EC2/RDS) currently runs on free tiers with no cost incurred to date.
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A, no contractors used, solo project.
- Other:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: N/A
- Total $(USD): 9,081.20

No

None

Yes

### Other Funding Sources Details

Separately preparing a Zcash Community Grants (ZCG) milestone-based application for future work (security audit, infrastructure redundancy), this retroactive request covers only work already completed and is independent of that forward-looking application.

### Success Metrics

- 38 weekly active users processing real mainnet ZEC deposits, quest rewards, and shielded withdrawals in closed beta, not a testnet demo.
- 33 mainnet transactions processed to date (deposits and withdrawals) between June 28 and August 12, 2026, spanning both sides of the July 28 Ironwood network upgrade; 21 confirmed on-chain, remainder attributable to a Nozy-side pending-transaction reconciliation gap (diagnosed and fixed, see below), not lost or unrecoverable funds.
- Merged upstream fix to Nozy Wallet (PR #180) resolving an Ironwood-migration-breaking Axum routing incompatibility, restoring Ironwood pool deposit compatibility for Gleyo and other Nozy-dependent projects.
- Diagnosed and helped resolve a Nozy pending-transaction reconciliation issue (balance/state sync gap between Nozy and client polling logic causing some confirmed withdrawals to surface as failed), improving reliability for all builders on Nozy's API.
- Reported a Unified Address validation bug in Dizzy where Orchard-only addresses were incorrectly rejected despite valid checksums; confirmed and fixed by the Dizzy team following the report.
- Reported two UX issues on LiveZEC (zec.live) during beta testing (a persistently re-triggering wallet setup modal, and unclear account-deletion 2FA messaging); both fixed by the LiveZEC team following the reports.
- Full end-to-end ZEC flow live and verifiable on mainnet: deposit → quest reward → shielded withdrawal, confirmed within ~3 minutes per transaction.
- Externally tested during ZecHub Hackathon 2026 judging by dismad, an active ZecHub and Zcash ecosystem contributor, who ran Gleyo's full local setup process on a fresh environment and surfaced real, previously undocumented setup requirements (a required Supabase storage bucket, a Python version incompatibility, and a dependency fix later merged upstream to Nozy itself); this feedback directly improved Gleyo's SETUP.md and was later independently re-verified end-to-end on a clean Linux environment.

**Ecosystem Adoption Signals**
- Zcash Nigeria actively testing Gleyo.
- Paul Brigner (ZCG) independently discovered and tested the platform, evaluating it for a PGPZ test community.
- ZecForge members have tested Gleyo directly, connecting wallets and completing shielded withdrawals, with further discussions underway to expand usage for their ambassador program and Heat Index tracking.

**Path to Self-Sufficiency**
Gleyo operates a Free and Pro tier model. Zcash-native projects, communities, and creators remain free on Gleyo permanently, including premium collaboration features such as community analytics and engagement insights, ensuring no Zcash builder is ever gated behind a paywall to grow their community. Revenue is instead generated by offering the Pro tier to communities and projects outside the Zcash ecosystem who want the same quest, retention-analytics, and ZEC-reward tooling for their own communities, with initial Pro tier pricing planned in the $60-100/month range, notably below comparable platforms such as Zealy ($250–500/month), positioning Gleyo as the more accessible option for external adoption. This mirrors the sustainability model already outlined in Gleyo's parallel ZCG application: monetizing external demand to fund ongoing development and infrastructure costs, rather than relying on continued grant funding or monetizing the Zcash community itself. As Gleyo's user base grows beyond closed beta, this Pro-tier revenue is intended to make the platform increasingly self-sustaining.

- Other Evidence: Demo video, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Har9yk9Ep04, full walkthrough of Gleyo including wallet verification, community funding, quest creation, task verification, reward crediting, community chat, retention analytics, and shielded withdrawals via Nozy on Zcash mainnet (published July 14, 2026, as part of the ZecHub Hackathon 2026 submission)

# Retroactive Grant Application: ZecLedger

*Matched to the Coinholder-Directed Retroactive Grants Program (Q3 2026) template. Fill in any remaining brackets, then copy into the GitHub issue template and mirror as a new forum thread.*

---

### Terms and Conditions
- [x] I agree to the Grant Agreement terms if funded
- [x] I agree to provide KYC information if funded above $50,000 USD (not applicable at this request size)
- [x] I agree to disclose conflicts of interest
- [x] I understand this grant program is only eligible for completed work
- [x] I agree to maintain a CONTRIBUTING.md reflecting the librustzcash style guides for any new open-source software
- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but disbursed in shielded ZEC

### Application Owners
@vancube2

### Organization or Individual Name
Zecledger

### Additional Team Members
None. Solo project.

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?
Zcash Community Forum / ZecHub

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)
$10,000

### Category
Tools (Accounting)

### Project Summary

Zcash's shielded pools hide transaction details by design, which is exactly what makes them private, and exactly what makes them impossible to audit with ordinary tools. ZecLedger solves that problem. It is a read-only accounting tool built entirely around a viewing key rather than a spending key: it can see a wallet's shielded activity but can never move a single zatoshi. From that read-only view it produces real books, balances, transaction history, cost-basis and gain/loss reports, payment reconciliation, and privacy checks, verified against a real mainnet wallet spanning 108 transactions and tested independently by a third party. It ships as an open-source Rust CLI, alongside a companion public dashboard, ZecLedger Web, that shows network-wide shielding statistics without ever touching a private key.

### Project Description

**The problem.** Zcash's shielded pools hide transaction details by design, which is the whole point of the privacy, but it creates a real bookkeeping problem. Most crypto accounting tools assume a public, transparent ledger to read from. Shielded ZEC gives third-party tools nothing to read by default, so shielded users have had no honest way to produce a cost-basis report, reconcile payments, or audit their own activity without exposing a spend key to some outside service.

**The approach.** ZecLedger takes a Unified Full Viewing Key, which can see incoming and outgoing shielded activity but cannot authorize a spend. The key never leaves the user's machine and is encrypted at rest with a user-chosen passphrase. From that read-only view it produces:
- Balances per pool (transparent, Sapling, Orchard)
- Full transaction history with decoded memos
- Cost-basis and realized gain/loss reports under FIFO, LIFO, or average-cost methods, with holding period in days and an optional historical price fetch
- Reconciliation of expected payments against what was actually received, flagging partial matches instead of silently accepting them
- A privacy check that flags pool-usage and amount patterns that could weaken privacy
- ZIP-321 payment request generation, so payments are requested, never sent, by the tool itself

An optional copilot feature lets a user query their own wallet in plain language. It only ever sends aggregate totals off the local machine, and only after the user explicitly confirms what will be shared.

**Verified in production.** ZecLedger's cost-basis engine has been run against a real mainnet wallet spanning 108 transactions from September 2025 through July 2026, correctly computing per-lot gain and loss under FIFO with holding periods in days. This is not a synthetic demo, it is the actual output the tool produces against a real transaction history.

**Engineering discipline.** Every release ships with SHA256 checksums and public GitHub Actions build provenance, so anyone can verify a binary was built from the published source rather than trusting a download blindly. The README is explicit about where the tool's current limits are. The Ironwood network upgrade (NU6.3, activated July 28, 2026) introduced a new shielded pool and transaction format that the initial v0.1.x releases cannot yet see, and the README says so plainly rather than letting the tool silently misreport. That fix, v0.2.0, is in active development now and is expected to land within the current review window, ahead of the coinholder vote.

**ZecLedger Web** is a separate, complementary public dashboard at zecledger-web.vercel.app, built to serve a different purpose than the CLI. Where the CLI is for a single wallet holder auditing their own shielded activity with a key, ZecLedger Web is for anyone who wants a public window into the network with no key of any kind. It offers three real, working views:

- **Shield rate**: a live, classified sample of recent chain activity, sorted into shielding, deshielding, fully private, transparent, and coinbase transactions, using a corrected classification method
- **Network and fees**: live block height, price, market cap, node count, fees, and chain size
- **Address lookup**: full public balance and history for any transparent address. Shielded addresses are deliberately declined, with an explanation shown instead of a fake or partial result, respecting the privacy that shielded addresses are built to have rather than working around it

The app touches only public data, fetched server-side through a single data-source module, and never asks for or handles a private key or viewing key of any kind. Its own documentation is candid about its limits in the same spirit as the CLI: shield-rate figures are explicitly labeled as a floor, not a total, since fully private shielded-to-shielded transactions cannot be observed from outside the pool by any tool, a limitation stated plainly rather than glossed over. The data layer is deliberately isolated in one file specifically so a public Zaino or lightwalletd source can replace the current third-party data provider later without any change to the interface, a real piece of forward planning already built into the architecture.

**External testing.** On July 24, 2026, dismad, an active ZecHub and Zcash ecosystem contributor, tested ZecLedger directly against a real mainnet wallet, running the wallet sync, the FIFO cost-basis report, and the monthly wallet-report command. The session surfaced a genuine bug: holding-period values in the cost-basis report appeared incorrect on repeated runs. That issue is acknowledged and is being fixed alongside the Ironwood work. In the same session, the wallet-report command, which produces a monthly received/sent/net summary and exports a CSV, was confirmed working correctly against real transaction data ("looks good here"). This is disclosed here in the same spirit as the tool's own README: real testing surfaces real issues, and reporting them plainly is more valuable than hiding them.

### Time Period of Work Completion

Development began full time around May 18, 2026, roughly a week ahead of the official ZecHub Hackathon 3.0 kickoff on May 25, 2026, and continued full time through the hackathon submission window, which closed July 15, 2026. The CLI's first public release shipped July 16, 2026, followed by three further releases on July 18, 2026. Development has continued part time since, including the external testing session on July 24, 2026, and Ironwood support now in progress.

### Total Budget (USD)
$10,000

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation: $10,000, retroactive recognition for two shipped products. The CLI accounting engine (sync, balances, history, cost-basis under three methods, reconciliation, privacy checks, ZIP-321 requests, encrypted key storage, release engineering with checksums and build provenance), and ZecLedger Web, a separate public dashboard with its own three working views (shield rate classification, network and fee statistics, transparent address lookup), its own honest data-limitation notes, and an architecture deliberately built to swap in a public Zcash-native data source later without a UI rewrite. Justification: approximately 8 weeks of full-time solo development (May 18 to July 15, 2026, roughly 320 hours at 40 hours per week) covering the core build through hackathon submission, plus continued part-time work since (releases, documentation, external-testing follow-up, ongoing Ironwood support), estimated at roughly 40 to 60 additional hours. Against a conservative total of roughly 360 to 380 hours across both products, this ask prices the work at approximately $26 to $28 per hour, below typical market rates for systems-level Rust and cryptography development, reflecting the retroactive, already-completed nature of the request.
- Technology/Software: $0, no paid infrastructure required for the CLI; the web dashboard runs on Vercel's free tier.
- Infrastructure/Hosting: $0, user-run tool; no hosted service to fund.
- Services/Contractors: $0, solo project, no contractors.
- Other: $0
- Total: $10,000

### Previous Funding
No

### Previous Funding Details
N/A

### Other Funding Sources
No

### Other Funding Sources Details
N/A

### Success Metrics

- Built for and submitted to the Accounting track of ZecHub Hackathon 3.0, a real deadline that forced a working, shippable tool rather than a slide deck
- Four public, versioned releases (v0.1.0 through v0.1.3) in nine days, each with reproducible builds, SHA256 checksums, and cryptographic build provenance so anyone can verify what they downloaded
- A cost-basis engine verified against 108 real mainnet transactions spanning eleven months, correctly computing FIFO gain and loss with per-lot holding periods, not a synthetic test case
- Independently tested against a real mainnet wallet by dismad, an active ZecHub and Zcash ecosystem contributor, on July 24, 2026, exercising wallet sync, cost-basis reporting, and the monthly wallet-report command, with real feedback that surfaced and is now driving a fix to a holding-period calculation bug
- A README that discloses the tool's current limits plainly, including the Ironwood coverage gap and its fix timeline, instead of overstating what it does
- A live, publicly reachable companion dashboard with three working views and zero key collection of any kind, whose own documentation honestly labels its shield-rate figures as a floor rather than a total, and whose data layer is architected to swap in a public Zcash-native source later without a UI rewrite
- Zero incidents of fund loss or key exposure, guaranteed structurally by the read-only, viewing-key-only design, not by policy alone
- v0.2.0 Ironwood support targeted within the review period, independently checkable before the coinholder vote closes

### Proof of completion

- CLI repository: https://github.com/vancube2/zecledger
- CLI releases with checksums and build provenance: https://github.com/vancube2/zecledger/releases
- Web dashboard repository: https://github.com/vancube2/zecledger-web
- Live web dashboard: https://zecledger-web.vercel.app/
- Demo video: https://youtu.be/7emZKHAH7TQ
- Real cost-basis report generated from actual mainnet wallet history (108 transactions, September 2025 to July 2026), available on request or postable in the review thread
- README, design, and security documentation: https://github.com/vancube2/zecledger/blob/master/README.md, /DESIGN.md, /SECURITY.md

### Conflict of Interest Disclosure

None known beyond being the sole author and maintainer of ZecLedger and ZecLedger Web.

### Community Forum Posting
- [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the Zcash Community Forums after this application has been submitted so the community can give input.

- [x] I understand all grants are valued in USD but will be disbursed in Shielded ZEC. I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment.

### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1)

@jpgonzalezra

### Organization or Individual Name

jpgonzalezra

### Additional Team Members

```team-members.yaml
None
```

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Pacu told me about the program. I had been following the coinholder grants threads on the Zcash Community Forum, but it was his suggestion that I apply with this project.

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$10,720

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

lightwalletd-rs is an independent Rust implementation of the Zcash light-client server, the caching proxy that sits between zebrad and shielded wallets; I built it from scratch between June and August 2026. It implements all 20 CompactTxStreamer gRPC methods, serves the currently active network upgrade (NU6.3), and is public under MIT, CI-tested, and benchmarked against the Go reference implementation.


### Project Description

The Zcash core stack has moved to Rust (zebrad, librustzcash), but the server that light wallets actually talk to has remained a separate Go stack. I wanted a light-client server that fits the Rust ecosystem. That meant a codebase small enough to audit, librustzcash for all consensus-critical parsing instead of reimplementing it, and zebrad accessed only through its public JSON-RPC interface. The whole server is a single crate of roughly 19k lines, so the trust boundary stays clean and the dependency surface small.

The work is complete as an implementation of the light-client protocol. All 20 CompactTxStreamer methods are implemented and tested: compact block streaming, transactions, tree state, subtree roots, mempool streaming, and the transparent-address queries. Blocks are ingested from zebrad, converted to compact blocks and cached on disk with redb; a reorg rolls the cache back, and it recovers automatically from corruption or gaps. It ships ready for a public endpoint, with TLS on by default, hardened input validation and per-connection limits. Day-to-day operation gets Prometheus metrics, gRPC server reflection, gRPC-web and graceful shutdown. For wallet developers there is a darkside mode, which stages a controllable mock chain for deterministic tests.

It also serves NU6.3 (Ironwood). Support was merged on July 7, three weeks before mainnet activation at height 3,428,143, and verified end-to-end against testnet past the activation height, with hashes, txids, tree states and subtree roots byte-identical to zebra's responses. An ingestor that does not understand v6 transactions stalls at the first v6 block.

This is beta software. It has not had a security audit, and the only instance I know to be running is my own, which I use for development. The next step is an audit by the Zcash Ecosystem Security Lead team (Least Authority), likely via a ZCG micro-grant; that is future work, outside this application. What I'm claiming here is a complete, tested, benchmarked and publicly verifiable implementation, not an adopted one.

Zaino, the ecosystem's new Rust indexer, covers a much broader surface. This project is deliberately narrow. I think critical serving infrastructure benefits from more than one independent implementation, and a lean one is something an operator can read end to end.


### Technical Approach (how you did it)

The backend is zebrad over plain JSON-RPC. Transactions are parsed with librustzcash (zcash_primitives and friends). Only the block header and framing are parsed by hand. Txids are computed locally, including v5/ZIP-244, so a single non-verbose getblock supplies all transaction data for a block; the only other per-block call is a verbose one for the note-commitment tree sizes. The cache is redb, one compact block per height; a reorg truncates and re-ingests, and ranges are served through MVCC chunked reads, which keeps a wallet from ever seeing a torn range. A slow client throttles only its own stream, because range streams are produced lazily under gRPC flow control. Every node call has a timeout; if zebrad stalls or goes away, the server keeps serving what it has cached while the ingestor retries with backoff. Ingestion runs in concurrent windows with batched commits. An A/B against the sequential baseline measured this at 6.6-9x. There is also an optional in-process Zebra ReadStateService backend behind the same node-access seam, contributed by Pacu and validated for wire parity against the default backend (5,997 compact blocks compared, byte-identical).

Tests are layered, from fakes at the node seam, through golden fixtures compared byte-for-byte against captured reference output, to in-process end-to-end tests. CI runs 433 test functions along with clippy (warnings as errors) and fmt. Every architectural decision is recorded as a short ADR; there are 30 so far in docs/decisions/. The file docs/protocol-references.md maps each spec the code relies on to the module that implements it.

Performance was measured against the Go reference on a live mainnet zebrad, with the methodology written down in ADR 0017 and the full reports committed to the repo. The harness runs both servers in containers capped at 2 vCPUs and 2 GiB, and verifies before measuring that both answer every request from a fully populated cache with byte-identical streams. Block-range streaming then plateaus around 330k blocks/s (321k on the 1,000-block ranges charted below) where the reference reaches 60-140k once concurrency goes above 2, and GetBlock p99 stays near 2.7 ms at 64 concurrent clients, against 33-55 ms for the reference. Ingest from live mainnet is 1.4x on modern blocks and 5.6x on sandblasting-era blocks, with peak RSS around 79 MiB versus 250 MiB. The reference wins single-stream dense range streaming and p50 at moderate concurrency, and my on-disk cache is about 2.3x larger. All of it is in the reports.

![GetBlockRange throughput by concurrency on dense mainnet blocks: the Go reference wins at 1-2 streams, lightwalletd-rs plateaus around 321k blocks per second from 8 streams up](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jpgonzalezra/lightwalletd-rs/e6e5e1fdcf4c759d3552f69f9fde3cfdccb5f95f/contrib/bench/results/getblockrange-throughput-dense.svg)

![GetBlock p99 latency by concurrency, log scale: both servers stay under a millisecond up to 8 clients, then the Go reference climbs to 53 ms at 64 while lightwalletd-rs holds 2.7 ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jpgonzalezra/lightwalletd-rs/e6e5e1fdcf4c759d3552f69f9fde3cfdccb5f95f/contrib/bench/results/getblock-p99-dense.svg)

I also want to disclose how this was built. I used AI coding assistants throughout (Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5, driven through Claude Code). I researched each piece first (including how the Go reference handles it), wrote a plan, and only then implemented it in short iterations. The design decisions were mine, each one documented in an ADR, and I reviewed every change that landed on main. The verification discipline described above exists for exactly this reason. Anyone can rerun the checks instead of taking my word for it.



### Time Period of Work Completion

June 12, 2026 to August 6, 2026.

### Total Budget (USD)

$10,720

### Budget Breakdown

- Compensation:
  - $(USD): 10,720
  - Justification: 160 hours at $67/h. The hours are a conservative reconstruction from the public commit history. Between June 12 and August 6 there are 30 active days, and 89 hours fall inside first-to-last-commit windows. The rest is design, debugging, benchmarking runs and end-to-end validation, none of which shows up in commit timestamps.
- Technology/Software:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: Personal tooling paid out of pocket; not claimed.
- Infrastructure/Hosting:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: Developed and tested on my own hardware; no hosting costs claimed.
- Services/Contractors:
  - $(USD): 0
  - Justification: Pacu volunteered his two contributions; nothing was paid to anyone.
- Total $(USD): 10,720


### Previous Funding

No

_No response_

No

_No response_

### Success Metrics

- All 20 CompactTxStreamer methods implemented and tested.
- Responses verified byte-identical against zebra on live testnet, including the NU6.3 activation boundary. A golden-fixture suite backs this, and 433 tests run green in CI.
- Performance measured against the reference implementation on live mainnet data; the reports are committed in the repo, with numbers and caveats in the Technical Approach section above.
- NU6.3 support merged three weeks before mainnet activation.
- 30 ADRs, a spec-to-code reference map, and a benchmark methodology that anyone can rerun.

### Proof of completion

- Repository/Commit:
  - [Repository](https://github.com/jpgonzalezra/lightwalletd-rs) - public, MIT
  - Full history: 228 commits on main from June 12 to August 6, 2026; every PR reviewable
  - CI: GitHub Actions on every push (build, tests, clippy -D warnings, fmt)
- Deployment/Release:
  - [Release](https://github.com/jpgonzalezra/lightwalletd-rs/releases/tag/v0.1.0) - v0.1.0, signed tag, published August 9, 2026
- Other Evidence:
  - Architecture and decisions: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and 30 ADRs under docs/decisions/
  - Spec mapping: docs/protocol-references.md
  - Benchmark reports: contrib/bench/results/ (mainnet-2026-07-summary.md and companions), with the harness in contrib/bench/ so the runs can be reproduced

Zapp is a serverless, end-to-end encrypted P2P messenger that fuses chat with shielded Zcash payments, enabling in-thread transactions and real-world scan-and-pay. Live on Google Play, it supports fiat offramps across seven emerging-market rails (UPI (India), PIX (Brazil), QRIS (Indonesia), NIP (Nigeria), Mercado Pago (Argentina), PagoMovil and Transferencia (Venezuela)), without requiring a phone number or central server.

### Project Description

**Overview and goals.** Zapp (`android-zapp`, a fork of Zodl/Zashi) and its companion SDK ZappMessaging give Zcash users a way to message and pay in one motion: send an address, a payment request, or shielded ZEC itself inside an encrypted conversation, with no server relaying the content and no phone number tying the identity to a real-world number. On top of that, Zapp built scan-and-pay support against seven local instant-payment rails (UPI in India, PIX in Brazil, QRIS in Indonesia, NIP in Nigeria, Mercado Pago in Argentina, PagoMovil and Transferencia in Venezuela, and a rail in Colombia), so ZEC can become spendable local currency without a custodial exchange in the middle.

**Payments where the conversation already is.** The chat layer is not a bolt-on notification feed; it carries typed message bubbles for wallet addresses, payment requests, media, and transaction references, wired through a real IPC bridge between the Kotlin wallet and a JS/Hyperswarm worklet running on-device. A "blind peer" relay and invite-mailbox service (also open-source) let peers behind restrictive networks connect, demonstrated working across a China ↔ non-China link.

**Reusable infrastructure: ZappMessaging.** The messaging core is not walled into Zapp. It's dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0, ships as a standalone SDK with native Android and iOS bindings, and any other Zcash wallet or app could integrate it for the same serverless-messaging capability.

**Real-world liquidity: a multi-country scan-and-pay corridor.** Rather than building a separate, generic crypto off-ramp, Zapp's corridor is layered directly on top of Electric Coin Company's existing NEAR-intents swap screens already shipped in the upstream wallet: a `swap/upi/` package (named for where it started, India's UPI) that has grown into a shared scan-and-pay flow with checkpointed/resumable order orchestration and a dedicated QR parser per rail: `PixQrParser`/`DirectPixResolver`/`DynamicPixResolver` (Brazil), `QrisQrParser` (Indonesia), `NgnQrParser` (Nigeria/NIP), `MercadoPagoQrParser` (Argentina), `PagoMovilQrParser` (Venezuela, alongside a Transferencia bank-transfer path), and `CopQrParser` (Colombia), each with its own test coverage. `OfframpCorridorUi.kt` is the user-facing corridor picker, one flag/currency/country per supported rail, confirming these are shipped, selectable options, not backend scaffolding. A privacy-preserving, no-custodial-KYC identity check (ZKPassport) gates the USDC leg of the onramp side, so users aren't required to hand identity documents to a custodian to get in.

**Hardware-wallet and protocol hygiene.** Zapp also shipped a Keystone hardware-wallet security fix (the app now refuses a signature if the connected firmware can't actually produce a transaction the app can broadcast; firmware ≥3.0.1 required), and shipped Ironwood (NU6.3) readiness UI (per-pool balance breakdown, a one-time upgrade explainer) ahead of network-upgrade activation.

**Ecosystem goal.** Every piece above is additive to, not a replacement for, the underlying Zcash wallet SDK and protocol: no transaction construction, signing, or chain-sync code was modified. The goal is a second, genuinely different on-ramp into ZEC usage (conversational payments) and a second on-ramp into ZEC liquidity (a regional cash-out corridor), both reproducible by other teams.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

**Architecture:**
- Kotlin/Compose Android app (Swift/SwiftUI iOS counterpart, in progress — not part of this claim), forked from Zodl v3.3.1 / Electric Coin Company's Zashi, with no modification to SDK-level transaction construction, signing, or chain sync.
- ZappMessaging: a Bare/Hyperswarm JS runtime, packed into a worklet bundle and executed on-device via `bare-kit` (unmodified, upstream Holepunch); a typed JSON IPC wire format bridges it to native Kotlin.
- `offramp-lib` (~13k lines) and `evm-lib` (~4.8k lines): new Kotlin modules orchestrating the multi-corridor scan-and-pay flow (UPI, PIX, QRIS, NIP, Mercado Pago, PagoMovil/Transferencia, and Colombia's rail) — quote via ECC's existing NEAR-intents swap infrastructure, per-rail QR parsing (`offramp-lib/src/commonMain/kotlin/xyz/justzappit/offramp/p2p/`), then a checkpointed state machine (`OfframpOrchestrator`, `OfframpCheckpoint`) so an interrupted order can resume rather than lose funds in transit.
- A minimal server component (`blind-peer-relay.js`, `blind-relay.js`, `invite-mailbox.js`) — a single lightweight Node service, not a fleet — for peers that can't reach each other directly over the DHT.

**Reviewer verification:**
- Public repository with full commit history; the corridor's novelty (vs. upstream) is directly reproducible: `git diff upstream/zodl-3.3.1 HEAD -- ui-lib/src/main/java/co/electriccoin/zcash/ui/screen/swap/upi/` shows the entire package as new files, not modifications.


### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Research on the web then through the forum

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$17,000

### Category

Infrastructure

### Project Summary

Blindvault is a privacy-preserving credential issuance service that allows clients(applications) to issue and verify one time anonymous credentials without tracking users. It makes uses of BLS12-381 blind signatures and DLEQ proofs alongside deterministic key derivation. Blindvault ultimately serves as a middleware (infrastructure) that can be used by any application through API calls to perverse users privacy, it can be used for private airdrop, access controls, community votes and similar apps.


### Project Description

# Blindvault
## Description
Blindvault is a middleware service that only focus on issue and verifying credentials, it let the application handles all the logic(e.g: eligibility checks…)

Many apps tries to preverse users privacy but still fail to do so, either because they need to track a users(accounts) to ensure their are ideed eligibile for rewards or other identifiers. All this weaken users privacy.

Blindvault stays stateless, application remains responsible for deciding who’s eligible to receive a credentials, while blindvault issues unlinkable blind signatures that can be redeemed later(technically redemption must only be done once, but it’ll be up to the application to either decide to allow double/more redemption or not). During redemption the service verifies the credentials without learning which credential is being redeemed

Blindvault was designed as a reusable infrastructure, instead of having every project to implement blind signature, replay attacks protection and key management independently.

Blindvault is centered around those contraints:

- Privacy by default
The service (should) never learn enough information to correlate issuance with redemption. Applications determine eligibility, while the middleware only performs cryptographic operations required for issuance and verification.

- Reusable infrastructure
The cryptography doesn't need to be written every time another project wants anonymous credentials(or a similar capability). Integrating the service only require calling an HTTP API instead of a good understanding blind signature protocols.

- Operational simplicity
Running BlindVault doesn't require specialized infrastructure. A deployment consists of the service itself together with a Redis instance for replay protection. Everything else is self-contained.

- Clear security boundaries
The service performs one job:

1- issues credentials.
2- verifies credentials.
3- prevents replay.


Ensures that unlinkability between issuance and redemption
Authorization, user accounts, payments, KYC, and application-specific logic doesn't concern the blindvault.

## Cryptography

BlindVault implements blind signatures over the BLS12-381 pairing-friendly curve together with Discrete Logarithm Equality (DLEQ) proofs.
This provides three properties that blindvault relies on to work:

The server can sign a blinded message without knowing the message
The client can prove ownership of a valid signature after unblinding
The client can verify that the signature was produced by the correct key(signing key)

### DLEQ Proof

Blind signatures only proves that a signature is mathematically valid.
This doesn't prove that it was signed by the correct server or service, this allows anyone to generate blind signatures and pose as the service.
Therefore DLEQ proofs are used to ensure that it was indeed the service, and that it used to correct keys to sign the blinded message.
Blindvault returns a DLEQ proof on each issuance so the client can verify that it's valid, the verification can be done by anyone without having to unblind the signature.

The proof provides the following:

The blind signature was produce with the requested credentials
The blind signature comes from the correct server (not a malicious one)
The verification happens on the client side and require no interaction with the server.

### Credentials Class
Credentials class provide clear separation and isolation.
Examples:
```
airdrop_2026
faucet
event_registration
tier_gold
```

This isolation is possible because each credentials have their own key which is derived from the Master Seed.
A credentials for class "faucet" can't be used to redeem for class "airdrop", therefore it prevents accidental reuse across application while, also allowing revocation of a specific class of credentials

### Deterministic Key Derivation
Blindvault doesn't require the use of different private key for every credentials class, it makes use of a single Master Seed to generate all other keys, although this simplifies usage. It comes with a heavy cost, which is in the event the master seed(key) is compromised.

### Replay Protection
Anonymous credentials is mostly useful for one time use. Although based on the application logic, multiple use might be require.
Blindvault prevents replays using deterministic nullifiers.
During redemption, the service derive the nullifier from the redeemed credentials. The resulting value does in any case allow us to know who's credential was used. Blindvault for a unique nullifier returns a 200 code but when duplicate(on second or more redemption of the same credentials) it return 409 code. Blindvault interpret this as double spend and reply back with the 409 code, It 'll be up to the application to handle it.

### Security Model
Blindvault was designed as a dumb service. In other words it assumes that the application correctly determine and validate the user eligibility before requesting a credentials

Blindvault guarantees:

- unlinkability between issuance and redemption
- cryptographic verification of issued credentials
- detection of replay attempts
- namespace isolation between credential classes
- verification that signatures originate from the expected derived key

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

# Technical Approach

## Overview

Blindvault is a privacy-preserving credential issuance service that allows clients(applications) to issue and verify one time anonymous credentials without tracking users. It makes uses of BLS12-381 blind signatures and DLEQ proofs alongside deterministic key derivation

## System Architecture

Blindvault follows a layered architecture with separation of concerns
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     HTTP Transport Layer                    │
│  (REST API, JWT Authentication, Rate Limiting, Middleware)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                      Service Logic Layer                    │
│    (Credential Issuance, Consumption, Revocation Logic)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                      Storage Abstraction                    │
│         (Nullifier Store, Revocation Store Interfaces)      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Cryptographic Core Layer                 │
│ (BLS12-381 Blind Signatures, DLEQ Proofs, Key Derivation)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Cryptographic Design

### BLS12-381 Blind Signatures
Blindvault mainly uses BLS12-381 blind signatures, using [blst](https://github.com/supranational/blst) go library.
The whole process is as follows:

1- **Client** hashes a message to a G1 point: B = HashToCurve(message, DST)
2- **Client** generates a random blinding scalar r and computes B' = r * B
3- **Client** sends B' (blinded message) to the server
4- **Server** derives the signing key sk for the requested epoch and credential class
5 -**Server** computes σ' = sk * B' (blind signature)
6- **Server** returns σ' with a DLEQ proof
7- **Client** verifies the DLEQ proof and unblinds: σ = r^(-1) * σ'

This ensures the server never learns the final credential, preserving unlinkability.

### Deterministic Key Derivation

We avoid storing private keys for each credentials by deriving keys from a Master Seed.
```
Derivation hierarchy:

	Master Seed
	    │
	    └── HKDF-Expand(salt="BCIS-V1-SALT", info="BCIS" || "SIGNING_KEY" || epoch || class)
	            │
	            └── 64 bytes → modulo r → BLS12-381 Scalar
```

This provides:
- Protocol isolation (fixed "BCIS" tag)
- Purpose isolation (fixed "SIGNING_KEY" tag)
- Lifecycle rotation (epoch)
- Application namespace isolation (credential class)

### DLEQ Proofs

Every issuance includes a zero-knowledge proof proving that the server  used the correct signing key. This proof prevent malicious server from signing, and also prevents the incorrect signing by legitimate server

### Nullifier-Based Replay Protection

Replay attacks are prevented with nullifiers
```
nullifier = SHA256("BCIS-V1" || epoch || credential_class || Serialize(σ))
```

The nullifier is stored atomatically in redis. If nullifier exists, the redemption is rejected with 409 error. This preserve unlinkability even further.

### Credential Revocation

Blindvault support revocation of class and epoch, specifically:

- Class-wide revocation: Invalidates all credentials for a given class across all epochs
- Epoch-specific revocation: Invalidates credentials for a specific class + epoch combination
- Time-limited revocation: Revocations can be set to expire automatically

Revocation checks are done during redemption, before signature verification.

## Technology stack

| Layer | Technology | Version |
|-------|------------|---------|
| **Language** | Go | 1.26.5 |
| **Cryptography** | `blst` (C bindings) | Latest |
| **HTTP Server** | Standard `net/http` | Go 1.26+ |
| **Storage** | Redis (via `go-redis`) | v9 |
| **Authentication** | JWT (via `golang-jwt`) | v5 |
| **Logging** | Zerolog | v1 |
| **Metrics** | Prometheus | v1 |
| **Dependency Management** | Go Modules | |
| **Containerization** | Docker + Docker Compose | |
| **CI/CD** | GitHub Actions | |

### Client SDKs

| Language | Use Case | Implementation |
|----------|----------|----------------|
| **Go** | CLI, Backend Integration | `pkg/client` + `cmd/bv` CLI |
| **TypeScript** | Browser Integration | `@noble/curves` BLS12-381 library |

## Engineering Decisions
### Minimal Persistent State

Blindvault stores as little information as possible:
- issued credential are never stored
- Replay protection uses hashes

### Storage Abstraction

Replay protection and Revocation storage is entirely abstracted into interfaces, allowing the use of any backend as long as it implements those interfaces

```go
type NullifierStore interface {
    CheckAndStore(nullifier []byte) (bool, error)
    Close() error
}

type RevocationStore interface {
    RevokeClass(class, epoch, reason, revokedBy string, revokedUntil *time.Time) error
    IsRevoked(class, epoch string) (bool, *RevocationEntry, error)
    ListRevocations() ([]RevocationEntry, error)
    UnrevokeClass(class, epoch string) error
    Close() error
}
```

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1:  Cryptography (Completed)
- BLS12-381 blind signatures
- DLEQ proof generation and verification
- HKDF-SHA256 key derivation
- Nullifiers

### Phase 2: Service Layer (Completed)
- Credential issuance and redemption logic
- JWT authentication
- Storage abstraction 
- In-memory and Redis implementations

### Phase 3: API (Completed)
- REST API with structured error responses
- Middleware (logging, recovery, rate limiting, CORS)
- Prometheus metrics
- Health checks

### Phase 4: Client SDKs (Completed)
- Go client library and CLI (`cmd/bv`)
- TypeScript browser SDK with interactive demo
- Cryptographic test vectors

### Phase 5: Operations & Deployment (Completed)
- Docker containerization
- Docker Compose for local development
- GitHub Actions CI/CD
- Structured logging with request tracking

### Phase 6: Airdrop Demo (Completed)
- Deterministic blinding from wallet signatures
- E2E encrypted credential storage
- Ticket-based redemption flow
- Three-mode demo interface (Vector, Core API, Airdrop)

### Go Server (cpu: INTEL(R) XEON(R) PLATINUM 8573C)
#### Cryptography
| Benchmark | Iterations (Ops) | Time per Op (ns/op) | Time per Op (ms) | Memory (B/op) | Allocations (allocs/op) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BenchmarkHashToCurve-4` | 19,671 | 60,913 | 0.061 ms | 152 | 2 |
| `BenchmarkBlindMessage-4` | 13,608 | 88,179 | 0.088 ms | 152 | 2 |

## Testing 

### Unit Tests
- Cryptographic primitives (`pkg/crypto`)
- Storage implementations (`internal/storage`)
- Service logic (`internal/service`)
- JWT validation (`internal/auth`)

### Integration Tests

### Benchmarks
- Cryptographic operations (`pkg/crypto/bench_test.go`)
- HTTP handlers (`internal/api/bench_test.go`)

## Security Considerations
### Trust Boundaries

BlindVault assumes:
- Applications ensure eligibility before requesting issuance
- The master seed is protected

### Guarantees Provided

1. **Unlinkability**: Issuance and redemption cannot be correlated
2. **Cryptographic Authenticity**: Credentials are mathematically verifiable
3. **Replay Detection**: Nullifiers prevent double-spending
4. **Namespace Isolation**: Credential classes use independent signing keys
5. **Public Verifiability**: Clients verify DLEQ proofs without trusting the server

### Out of Scope

- User authentication and identity management
- Sybil resistance
- Application-level authorization
- Network-level privacy

### Success Metrics

# Success Metrics
## Quantitative Metrics:
- Production-Ready Codebase
- 100% Test Coverage on critical cryptographic operations and core business logic
- client SDK and interactive browser demo
- Comprehensive Documentation
- Test Vectors
## Qualitative Metrics:
- Reusable Infrastructure: blindvault can be used by any application. Other application don't need to build or design complex cryptography operation, they can just integrate blindvault
- Low Entry Barrier: HTTP API allows almost any app to benefits from it
- Alignment with Zcash Mission: It provides an infrastructure for application to offer unlinkable credentials. Helping advancing privacy technologies.
- Ecosystem Gap: Blindvault solves a lot of problem but the one which is directly addressed; is how to issue a one time credentials to a user without having to track them or compromising their privacy. While also ensuring that only the intended user can make use of them

## Values to Zcash community
The real value brought by blindvault, an infrastructure that allows issuance of credentials to users, and redeeming them later without creating a link between the person who received the credential and the person who's redeeming it.

1. Private Airdrops
Usually airdrop check eligibility of users, by the amount of token(crypto) present in their wallet then store the address of those users(for the simplest one) or either store a piece of information related to that user. This doesn't exactly protect the user identity.

That's exactly where Blindvault works. And allows for a complete private airdrop:
- The application verifies user eligibility
- Blindvault issues a blind credential to the user
- The user redeems the credentials to claim the airdrop
The server can't in most case link the claim to the original user that received the credentials. 
This allows Zcash to distribute airdrops privately

2. Community Voting & Governance
Voting and Governance is an important aspect of communities, but most voting systems are linkable, we can know who voted for what.

In that same scenario Blindvault ensures only eligible users can vote, eligibility is handled by the application:
- Each voter receives a single credential
- Voter casts vote(s) using it
- Once used the same credentials can't be reused(replay protection)
- The vote is recorded
The voter and the vote is protected, we can't know who is voting and the same goes for their vote

This allows Zcash to implement private voting, while preserving voters privacy

Blindvault brings more than that to the zcash because it enable development of applications that aims to preserve users privacy.
List of other uses of Blindvault includes:
- Privacy-Preserving Contributions: each eligible contributor receives a credentials and can from that point contribute without having to reveal their identity.
- Anonymous Access Control: eligible user receive a credential which allows them access to the resources and we can't know who accessed that specific resource preserving their privacy although we do know that the person who accessed it is authorized(eligible)

I acknowledge and accept that disbursement amounts may fluctuate based on the ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of payment. ### Application Owners (@octocat, @octocat1) @Lowo88 ### Organization or Individual Name Leonine DAO ### Additional Team Members ```team-members.yaml - Name: Lowo88 / LEONINE DAO Role: Lead maintainer (NozyWallet) Background: Orchard-first Zcash wallet engineering on Zebrad + lightwalletd Responsibilities: CLI, desktop, shared core, releases, evidence docs ``` ### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program? Zcash Community Forum ### Requested Grant Amount (USD) $60,000 ### Category Wallets ### Project Summary ### NozyWallet is Zcash privacy you run yourself Shielded-first on your Zebrad/Zakura + lightwalletd, with local witnesses, not a hosted light wallet that sees your sync graph. Most wallets trade convenience for someone else’s infrastructure. Nozy is built the other way: you self-host the node stack, keep keys on your machine, and sync/send over Zebrad/Zakura + lightwalletd with local Orchard/Ironwood proofs. Privacy at full strength for people who refuse to outsource the chain CLI, Desktop, and companion API on the same core. ### Project Description ## Overview and goals NozyWallet (https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet) is a shielded-first Zcash wallet stack for people and businesses who want privacy without outsourcing the chain to someone else’s node. It is a wallet + companion services not a consensus node. Users run (or point at) their own Zebrad/Zakura + lightwalletd; Orchard/Ironwood proofs use local witness derivation. ### Privacy = your node, not someone else’s The privacy hole is not “who holds the seed phrase in a slogan.” It is what you give away when you connect a wallet to other people’s nodes hosted light servers, remote WalletConnect-style backends, or any third-party sync path that sees your IP, compact-block requests, and usage pattern. Shielded on-chain still leaks if the sync and broadcast path is someone else’s. NozyWallet is built the other way: - Default product path: self-host Zebrad/Zakura + lightwalletd (or infra you operate). - Local witness derivation proofs do not depend on a remote prove/sync provider seeing your wallet graph. - Companion API defaults to localhost (127.0.0.1); remote bind is explicit. - Merchants who choose privacy settle shielded on infra they run; business payment/wallet operational data stays on that stack. - Network privacy for sensitive flows prefers loopback and supports Tor/I2P / opt-in Nym not silent clearnet when policy says otherwise. ### Developers — build on nozywallet-api The companion HTTP API (`nozywallet-api`) is a first-class surface for builders. Apps can sync, read balances, send shielded ZEC, estimate ZIP-317 fees, track history/confirmations, and use Business/invoice helpers without embedding the full Desktop UI. Production integrators already run the API headlessly on VPS (Gleyo-style withdrawal / product backends and similar). Goal: “build a Zcash app” means “talk to a self-hosted Nozy companion,” not invent a new wallet stack or route users through a third-party node. ### Merchants — run a business on Nozy Desktop and API expose Business profile / invoice-oriented flows so merchants can accept shielded ZEC on their own node stack. Invoices and Business wallet tooling live in-repo on a native path not a third-party payment processor or someone else’s light wallet. Merchants who want privacy keep operational control of node + wallet/business data. ### Ecosystem goal — more Zcash nodes Nozy’s default product path assumes Zebrad/Zakura + lightwalletd. When more people adopt NozyWallet for personal use, merchant ops, or API-backed apps, more operators stand up or keep. Zcash nodes instead of concentrating sync on a few hosted light servers. Wallet growth and node growth move together. ### Technical Approach (how you did it) **Architecture:** - Shared Rust core (`nozy`) + CLI; Desktop Tauri and api-server reuse the library. - api-server: Axum HTTP companion (loopback by default) exposing wallet/sync/send/fee/history and related routes for GUI and headless integrators. - Sync: lightwalletd compact blocks + Zebrad JSON-RPC; local witness derivation. - Fees: client-side ZIP-317 with Nozy mandatory priority ×4 on send surfaces. - Ironwood: ZIP 318–shaped migrate path; network privacy gate for broadcast. - Releases: CLI via GitHub Actions; desktop under desktop-v* tags; api-server as workspace package. **Reviewer verification:** - Public repo + CLI/Desktop release artifacts. - api-server source and docs under api-server/. - Mainnet TXID evidence for send + Ironwood turnstile. ### Time Period of Work Completion June 2025 – August 2026 (CLI/Desktop production path and Ironwood mainnet migration evidence; releases through v2.4.4 / desktop-v1.0.0-beta.5) ### Total Budget (USD) $60,000 ### Budget Breakdown - Compensation: - $(USD): 60000 - Justification: Retroactive recognition for completed CLI + Desktop + companion API engineering (~600h blended at ~$100/hr narrative). - Technology/Software: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: Covered under compensation. - Infrastructure/Hosting: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: Operator-run Zebrad/LWD; not requesting hosted node funding. - Services/Contractors: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: No third-party audit engagement in this ask. - Other: - $(USD): 0 - Justification: N/A - Total $(USD): 60000 Split (informational): - CLI (`nozy`): $25,000 - Desktop (Tauri): $25,000 - Companion API (`nozywallet-api`): $10,000 ### Previous Funding No ### Previous Funding Details N/A ### Other Funding Sources No ### Other Funding Sources Details N/A ### Success Metrics - Verifiable mainnet Orchard send + Ironwood turnstile TXIDs (published evidence docs). - Public CLI + Desktop releases on GitHub (v2.4.x / desktop-v*). - Companion API (`nozywallet-api`) used in production by headless VPS integrators (Gleyo-style apps) and merchant/Business flows — not GUI-only. - Product path couples wallet adoption to self-hosted Zebrad + lightwalletd (more Nozy users → more Zcash nodes) instead of third-party node / WalletConnect-style sync. - Localhost-default companion API; privacy posture is “your node,” not “someone else’s light server.” - Zcash Names (ZNS) resolve shipped across CLI, Desktop Send, and companion API — recipients by name, not raw address-only. - Opt-in Nym network privacy shipped in Desktop (Settings → Network privacy) for sensitive broadcast/submit paths — Tor/I2P-friendly posture, not silent clearnet-only. - Ironwood readiness + migrate path (ZIP 318–shaped) on CLI/Desktop with mainnet turnstile confirmation. - ZIP-317 priority ×4 fee policy on send surfaces; fee-estimate on API. - Business profile + invoice flows on Desktop/API for merchants who choose shielded settle on self-hosted infra. ### Proof of completion Repository: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet - CLI releases: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/releases (e.g. v2.4.4 / v2.4.5) - Desktop releases: desktop-v* tags (e.g. desktop-v1.0.0-beta.5 / beta.6) - Companion API source: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/tree/master/api-server - https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/blob/master/api-server/scripts/companion-api-smoke-proof.png - API docs: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/blob/master/api-server/README.md - Mainnet send evidence: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/blob/master/docs/reference/MAINNET_SEND_READINESS_EVIDENCE.md - TXID: ecbd068880e9512983f9ec36a1014c84ed51065886b0bcc657415feaccd4016b - Ironwood migration evidence: https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/blob/master/docs/reference/MAINNET_IRONWOOD_MIGRATION_EVIDENCE.md - TXID: ea2fa4e64a5ca3f588dea58f38feb2a72a8d4e30292ac012d983e23bde7048fd @ 3430663 - Security self-review (not LA cert): https://github.com/LEONINE-DAO/Nozy-wallet/tree/master/docs/reference/security-audit - Prior rejected application: https://github.com/Financial-Privacy-Foundation/ZcashCoinholderGrantsProgram/issues/6 ### Conflict of Interest Disclosure None known beyond being the maintainers of NozyWallet. ### Community Forum Posting - [x] I understand it is my responsibility to post a link to this issue on the [Zcash Community Forums](https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/about-the-retroactive-grants-category/52106) after this application has been submitted so the community can give input. ### Project Summary

BlindVault is a privacy-preserving credential issuance service that enables applications to issue and verify one-time anonymous credentials without tracking users. By combining BLS12-381 blind signatures, DLEQ proofs and deterministic key derivation, it provides reusable infrastructure for privacy-preserving airdrops, faucets, access control and similar applications.

### Project Description

BlindVault is an open-source middleware service that separates application-specific eligibility checks from the cryptographic process of issuing anonymous credentials.

Many applications need to answer a simple question: *has this user already claimed a reward or consumed a resource?* The common solution is to track users through accounts, IP addresses, browser fingerprints or other identifiers. These approaches either weaken user privacy or become unreliable as users change devices, networks or use privacy tools such as VPNs.

BlindVault approaches the problem differently. Applications remain responsible for determining who is eligible to receive a credential, while BlindVault issues an unlinkable blind signature that can later be redeemed exactly once. During redemption, the service verifies the credential and prevents replay attacks without learning which issued credential is being redeemed.

The project was designed as reusable infrastructure rather than application-specific software. Instead of requiring every project to implement blind signatures, replay protection and key management independently, BlindVault exposes a simple HTTP API that any application can integrate regardless of the programming language or framework it uses.

The implementation includes deterministic key derivation for credential namespaces, DLEQ proofs to verify correct key usage, replay protection through deterministic nullifiers, REST APIs, Redis-backed storage, Docker deployment, automated testing, continuous integration and comprehensive documentation.

BlindVault is intended to reduce the complexity of building privacy-preserving applications while making anonymous credential issuance practical for developers who do not specialize in applied cryptography.

Built with Go

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

BlindVault was developed as a layered system that separates cryptographic operations, business logic, storage and transport into independent components. This organization allows each layer to be tested, audited and maintained independently while keeping the security-critical cryptographic implementation isolated from operational concerns.

The cryptographic core is implemented using BLS12-381 blind signatures. Each credential belongs to a **credential class**, with signing keys derived deterministically from a protected master secret using HKDF-SHA256 and explicit domain separation. This removes the need to store independent private keys while maintaining cryptographic isolation between credential namespaces. Every issued credential also includes a DLEQ proof, allowing clients to verify that the server used the correct derived signing key.

Replay protection is implemented using deterministic nullifiers derived from the credential, credential class and signing epoch. During redemption, BlindVault performs an atomic insertion into the configured nullifier store. A successful insertion indicates the credential is being redeemed for the first time, while an existing nullifier identifies a replay attempt. Redis serves as the default backend because its atomic operations match the protocol requirements, although storage is abstracted behind an interface to support alternative implementations.

The service exposes REST endpoints for credential issuance and redemption. Issuance endpoints are protected with JWT authentication, while redemption endpoints remain public so applications can verify anonymous credentials without requiring user accounts. The service is instrumented with structured logging, Prometheus metrics and health endpoints to simplify deployment and operational monitoring.

Development followed an implementation-first approach, with testing and operational tooling built alongside the protocol rather than after it. The project includes comprehensive unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end protocol tests, GitHub Actions continuous integration, Docker images, Docker Compose deployment, API documentation, cryptographic specifications and reproducible test vectors.

During development, several architectural decisions were refined to simplify the protocol and improve maintainability. The API evolved from exposing `key_id` values to using `credential_class`, reflecting the application's domain rather than implementation details. Credential classes became cryptographic namespaces with independently derived signing keys, deterministic key derivation replaced per-class key storage, DLEQ proofs became mandatory to prevent key substitution, and storage was abstracted behind interfaces to keep the cryptographic protocol independent of deployment choices. The final architecture emphasizes minimal persistent state, clear security boundaries and reusable infrastructure that can be integrated into a wide range of privacy-preserving applications.

Engineering Deliverables:

### How did you learn about the Lockbox: Coinholder Retroactive Grants Program?

Word-of-mouth (previous applicant, Q1 2026 round)

### Requested Grant Amount (USD)

$122,400

### Category

Non-Wallet Applications

### Project Summary

ZcashMe made Zcash easier to use by letting people create a public profile page and share a simple link instead of a long address. People who received the link could pay quickly from QR or wallet URI, while profile owners could manage their display name, bio, nearest city, avatar, and social media links. ZcashMe also introduced memo + OTP verification to confirm address ownership before profile edits and social authentication.

That usability win came with an important trust limitation: ZcashMe resolves payment destinations through a centrally managed database. Even with honest operators and verification controls, a privileged admin or compromised backend could alter a stored address mapping, creating a man-in-the-middle risk where funds could be redirected or payment relationships surveilled. ZcashNames is the completed next step that removes this trust bottleneck by moving name-to-address resolution on-chain.

ZcashNames is an on-chain naming system for Zcash that maps human-readable names like alice.zcash to shielded addresses. The completed work delivered a live beta web app, public explorer, open documentation, integration guides, and supporting developer infrastructure that makes ZNS usable and testable by end users, wallet teams, and app builders.

In addition to the ZcashMe and ZcashNames product work, we built supporting open-source infrastructure for authentication, chain synchronization, transaction ingestion, and Zebra integration. This includes ZNS Login, seer-sync, ZNS Postgres Sync, and zebra-indexer-proto. These components were created for ZcashMe and ZcashNames but are published so other Zcash projects can use or adapt them.

### Project Description

ZcashMe proved there is strong demand for human-readable payments, public recipient discovery, and lightweight identity around shielded addresses. It helped users share a memorable payment destination, build a public profile, and receive funds more easily than copying raw addresses in chat. In practice, it served as an onboarding and usability layer for Zcash.

However, ZcashMe also exposed a structural limitation of centralized name resolution. Because the username-to-address mapping lives in a server-controlled database, users and integrators must trust the operator not only to stay online, but also to preserve the correctness of the mapping at all times. A malicious or compromised administrator could substitute a different address, intercept funds, or observe and influence payment flows. This is not a flaw in Zcash itself; it is the trust model imposed by an off-chain directory.

ZcashNames is the solution to that problem. Instead of relying on a mutable central database, ZcashNames anchors human-readable name resolution on-chain, so wallets and applications can verify name-to-address mappings directly from Zcash state. ZcashMe demonstrated the product need, and ZcashNames completes the architecture needed to satisfy that need without introducing a centralized interception point.

The transition path is straightforward and practical. ZcashMe can evolve from being the source of truth for payment destinations into a discovery, profile, and social UX layer that sits on top of ZcashNames. Public profiles, avatars, bios, verified links, and discovery features can remain useful, but the canonical payment destination should become the user's `.zcash` name and its on-chain mapping. This preserves the usability benefits of ZcashMe while eliminating its most important trust assumption.

ZcashNames includes a production website, claim/update/list/buy/release flows for names (plus protected-name suggestion, dispute, unlock-code request, and gated claim paths), OTP and keypair-based authorization paths, a live explorer and marketplace view, a public roadmap, waitlist and referral onboarding, beta application flows, a share kit for community distribution, and a docs portal that explains usage, protocol rules, wallet integration, RPC methods, and SDK usage. Taken together, this lowers the barrier to Zcash adoption by making shielded addresses easier to use while preserving the verification and privacy properties of the underlying chain.

As part of this work, we also built reusable infrastructure around Zcash application development. ZNS Login provides OAuth2/OpenID Connect authentication using Zcash identities and encrypted memo OTPs. seer-sync provides viewing-key chain synchronization, including compact-block scanning, spend detection, memo recovery, persistence, and reorg handling. ZNS Postgres Sync routes transactions for configured viewing keys into Postgres tables without requiring a self-hosted lightwalletd. zebra-indexer-proto packages Zebra’s indexer gRPC definitions and Rust bindings so developers can integrate Zebra without maintaining their own protobuf generation pipeline.

### Technical Approach (how you did it)

[Zcash.me](http://zcash.me/) is a Next.js web application with a Postgres SQL database. It features a stand-alone background verification service to decrypt incoming requests and generate OTP responses. Social OAuth is integrated via Supabase. 1Click swap APIs are used for cross-chain execution. External market pricing provided by CoinGecko, Coinbase.

ZcashNames uses a Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript web app and docs site, aligned to zcashname-sdk and the canonical ZNS OpenRPC spec. State-changing actions are encoded as signed ZNS: memos inside standard Orchard shielded transactions and delivered through ZIP-321 wallet flows. Reads come from the Rust ZNS indexer over JSON-RPC; address ownership proofs use the separate ZVS OTP flow; the explorer is SDK-first and server-rendered; and the docs are published from MDX/Nextra in the same repo so protocol, integration, and user-facing guidance stay synchronized. The completed work covers Alpha v1 (2026-03-09 to 2026-04-19), Alpha v2 (2026-04-20 to 2026-05-08), and the associated public onboarding / referral / beta-prep surfaces completed by 2026-05-14.

Supporting infrastructure includes ZNS Login for Zcash-based OAuth authentication, seer-sync for viewing-key chain synchronization, ZNS Postgres Sync for transaction ingestion into Postgres, and zebra-indexer-proto for consuming Zebra indexer gRPC interfaces from Rust. These components separate authentication, synchronization, data ingestion, and Zebra integration from the application layer and are published for reuse outside ZcashMe and ZcashNames.

Q2 2020, Q3 2025, October 2025 - August 2026
